BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(27), 92(4), (7), (13), (14), and (16), together with Faber v. The Queen, Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, Attorney General (Que.) and Keable v. Attorney General (Can.), and O'Hara v. British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal causation test: the accused’s unlawful act must be at least a contributing cause of death outside the de minimis range, proved beyond a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, s. 205(1), and common-law causation and thin-skull principles reflected in R. v. Larkin, R. v. Cato, R. v. Garforth, R. v. Blaue, and R. v. Nicholson
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage test for recognizing a novel duty of care for pure economic loss arising from commercial negotiations
BaselineB: Common law — the two-stage analysis from Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, adopted in Canada in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and applied within the pure economic loss framework developed in cases including Canadian National Railway Co. v. Norsk Pacific Steamship Co.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rule of specialty duration: an extradition undertaking must be interpreted in context and in light of its object, purpose, and general international-law principles; absent clear terms, immunity ends once the extraditee has had a reasonable opportunity to return and remains voluntarily.
BaselineA: Combination of the extradition arrangement, the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, ss. 2, 3, 33 and 40, and international-law principles governing treaty interpretation and specialty.
CaseB_TestB: No-separate-leave rule for the curative proviso: where an alleged error of law is properly before the Court and the Crown invokes s. 686(1)(b)(iii), the proviso is always intertwined with that error and may be addressed without separate leave to appeal.
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), and the appellate principle established in R. v. Keegstra.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal licensing-power test: a council may refuse a licence only on grounds peculiar to the applicant and within its licensing jurisdiction; absent express prohibitory authority, it cannot use licensing discretion to prohibit a lawful type of business or rely on extraneous moral-policy grounds.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, especially s. 455, read in the context of ss. 458, 458M, 458N, 870 and 871; and the rule from Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo that regulatory authority does not, absent express authority, include power to prohibit a lawful trade conducted lawfully.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 fair-process test for the IRPA security-certificate scheme: the process must substantially substitute for full disclosure and participation, keep the named person reasonably informed through an incompressible minimum of disclosure, and remain fair through the designated judge's ongoing gatekeeping and remedial discretion.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional law and statute: s. 7 and s. 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms; IRPA Division 9, particularly ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1), 85.1, 85.2, 85.4 and 85.5; and the fair-process principles established in Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility at sentencing of evidence tending to establish another untried offence, based on its purpose and procedural safeguards
BaselineA: Criminal Code, Part XXIII, especially ss. 718 to 718.2, 724(3)(e), 725 and 726.1, combined with the common-law principles in Lees v. The Queen and R. v. Gardiner
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in online communications with an unknown child during a police-created sting
BaselineB: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the common-law reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework developed in Marakah, Cole, Spencer, Tessling, Edwards and Hunter
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation: representation by words or conduct inducing detrimental reliance; silence or inaction qualifies only where there is a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law estoppel by representation, including Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd. and Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha v. Dawson’s Bank, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the presumption of living on the avails of prostitution: the jury may consider all relevant evidence, without isolating a particular and severable item of evidence to the contrary
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contextual inference of possession from fingerprint evidence based on all the circumstances and evidence
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. O'Keefe and R. v. Mehrabnia, applied alongside the statutory definition of possession in Criminal Code, s. 4(3), incorporated by Food and Drugs Act, ss. 46 and 48(2)
CaseB_TestB: Review Board authority to bind hospital authorities and supervise, but not prescribe, medical treatment of an NCR accused
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, Part XX.1, principally ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Refined three-stage test for whether conferring jurisdiction on a provincial tribunal violates s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, and the common law three-stage framework established in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714
CaseB_TestB: Flexible three-factor test for granting public interest standing, including the sufficient factual setting requirement
BaselineB: Common law framework established in Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examination on a former juvenile delinquency: a Criminal Code delinquency is an “offence,” its adjudication is a “conviction,” and cross-examination may expose the falsity of evidence-in-chief.
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Evidence Act, s. 12(1), read with the Juvenile Delinquents Act, particularly ss. 2, 3 and 20(1); Criminal Code, s. 593 provided an alternative basis.
CaseB_TestB: Amendment of an indictment where the proved narcotic differs from the particular specified: amendment is available unless the variance causes prejudice that cannot be cured without injustice.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 529(4)-(5) and 613(1)(b)(i), (3), read with the Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 and 4 and Schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional assessment of non-pecuniary damages subject to a rough $100,000 upper limit, exceeded only in rare circumstances or adjusted upon proof or agreement of inflation
BaselineA: Common law: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Arnold v. Teno, and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57 (Prince George), as refined in Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: Inadequately insured motorist coverage requires use of a vehicle as a motor vehicle and an unbroken chain of causation linking the tortfeasor's conduct as a motorist to the injuries, beyond a merely incidental, fortuitous, or but-for connection
BaselineB: Combination of statute and insurance policy: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a), and s. 3 of Ontario Policy Change Form 44R, informed by but distinguished from the common law test in Amos v. Insurance Corp. of British Columbia
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 27(2)(e) hypothetical infringement test: an importer is liable only if the foreign maker would have infringed copyright by making the work in Canada; an owner-licensor cannot infringe its own copyright and may be sued by an exclusive licensee only in contract, not for infringement.
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, principally ss. 2.7, 13(4)-(7), 27(1), 27(2)(e), and 36(1)-(2), informed by the common-law distinction between assignments and licences.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) retrospective double-punishment test: the dominant consideration is the extent to which retrospective legislative action thwarts an offender’s settled expectation of liberty; automatic lengthening of incarceration is punishment, while less drastic changes depend on whether they substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and prior jurisprudence — Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h), building on R. v. Wigglesworth, R. v. Rodgers, and Cunningham v. Canada.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual characterization test for a voluntary association’s breach of its by-laws and natural justice obligations
BaselineA: Combination of Quebec civil law and jurisprudence, principally Civil Code arts. 361, 1024, 1057, 2242 and 2261(2), the Companies Act, and prior decisions treating voluntary-association by-laws as contractual.
CaseB_TestB: Priority-of-registration test for a mechanic’s lien and competing mortgage where statutory priorities do not otherwise govern
BaselineB: Statute, principally The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 16 and 20-22, together with The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Essence-of-the-crime test for determining whether an offence falls within an extradition arrangement
BaselineA: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2, and the 1925 Supplementary Convention, s. 17
CaseB_TestB: Purpose-of-use test distinguishing credibility impeachment from incriminating use of prior testimony
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13, and Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2), informed by R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unified three-step BFOR (Meiorin) test: the employer must prove a rationally job-connected purpose, an honest and good-faith belief in the standard's necessity, and reasonable necessity, meaning that accommodation is impossible without undue hardship.
BaselineA: Statute and prior jurisprudence: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1) and 13(4), interpreted against the earlier bifurcated discrimination and accommodation frameworks from O'Malley, Etobicoke, Central Alberta Dairy Pool, and related cases.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage pursuit-of-profit source-of-income test: determine whether the activity is undertaken for profit rather than as a personal endeavour, and, if so, classify the source as business or property; clearly commercial activities require no further inquiry.
BaselineB: Statute and prior jurisprudence: Income Tax Act, principally ss. 3 and 9, with ss. 18(1)(a), 18(1)(h), 20(1)(c)(i), 67, and 248(1), together with the reasonable-expectation-of-profit approach associated with Moldowan v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority test for a statutory wage lien: the lien attaches from the date wages were earned, does not affect prior mortgages, and attaches only to the employer’s equity in encumbered property
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), ss. 5 and 5A, particularly s. 5A(1)-(2)
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive Civil Code framework for forced dissolution: special legislation governs first, but arts. 355 to 364 C.C.Q. apply insofar as necessary to fill gaps in the special statutory scheme
BaselineB: Statute — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334 and 355 to 364, read with Part III of the Companies Act and art. 829 of the Code of Civil Procedure
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal criminal law validity test: a prohibition backed by a penalty and directed at a legitimate criminal public purpose, without colourability.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(27), combined with the common law framework from the Margarine Reference, PATA, and Scowby.
CaseB_TestB: Individualized reasonable accommodation and undue hardship test for applying a collectively bargained termination-after-absence clause.
BaselineB: Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20, the collective agreement, and the common law Meiorin accommodation framework.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Identifiability or traceability test for whether a statutory tax trust is excluded from the bankrupt estate under s. 47(a) or ranked as a Crown claim under s. 107(1)(j)
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j); Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18; general principles of trust law; Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville; and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 numbers-warrant and management-and-control test for locating minority-language instruction and limiting ministerial interference
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional, statutory, and regulatory law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23; School Act, R.S.P.E.I. 1988, particularly ss. 112 and 128; School Act Regulations, particularly ss. 6.01(f), 6.07, 6.08, and 6.11; and the sliding-scale framework established in Mahe v. Alberta
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory accomplice-evidence caution for testimony of an accessory after the fact
BaselineA: Common-law rule of practice governing accomplice evidence, including the definition adopted in Davies v. Director of Public Prosecutions and accepted in Horsburgh v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Unlawful-object murder test under Criminal Code s. 212(c)
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Manslaughter liability under Criminal Code s. 21(2): a party to a common unlawful purpose may be convicted where the party did not foresee probable murder but a reasonable person in all the circumstances would have foreseen at least a risk of harm resulting in death.
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(2), and the manslaughter principles in R. v. Creighton, R. v. Trinneer, and R. v. Kirkness.
CaseB_TestB: GST overpayment rebate and mandatory reassessment set-off: the actual payer may obtain a rebate under s. 261(1), and the Minister must apply an otherwise allowable but unclaimed or time-barred rebate against assessed net tax under s. 296(2.1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Prejudgment interest for an improperly withheld just debt: where compensation by interest is fair and equitable, the court may select the appropriate period and rate; for the withheld costs under this cost-plus contract, the rate was the contractor's actual bank borrowing rate.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: s. 46 of The Queen's Bench Act, R.S.S. 1965, c. 73, as interpreted in Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto and followed in The Custodian v. Blucher; ss. 3, 12 and 13 of the Interest Act were also interpreted.
CaseB_TestB: Two-step test for impairment of full answer and defence by non-disclosure: determine whether there is a reasonable possibility that the undisclosed information affected the conviction's reliability; if not, determine whether it affected overall trial fairness through lost realistic investigative or evidentiary opportunities, taking defence diligence into account.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1), together with the disclosure and full-answer-and-defence principles established in R. v. Stinchcombe, R. v. C. (M.H.), R. v. Carosella and R. v. Collins.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Arbitrator's authority to substitute a lesser penalty where the collective agreement specifies no penalty for the infraction
BaselineA: Combination of statute and collective agreement: The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3), read with collective agreement arts. 6(4) and 12(12)(a).
CaseB_TestB: Contribution-based test for complicity in international crimes under the refugee exclusion clause
BaselineB: Statute and treaty: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s. 98, incorporating Refugee Convention art. 1F(a), informed by international criminal law, including Rome Statute arts. 25, 30 and 31(1)(d).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Recent-possession jury instruction where no explanation is in evidence: once possession of recently stolen goods is proved, the judge must instruct that it raises a prima facie case permitting conviction, omitting the phrase “in the absence of any reasonable explanation”; the Crown need not prove that no explanation was given.
BaselineA: Common-law doctrine of recent possession from R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch, as approved in Richler, Ungaro, Graham, Tremblay and R. v. Graham, interpreted alongside s. 4(5) of the Canada Evidence Act.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage test for the territorial validity of provincial legislation: characterize and classify the law by its pith and substance, then determine whether it has a meaningful connection to the province and respects other provinces’ legislative sovereignty.
BaselineB: Section 92 of the Constitution Act, 1867 and the two-stage constitutional framework established in British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust for unjust enrichment: enrichment, corresponding deprivation, absence of juristic reason, and a sufficient causal connection to property, with the interest proportionate to the claimant’s contribution.
BaselineA: Common law and equity, principally the unjust-enrichment constructive trust developed in Murdoch v. Murdoch and Rathwell v. Rathwell.
CaseB_TestB: Substantive solicitor-client confidentiality rule and safeguards for searching a lawyer’s office: confidentiality prevails unless law provides otherwise, interference must be absolutely necessary, no reasonable search alternative may exist, and protective execution terms must be imposed.
BaselineB: Combination of common law solicitor-client privilege, including Solosky v. The Queen, and the search-warrant power under Criminal Code, s. 443, particularly s. 443(1)(b).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional approach to non-pecuniary damages, subject to a presumptive $100,000 upper limit with flexibility for exceptional cases
BaselineA: Common law personal-injury damages, particularly Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Thornton v. Board of School Trustees and Warren v. King
CaseB_TestB: Fire-damage election under clause 5: the purchaser must either complete for whatever insurance proceeds are owing or cancel; imposing additional conditions constitutes repudiation
BaselineB: Common law of contract and repudiation, applied through clauses 5 and 9 of the agreement of purchase and sale
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore four-criterion test for case-by-case privilege over journalist-source communications
BaselineA: Common law: Wigmore’s four criteria, as discussed by the SCC in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness test for a Crown corporation’s determination of the effective tax rate for payments in lieu of taxes
BaselineB: Combination of statute and regulation: Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, especially ss. 2, 2.1, 4(1), 9(1)(f) and 15, and Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, especially ss. 2 and 7(1), reviewed under the reasonableness principles from Dunsmuir and Khosa.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual arbitrator’s award: an error of law on the face of the award is reviewable unless the parties specifically submitted the legal question for a binding, unreviewable determination
BaselineA: Common law, principally Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd. and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131, informed by the arbitration agreement’s limits on the arbitrator’s powers
CaseB_TestB: Morin framework for determining unreasonable trial delay under Charter s. 11(b), including attribution of delay and inference of prejudice
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), as interpreted in R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use: applying new knowledge to achieve a useful, commercially valuable result is a patentable “new and useful art” when it has a method of practical application; no further inventive step in implementation is required.
BaselineA: Statute: Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, ss. 2 and 36, with s. 41 distinguished.
CaseB_TestB: Purchaser-assistance exception to trafficking liability: a person whose conduct amounts only to incidental assistance to a drug purchaser is treated as a purchaser rather than a trafficker, but a concerted effort to effect the drug transfer constitutes aiding trafficking if accompanied by the required intent.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention under s. 2(c) of the Canadian Bill of Rights requires compulsory restraint, associated with custody or actual physical restraint; merely complying with a roadside breath demand is not detention and does not provide a reasonable excuse for refusal.

BaselineB: Common law: Quinn v. Leathem, Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch, Sorrell v. Smith, Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited, Southam Co. Ltd. v. Gouthro, and Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 13 test barring the incriminating use of prior testimony in other proceedings, including a retrial
BaselineA: Constitutional text — Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 13 and 11(c)-(d), considered alongside s. 5 of the Canada Evidence Act
CaseB_TestB: K.G.B. test for the substantive admissibility of a witness's prior inconsistent statement
BaselineB: Common law — the necessity-and-reliability approach from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith, replacing the orthodox rule adopted in Deacon v. The King and operating through s. 9 of the Canada Evidence Act
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Jurisdiction under art. 68 based on the defendant’s domicile or, failing that, residence, assessed from the evidence as a whole
BaselineA: Statute: Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68, with Canadian Citizenship Act, s. 10 used to support a presumption concerning principal residence.
CaseB_TestB: Considering related state misconduct as a mitigating factor in determining a fit and proportionate sentence
BaselineB: Statute and Constitution: Criminal Code, ss. 718 to 718.2, especially s. 718.2(a), operating within the framework of Charter s. 24(1).

BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, principally ss. 3(1), 27(1), 28.2 and 38(1), read with art. 734 of the Quebec Code of Civil Procedure.

BaselineB: Common law — the reasonableness standard from Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., within the pragmatic and functional framework established in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and refined in Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

BaselineA: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, ss. 137.1(2)-(4), especially the dismissal framework in ss. 137.1(3) and 137.1(4).

BaselineB: Common law: the corporate attribution doctrine established and developed in Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen, Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of), and Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd., and summarized in Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co.; applied in light of the purposes of the Limitations Act, 2002 and the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act.

The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference; applied to Provincial Court Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. P-21, s. 4.1, and Bill 7.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exclusive statutory obscenity test for publications under Criminal Code s. 159(8), including articles publicly displayed with sexually explicit descriptions
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), with the exclusivity of the statutory test previously recognized in Brodie v. The Queen.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant-purpose test for exemption from compelled testimony
BaselineA: Sections 7 and 13 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, building on the self-incrimination and derivative-use-immunity principles in R. v. S. (R.J.)

BaselineB: Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the framework from Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, Withler v. Canada (Attorney General), R. v. Kapp, and Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia

CaseA_TestA: Conspiracy to prevent or lessen competition unduly: the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended to enter the agreement and that, if carried into effect, the agreement would prevent or lessen competition unduly across the relevant industry.
BaselineA: Statute: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c), interpreted in light of Howard Smith Paper Mills Ltd. v. The Queen, Weidman v. Shragge, Stinson-Reeb Builders Supply Co. v. The King, and Container Materials Ltd. v. The King.
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable-verdict appellate review: determine whether a properly instructed jury or judge could reasonably have rendered the verdict; an essential factual finding may also make the verdict unreasonable if it is plainly contradicted by the evidence relied upon or incompatible with evidence not otherwise contradicted or rejected, while credibility findings may be disturbed only if unsupported on any reasonable view of the evidence.
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i), as interpreted in R. v. Yebes, R. v. Biniaris, R. v. Sinclair, R. v. Beaudry, and R. v. Burke.

CaseA_TestA: Valid consent to intercept a private communication: consent must be knowing and voluntary—meaning a conscious, intended decision free from external coercion—although promised or expected leniency does not itself invalidate consent.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, s. 178.11(2)(a), read with s. 178.16(1)(a).
CaseB_TestB: Determining whether hate speech targeted the particularized identifiable group: the court must consider the totality of the evidence and draw appropriate inferences; the Crown need not prove interchangeability between the hateful terminology used and the group's name in the information.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 319(2) and 318(4), informed by the law governing particulars.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rule prohibiting the joint trial of separate informations or indictments, even with consent, unless legislation expressly provides otherwise
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, incorporated by implication into the Criminal Code and applied to provincial proceedings absent an express statutory exception
CaseB_TestB: Credibility assessment using absence of motive to lie and lack of embellishment
BaselineB: Common law credibility principles, particularly R. v. Stirling, supplemented by R. v. Ignacio and R. v. Swain
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR abusive tax avoidance test: whether allowing the tax benefit would frustrate or defeat the object, spirit, or purpose of Income Tax Act provisions relied on by the taxpayer, determined through a unified textual, contextual, and purposive analysis
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 18(13), 96(1), 245(1)-(4), and 248(10), informed by Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun two-stage procedure and guiding rule requiring courts to protect informer privilege while minimizing, as much as possible, impairment of the open court principle, including use of a separate parallel proceeding where necessary
BaselineB: Common law — Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43, supplemented by the common law doctrines of informer privilege and the open court principle
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limits on a provincial commission’s inquiry into a federal agency: the province may investigate alleged criminal acts by RCMP members but may not inquire into the RCMP’s administration or management.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91 and 92(14), together with the provincial Public Inquiry Commission Act and the principles applied in Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail and Faber v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Paramount-welfare-of-the-child test for contested custody: consider all relevant factors affecting the child’s physical, psychological, spiritual, and emotional welfare, with parental claims subordinated where the child’s welfare requires.
BaselineB: Domestic Relations Ordinance, R.O.N.W.T. 1974, c. D-9, especially s. 39 and also ss. 28(1), 35(2), and 37, combined with the equitable parens patriae jurisdiction recognized in Re Moores and Feldstein, Beson v. Director of Child Welfare, and Racine v. Woods.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law defence of necessity: imminent peril, no reasonable legal alternative, and proportionality
BaselineA: Common law necessity defence, preserved by s. 7(3) of the Criminal Code and previously addressed in Morgentaler v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in an online undercover child-luring operation
BaselineB: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the common law reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework, including Marakah, Cole, Spencer, Patrick and Tessling
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant-purpose test for exemption from compelled testimony under Charter s. 7
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 13, and the principle against self-incrimination developed in R. v. S. (R.J.)
CaseB_TestB: Timing and voir dire framework for deciding a Corbett application
BaselineB: Canada Evidence Act, s. 12, and the judicial discretion to exclude prior convictions established in R. v. Corbett
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entitlement to immediate payment from the Highway Victims Indemnity Fund without first exhausting remedies against an insurer
BaselineA: Statute — Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39
CaseB_TestB: Calculation of Fatal Accidents Act dependency damages using the present value of lost net support, adjusted for investment returns, inflation, taxation, and contingencies
BaselineB: Statute and common law — The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164, together with the damages methodology discussed in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whether the circumstances warrant exercising the Court's discretion to vary the statutory default interest entitlement
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, s. 52; Interest Act, ss. 13-14; with Supreme Court Rule 61 governing an application to vary an unsettled judgment
CaseB_TestB: Whether procedural fairness is implied by the statutory scheme governing the Governor in Council's review power
BaselineB: Combination of the common law duty of procedural fairness, including Nicholson and Martineau, and the National Transportation Act, s. 64(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien owner and lien-attachment test: the party must have an estate or interest in the land, have requested the work, and have had the work done on its credit, on its behalf, with its privity or consent, or for its direct benefit, assessed from the overall arrangement.
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 1(1)(d), 5(1), 7 and 11.

BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b), informed by the realistic-potential test from R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 159(8) publication-based obscenity test: an article publicly displayed for sale with printed descriptions may constitute a “publication” and is governed exclusively by the statutory test of whether its dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), as informed by Brodie v. The Queen on the exclusivity of the statutory obscenity test for publications.
CaseB_TestB: Individualized reasonable-accommodation test for applying a collective agreement’s automatic termination clause: the negotiated absence period is a significant but non-determinative factor, and undue hardship must be assessed globally from the beginning of the absence in light of the employee’s particular circumstances.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20; the Meiorin reasonable-accommodation framework; and the collective agreement’s termination and disability provisions.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith-basis test for putting disputed or unproven facts to a witness in cross-examination
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. Bencardino and R. v. Shearing; the Court clarified and confined R. v. Howard. A question may be asked without independent proof if counsel has a good-faith basis, assessed through the available information, belief in its likely accuracy, and intended purpose, provided the suggestion is not reckless, knowingly false, misleading, or otherwise prohibited.
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test for operational conflict or frustration of federal purpose
BaselineB: Common-law constitutional doctrine developed in cases including Canadian Western Bank v. Alberta, Rothmans, Benson & Hedges Inc. v. Saskatchewan, and Quebec (Attorney General) v. Canadian Owners and Pilots Association, applied to Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act, ss. 243 and 244, and The Saskatchewan Farm Security Act, ss. 9 to 22. The party invoking paramountcy must establish the federal purpose by clear proof and prove that the provincial law is incompatible with it; the doctrine is construed narrowly and applied with restraint.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment for republished opinions: the defendant bears the burden of showing honest belief in the comment, and the defence fails absent evidence that the writer or publisher honestly held the expressed opinion.
BaselineA: Common law, particularly Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd., Silkin v. Beaverbrook Newspapers Ltd., and the republication principle in Truth (N.Z.) Ltd. v. Holloway.
CaseB_TestB: Contempt knowledge test: the party alleging contempt must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the alleged contemnor had actual personal knowledge of the order; service on counsel alone does not impute knowledge, although knowledge may be inferred from supporting circumstances.
BaselineB: Common law, particularly Kimpton v. Eve, Ex parte Langley, and Baxter Travenol Laboratories of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Canada), Ltd.; Federal Court Rules 308, 311, and 355 were held not to alter the common law requirement.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Police liability for false arrest: reasonable and probable grounds must account for all available information, except information reasonably considered unreliable
BaselineA: Combination of statute and civil law: Criminal Code, s. 435, and Civil Code, arts. 1053-1054; Coroners' Act, s. 38, governed the purported warrant
CaseB_TestB: Effective dismissal of a probationary constable by the exclusively authorized police board
BaselineB: Combination of regulation and collective agreement under statute: Regulation 680, s. 27(b), and collective agreement, s. 9, under The Police Act, s. 29
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of financial burdens imposed on holders of fully paid shares: an amendment is invalid if it imposes any financial burden in respect of those shares
BaselineA: Combination of the common-law limited-liability principle and The Companies Act of Alberta, R.S.A. 1970, c. 60, ss. 2(1)(10), 15(1), 16(c), 42(1), 68(4), and 193(1)(d)
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for identifying an Aboriginal right: precisely characterize the claimed activity and determine whether, before European contact, it was integral to the claimant group's distinctive culture
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1982, s. 35(1), as interpreted by R. v. Van der Peet
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown-binding test: the Crown is bound only when mentioned or referred to in legislation; at common law, necessary implication arises only where the legislation’s purpose would otherwise be wholly frustrated.

CaseB_TestB: Material contractual breach test: a material departure from an express contractual weight undertaking breaches the subsisting contract and attracts damages for resulting additional expenses.
BaselineB: Statute and contract: Civil Code arts. 992 and 1065, applied to the express weight undertaking in the contract of carriage.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional and integral-part test for federal jurisdiction over labour relations
BaselineA: Common law constitutional doctrine under ss. 91 and 92 of the British North America Act, 1867, particularly the Stevedoring Reference and related labour-jurisdiction precedents, combined with ss. 2 and 108(1) of the Canada Labour Code and ss. 88 and 91(24) concerning provincial laws applicable to Indians.
CaseB_TestB: Two-step substantive equality test under Charter s. 15(1) without a mandatory mirror comparator group
BaselineB: Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, as previously interpreted in Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, Law v. Canada, and R. v. Kapp.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Proof of breach of the contractual obligation to provide sewers that properly service each development stage

CaseB_TestB: Presumption against retrospective application of the statutory abolition of the presumption of advancement

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Four-factor test for whether an administrative decision must be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis
BaselineA: Federal Court Act, ss. 28 and 2, informed by common law natural justice principles
CaseB_TestB: Section 24(2) trial-fairness test classifying evidence as conscriptive or non-conscriptive and assessing discoverability
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), and the framework established in R. v. Collins
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea: proof that the accused trafficked in the restricted drug raises a presumption of intent and guilt unless evidence raises a reasonable doubt based on an honest belief negating mens rea.

BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy and R. v. Darlyn, supplemented by Jones v. National Coal Board, R. v. Torbiak and Campbell, Yuill v. Yuill, and R. v. Bateman.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b), as interpreted in Irwin Toy Ltd. v. Quebec (Attorney General), Ford v. Quebec (Attorney General), Rocket v. Royal College of Dental Surgeons of Ontario, and Ramsden v. Peterborough (City)
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights due process test for deprivation of property: procedural protection applies only in individualized adjudication, while clear and unambiguous legislation may expropriate property without compensation
BaselineB: Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e), Department of Veterans Affairs Act, s. 5.1(4), and the common law expropriation principles stated in Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen and Wells v. Newfoundland

CaseB_TestB: Elements of the secret-commission offence for an agent accepting a benefit

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

Assessors of the Town of Sunny Brae, Guaranty Trust Co. of Canada v. Minister of National Revenue, and Vancouver Society of Immigrant and Visible Minority Women v. M.N.R.

BaselineA: Common law — the proximity-based duty of care principles in Donoghue v. Stevenson, Hedley Byrne & Co. v. Heller & Partners Ltd., and Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, together with the contractual-limitation principle discussed in J. Nunes Diamonds Ltd. v. Dominion Electric Protection Co.
CaseB_TestB: Primacy of a valid and exclusive foreign choice-of-forum clause over incidental-demand jurisdiction

Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board; supplemented for the government claim by the Mining Safety Act, particularly ss. 42 and 43.

BaselineA: Common law principles reflected in Re West and Leonard v. Wharton, applied to a discharge order made under s. 62 of The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act

CaseA_TestA: Lease-based allocation of fire-loss risk where the tenant pays the insurance premiums
