CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso test: whether a properly instructed jury, acting reasonably, could have reached a different conclusion absent the error.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractor-method responsibility rule: barring specific arrangements to the contrary, the contractor is responsible for its chosen method of performing the work, and the owner or its design professionals have no duty to advise on that method or associated permit difficulties.
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. Paradis and Farley Inc. and Vermont Construction Inc. v. Beatson.
CaseB_TestB: Judicial review of prosecutorial discretion: decisions concerning the nature and extent of a prosecution are reviewable only for abuse of process, meaning egregious Crown conduct that seriously compromises trial fairness or the integrity of the justice system; the claimant must first establish a proper evidentiary foundation and ultimately prove abuse on a balance of probabilities.
BaselineB: Common law, principally Krieger v. Law Society of Alberta, R. v. Nixon, and Miazga v. Kvello Estate, applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code ss. 255 and 727(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Curative proviso test: the Crown must satisfy the appellate court that a properly instructed jury “could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty.”
BaselineA: Section 613(1)(b)(iii) of the Criminal Code, as interpreted in Colpitts v. R. and Brooks v. The King.
CaseB_TestB: Treaty interpretation test: ascertain the parties’ common intention from the treaty text and extrinsic historical and cultural context, even absent facial ambiguity, choosing the interpretation that best reconciles their interests and upholds the honour of the Crown.
BaselineB: The Mi’kmaq Treaties of 1760-61, s. 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, and common law treaty-interpretation principles from Sioui, Badger, Simon, Sundown, and Guerin.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability and inconsistency test for provincial laws affecting Indians: a provincial law that intrudes on Indian character or identity applies only through Indian Act s. 88 and only to the extent consistent with the Indian Act
BaselineA: Statutory and constitutional: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, ss. 2(1), 11 and 88; Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10; and British North America Act, 1867, s. 91(24)
CaseB_TestB: Collins three-category test for excluding Charter-infringing evidence under s. 24(2), emphasizing the seriousness and cumulative effect of the violations
BaselineB: Constitutional text and precedent: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), and the framework established in R. v. Collins, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Staged, individualized assessment of whether a conditional sentence is appropriate for an Indigenous offender, including mandatory consideration of Gladue factors and all sentencing purposes and principles
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 718 to 718.2, particularly s. 718.2(e), and s. 742.1, as previously interpreted in R. v. Gladue and R. v. Proulx.
CaseB_TestB: Balancing a claim of freedom of religion against countervailing rights, values, and harm under the Quebec Charter
BaselineB: Statute and jurisprudence: Charter of human rights and freedoms, R.S.Q., c. C-12, ss. 3 and 9.1, building on the religious-freedom test in Syndicat Northcrest v. Amselem and related Charter jurisprudence.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Purpose-of-producing-income test for capital cost allowance: if property produces revenue, the deduction is allowable unless the revenue is unreasonably low relative to the property’s value; if it produces no income, objectively assess whether it was acquired to produce income in light of the facts, jurisprudence, and reasonably acceptable commercial and business practices.
BaselineA: Income Tax Act, s. 20(1)(a), read with Income Tax Regulations, especially ss. 1100(1), 1102(1)(c), and 1102(14).
CaseB_TestB: Tertiary-ground bail test: bail may be denied only where, considering all circumstances through the four statutory factors, a properly informed reasonable member of the community would conclude that detention is necessary to maintain confidence in the administration of justice.
BaselineB: Criminal Code, s. 515(10)(c), interpreted under Charter s. 11(e) and the just-cause principles established in R. v. Pearson and R. v. Morales.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Lease-allocation test: read the lease reasonably and in a business sense to determine whether the tenant's payment of fire-insurance premiums transferred the risk of fire loss to the landlord
BaselineA: Common law principles of lease and contract interpretation, including Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd. v. Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd., informed by s. 118 of The Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 224
CaseB_TestB: Warsaw Convention ticket-delivery test: a carrier loses the passenger-liability limitation only if no passenger ticket was delivered; irregularity or illegibility does not suffice
BaselineB: Statute: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 45, Schedule I (Warsaw Convention), especially arts. 3(1), 3(2), and 22
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a damages award is permitted only where the trial judge applied a wrong principle of law or the overall award is a wholly erroneous estimate; an award merely considered “on the high side” is insufficient.
BaselineA: Common law, based on Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., [1978] 2 S.C.R. 229.
CaseB_TestB: Videotape-only identification test: an authenticated videotape may independently establish identity without corroboration where its clarity, quality, and duration permit identification beyond a reasonable doubt.
BaselineB: Common law evidentiary principles, particularly R. v. Leaney, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 393, together with the audio-recording principles discussed in R. v. Pleich and R. v. Rowbotham.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 16 “another good and sufficient reason” test: the employer must prove a substantial, non-pretextual reason that was the true reason for dismissal; the tribunal cannot review the proportionality of dismissal.
BaselineA: Statute: Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 14 and 16.
CaseB_TestB: Two-aspect section 12 gross-disproportionality test examining the actual offender and, if necessary, reasonable hypothetical circumstances.
BaselineB: Constitutional statute and precedent: s. 12 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the gross-disproportionality test established in R. v. Smith and reaffirmed in R. v. Lyons and R. v. Luxton.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for when a corporate mortgagor’s waiver binds a successor or assign: “successor” is limited to successor corporations, while an individual assign is bound only where the mortgage was assigned without the mortgagee’s consent and without an assumption agreement
BaselineA: Statute — The Limitation of Civil Rights Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-16, ss. 2(1), 2(2)(d), 40(1), and 40(2)
CaseB_TestB: Two-part test for a compensable de facto taking: acquisition of a beneficial interest in or flowing from the property and removal of all reasonable uses of the property
BaselineB: Common law — Mariner Real Estate Ltd. v. Nova Scotia (Attorney General), Manitoba Fisheries Ltd. v. The Queen, and The Queen in Right of British Columbia v. Tener; subject to statutory displacement by s. 569 of the Vancouver Charter
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment requires proof that the defamatory comment honestly expressed the opinion of its writer or publisher; each republisher stands in the same position as the original writer.
BaselineA: Common law fair-comment doctrine, particularly Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd., Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., and Truth (N.Z.) Ltd. v. Holloway.
CaseB_TestB: Review of a wiretap authorization containing erroneous affidavit information: errors, even deliberate or fraudulent ones, are factors rather than grounds for automatic invalidation; the court must determine whether the unaffected information remains sufficiently reliable to reasonably support the authorization.
BaselineB: Common law framework established in R. v. Garofoli for reviewing wiretap authorizations.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Leave-to-intervene test: whether the applicant has a sufficient interest and will bring a special perspective, subject to avoiding prejudice from new arguments or evidence
BaselineA: Common law and the Court's procedural discretion governing intervention applications
CaseB_TestB: Meaning of offering an indignity to human remains: physical contact is unnecessary; monuments are excluded unless they mark the presence of human remains
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 182(b)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Res ipsa loquitur test for proving gross negligence: the defendant controlled the instrumentality, the occurrence ordinarily would not happen without negligence, and no valid explanation displaces the inference
BaselineA: Combination of the common law res ipsa loquitur rule, including Walker v. Coates and Gauthier & Co. Ltd. v. The King, and the gross-negligence requirement in s. 132(3) of Ontario's Highway Traffic Act
CaseB_TestB: Two-part test for recognizing a vested right: the individual's juridical situation must be tangible and concrete, and sufficiently constituted when the new statute commences
BaselineB: The common law presumption against interference with vested rights, principally stated in Spooner Oils Ltd. v. Turner Valley Gas Conservation Board, and codified in s. 12 of Quebec's Interpretation Act
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 7 overbreadth test: whether the means chosen by the state are unnecessarily broad and go beyond what is needed to accomplish the governmental objective.
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 7, building on the overbreadth analysis discussed in R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society.
CaseB_TestB: Section 69(2) reasonable arm's-length transfer price test considering all economically relevant circumstances, including linked transactions and agreements.
BaselineB: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), s. 69(2), informed but not controlled by the OECD transfer-pricing guidelines.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for granting a limited defence reply to an improper Crown jury address
BaselineA: Common law inherent jurisdiction, including R. v. Osborn, Amato v. The Queen, and R. v. Young, applied alongside Criminal Code s. 651 and Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
CaseB_TestB: Three-step framework for the honest-belief-in-legal-age defence under Criminal Code s. 172.1(4)
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code ss. 172.1(1), (3), and (4), as previously interpreted in R. v. Levigne.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single transaction test for classifying murder under s. 214(5): the Crown must first prove the accused committed, or was a party to, both the underlying offence and the murder, after which the court asks whether the offences were sufficiently closely connected in time; the test does not apply to manslaughter.
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5)), and the single transaction principle from R. v. Paré.
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test: the party seeking a stay must show, through a global assessment of numerous and variable factors, that an alternative forum is clearly more appropriate.
BaselineB: Common law, principally the forum non conveniens framework reviewed in Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda and informed by Amchem Products Inc. v. British Columbia (Workers’ Compensation Board).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable-expectation-of-injury test for withholding personal information relating to lawful investigations
BaselineA: Statute: Privacy Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. P-21, ss. 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47 and 49, read harmoniously with Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 31 (4th Supp.), ss. 60, 72, 73 and 74.
CaseB_TestB: Permissive adverse inference or presumption of causation in medical liability cases
BaselineB: Combination of statute and jurisprudence: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2846 to 2849, particularly art. 2849, as informed by Snell v. Farrell and St-Jean v. Mercier.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 framework for granting letters rogatory seeking documentary production alone: the evidence must be for trial rather than discovery, relevant, within the scope permitted by local law, and adequately defined
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: s. 43 of the Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, interpreted through the liberal comity principle recognized in Zingre v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility test for defence-led evidence of an unknown third-party suspect: relevance to an available defence, followed by exclusion only if prejudice substantially outweighs probative value
BaselineB: Common law: the defence-evidence admissibility framework from R. v. Seaboyer and R. v. Corbett, informed by the air-of-reality test from R. v. Cinous and the sufficient-connection principles from McMillan v. The Queen and R. v. Grandinetti
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh-pursuit continuation of peace-officer status under s. 25(4)
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 25(4), 449(1)(b), and 450.
CaseB_TestB: Specific-penalty test limiting an arbitrator's power to substitute discipline
BaselineB: Statute: Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d)(ii), applied to the collective agreement.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Guidelines Order applicability test: a federal “decision making responsibility” exists only where an Act of Parliament imposes an affirmative regulatory duty relating to the proposed activity; the responsible department must then initiate the assessment process.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and regulation: Department of the Environment Act, ss. 4-6; Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, ss. 2, 3, 6, 10, 12 and 14; applied with the Navigable Waters Protection Act, s. 5, and Fisheries Act, ss. 35, 37 and 40.
CaseB_TestB: Contextual test for reviewable error in a jury charge: the alleged error must be assessed in the context of the entire charge, the evidence and the trial as a whole, and must engage a ground of appellate intervention under s. 686(1)(a).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a), together with the contextual jury-charge jurisprudence, including R. v. Morrissey.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 70(1) test for preserving the right to invoke interest arbitration after a collective agreement expires
BaselineA: Combination of statute and collective agreement: s. 70(1) of The Labour Relations Act and the interest-arbitration provisions in article 16 of the Haldimand agreement and article 15 of the Perth agreement
CaseB_TestB: Exception permitting review of an erroneous pre-trial division and severance order despite the rule against collateral attack
BaselineB: Common law rule against collateral attack stated in Wilson v. The Queen
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) is satisfied where the insured has an insurable interest; a tenant contractually obliged to insure the leased property has such an interest and need not separately specify its nature.
BaselineA: Statute: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240, statutory conditions 1 and 10(a), read with Civil Code arts. 2480, 2571, 2572 and 2584.
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 test for police appropriation of bodily samples initially obtained or seized for non-criminal purposes: the court must determine whether police conduct constitutes an independent seizure or makes the initial seizure unreasonable; appropriation for criminal use requires Hunter-compliant authorization.
BaselineB: Constitution and statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8, and Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, ss. 16(2), 16(4) and 16(5), informed by Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Dyment.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Justification for departing from the knock-and-announce rule: reasonable grounds to fear harm or destruction of evidence, assessed on information reasonably available at the time
BaselineA: Combination of s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the common law knock-and-announce framework established in Eccles v. Bourque and R. v. Genest, within the search-reasonableness framework from R. v. Collins.
CaseB_TestB: Hearsay treatment of implied verbal assertions tendered for the truth of their contents
BaselineB: Common law hearsay doctrine, particularly the defining features stated in R. v. Khelawon and the principled necessity-and-reliability framework developed in R. v. Khan and summarized in R. v. Mapara.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Property is used or held in carrying on a business when it is truly “employed and risked” to fulfil a business requirement, such that its withdrawal would have a “decidedly destabilizing effect” on corporate operations.
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii), incorporated into the definition of foreign investment income by s. 129(4)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Crown burden for obtaining a new trial after an acquittal: the Crown must satisfy the court, with a reasonable degree of certainty, that the verdict would not necessarily have been the same absent the legal error.
BaselineB: Statute and common law — Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and reaffirmed in R. v. Morin.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper duty-of-care test for statutory regulators
BaselineA: Common law — the Anns/Kamloops duty-of-care framework, as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart; proximity is assessed with reference to the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8, particularly ss. 9, 27, 33, 51, 60 and 61.
JudgeA: The Chief Justice and Major J.
CaseB_TestB: Fiscal-emergency justification for limiting Charter rights under s. 1
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 1, and the proportionality framework established in R. v. Oakes, informed by prior jurisprudence on budgetary justifications.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effective termination of a continuing guarantee requires written notice that is explicit and unequivocal, not merely an expression of wish or preference.
BaselineA: Contractual term interpreted through common-law principles: s. 4 of the Guarantee and Postponement of Claim permitted termination of liability for future advances by written notice delivered to the branch manager.
CaseB_TestB: Evidence of an accused’s silence is inadmissible unless the Crown establishes real relevance and a proper basis for its admission.
BaselineB: Combination of the common-law right to silence and evidentiary principles from Rothman v. The Queen, R. v. Robertson, and R. v. Symonds, reinforced by s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Hebert v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Article IV treaty-residence test: a person is a resident only if liable to tax by reason of an enumerated or genuinely similar criterion—one that grounds full taxation on worldwide income, not merely source taxation.
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I, incorporating the Canada-United States Income Tax Convention (1980), especially Article IV(1).
CaseB_TestB: Valid-refusal test for triggering the insurance limitation period: the insurer must adequately comply with SABS s. 71 by clearly explaining the dispute-resolution process to an unsophisticated person, including its principal steps and time limits.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, ss. 279-283 and 281(5), and the Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, especially ss. 62(8), 71, 72 and 94.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory limiting instruction for highly prejudicial bad-character evidence: the jury must be told the evidence is confined to its permissible purpose and cannot support propensity reasoning
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. D. (L.E.), with the bad-character admissibility rule drawn from Morris v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Recent-fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: once recent fabrication is alleged, prior complaints are admissible to prove that they were made, but not the truth of their contents
BaselineB: Common law rule against prior consistent statements and its recent-fabrication exception; no originating case is identified in the decision
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Witness-exclusion-order breach test: a witness who remains in court is not necessarily disqualified; the trial judge may exclude the evidence in certain circumstances, and otherwise its weight is for the trier of fact, without an express oral self-instruction for every witness where the judge has demonstrated awareness of the rule.
BaselineA: Common law, including Cook v. Nethercotte, Thomas v. David, Chandler v. Home, R. v. Briggs, R. v. Thompson, Black v. Besse, and R. v. Carefoot.
CaseB_TestB: Crown immunity from discovery test: immunity continues unless lifted by clear and unequivocal legislative language; section 27 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act lifts it only where the Crown is a party.
BaselineB: Combination of common law Crown immunity and statute, principally s. 17 of the Interpretation Act and ss. 27 and 34 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, considered with s. 7 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings (Provincial Court) Regulations.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec inter vivos trust for unborn primary beneficiaries: public-order prohibitions remain applicable, but constraints inherent to direct gifts do not; trustee acceptance makes the trust irrevocable, the trustee owns the property during the trust, and the trust requires actual or eventual beneficiaries.
BaselineA: Statute: former Civil Code of Lower Canada, especially arts. 981a, 981b and 981l, read with arts. 608, 755, 765, 771, 772 and 929; informed by Curran v. Davis on trustee acceptance.
CaseB_TestB: Enforceability of an interim injunction against non-parties: non-parties may be held in contempt only after being apprised of the order and given an opportunity to comply, and the order must be carefully worded, fair and not unduly broad.
BaselineB: Combination of common law and statute: courts' inherent equitable and contempt jurisdiction, reflected in Attorney-General v. Times Newspapers Ltd., Bartle & Gibson Co. and International Longshoremen's Association, together with s. 36 of British Columbia's Law and Equity Act; Criminal Code, s. 11 confirms that criminality does not displace civil remedies.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fraud by “other fraudulent means”: objectively dishonest conduct causing deprivation or risk, accompanied by subjective knowledge of the conduct and its potentially depriving consequence
BaselineA: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1), as interpreted in R. v. Olan and R. v. Théroux
CaseB_TestB: Union’s duty of diligent and competent representation toward former employees in collective bargaining
BaselineB: Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2, informed by Noël v. Société d’énergie de la Baie James and Centre hospitalier Régina Ltée v. Labour Court
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unfairness test for reapportioning family assets: equal division may be displaced under s. 51 after considering the statutory criteria, without mandatory asset-by-asset or contribution-proportionate analysis
BaselineA: Statute: Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, ss. 43 and 51
CaseB_TestB: Duty-to-comment test for prejudicial Crown remarks: remarks sufficiently prejudicial to prevent the defence from being fairly put require corrective jury instructions, subject to the curative proviso
BaselineB: Combination of common law, adopting the formulation in Ayles J.A.'s dissent below, and Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(b)(iii)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid partnership for s. 96: carrying on a business, in common, with a view to profit, assessed pragmatically in all the circumstances
BaselineA: Common law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada, applied through s. 96 of the Income Tax Act
CaseB_TestB: Substantive W. (D.) jury-instruction test: the charge as a whole must clearly preserve the Crown's burden and avoid a credibility contest
BaselineB: Common law test established in R. v. W. (D.) and clarified in R. v. S. (W.D.) and R. v. Avetysan
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accused-presence test: examination of prospective jurors concerning partiality after arraignment and plea forms part of the “whole of the trial” and must be heard by the accused.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, principally ss. 577(1) and 569(2), read with ss. 598-600 and 613(1)(b)(iii), and Nova Scotia Juries Act, s. 4(2).
CaseB_TestB: Appellate conviction-substitution test: an acquittal may be replaced by a conviction only if the Crown establishes that the accused should have been found guilty but for the legal error and all findings necessary for guilt were made explicitly or implicitly, or were not in issue.
BaselineB: Common law — Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Courville, applied under Criminal Code, s. 613(4)(b)(ii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law test for a lawful frisk search incident to arrest
BaselineA: Common law search-incident-to-arrest doctrine recognized in R. v. Brezack, R. v. Morrison, and R. v. Miller.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 requirements for warrantless child apprehension: serious harm threshold and a fair, prompt post-apprehension hearing
BaselineB: Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, applied to ss. 17, 21(1), 27(1), and 29(1) of Manitoba's Child and Family Services Act and informed by B. (R.) v. Children's Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto and New Brunswick (Minister of Health and Community Services) v. G. (J.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused a police line-up: the evidence is admissible where the Crown must explain the omission of a line-up or risk an adverse inference; otherwise it should not normally be tendered.
BaselineA: Common law principles of relevance and admissibility, informed by R. v. Brager and R. v. John.
CaseB_TestB: Pith-and-substance test for provincial inquiries: an inquiry is ultra vires where its overall purpose and effect make it a substitute police investigation or preliminary inquiry into a specific criminal offence by named individuals.
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(27) and 92, together with the commission-of-inquiry jurisprudence in Faber v. The Queen, Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, Attorney General (Que.) and Keable v. Attorney General (Can.), and O'Hara v. British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Homicide causation: the accused’s unlawful act must be a contributing cause of death outside the de minimis range, proved beyond a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, s. 205(1), and common-law causation and thin-skull principles reflected in R. v. Larkin, R. v. Cato, R. v. Garforth, R. v. Blaue, and R. v. Nicholson
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage Anns analysis for recognizing a novel duty of care for pure economic loss arising from commercial negotiations
BaselineB: Common law—Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, as adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and developed in Canadian pure-economic-loss cases including Canadian National Railway Co. v. Norsk Pacific Steamship Co.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rule of specialty: absent clear terms, immunity ends once the extraditee has had a reasonable opportunity to return and remains voluntarily rather than by reason of surrender
BaselineA: Combination of the extradition arrangement, the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, ss. 2, 3 and 33, and international-law principles for interpreting international agreements
CaseB_TestB: No separate leave is required to address the curative proviso because its application is always intertwined with the alleged error of law under appeal
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), and the common-law appellate principle stated in R. v. Keegstra
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal licensing-discretion test: a council may refuse a licence only on applicant-specific licensing grounds, not to prohibit a lawful type of business absent express statutory authority
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 455, read in the context of the Act's licensing, zoning, and by-law provisions and the non-prohibition principle from Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 fair-process framework for IRPA security-certificate proceedings, including the incompressible minimum disclosure requirement
BaselineB: Constitution and statute: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1), as interpreted in Charkaoui I and Ruby, together with IRPA Division 9, especially ss. 77(2), 83(1), 85.1, 85.2 and 85.4
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Purpose-based admissibility test for extrinsic evidence suggesting uncharged offences at sentencing
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code sentencing provisions, particularly ss. 718 to 718.2, 724(3)(e), 725 and 726.1, and the common law reflected in Lees v. The Queen and R. v. Gardiner
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in an online police sting involving an adult communicating with an unknown child
BaselineB: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the common law reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework from cases including R. v. Marakah, R. v. Cole, R. v. Spencer and R. v. Tessling
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contextual test for inferring possession from fingerprint evidence: the inference depends on all the circumstances and all the evidence, not a hard-and-fast rule.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Food and Drugs Act, ss. 46 and 48(2); Criminal Code, s. 4(3); and the fingerprint-possession principles discussed in R. v. O'Keefe and R. v. Mehrabnia.
CaseB_TestB: Review Board treatment-condition jurisdiction: Boards may bind hospital authorities and supervise treatment, but may not prescribe, impose, or require delivery of treatment.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, Part XX.1, especially ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examination on a former juvenile's record: a delinquency based on a Criminal Code violation is an “offence,” its adjudication is a “conviction,” and it may be used to contradict evidence-in-chief under s. 12(1) of the Canada Evidence Act.
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1), read with the Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3, ss. 2(1), 3 and 20(1), and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593.
CaseB_TestB: Amendment of an indictment where the narcotic proved differs from the particular specified: the substance is a particular rather than a distinct offence, and amendment is permitted unless prejudice or injustice is irreparable.
BaselineB: Statute — Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2 and 4 and Schedule item 3, together with Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) and 613(1)(b)(i), (3).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 27(2)(e) hypothetical-infringement test: an exclusive licensee cannot establish hypothetical primary infringement where the foreign maker is the Canadian copyright owner, because an owner-licensor cannot infringe its own copyright.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) test for retrospective changes to sentence conditions: the dominant consideration is the extent to which the change thwarts the offender's settled expectation of liberty; an automatic extension of incarceration is additional punishment, while less drastic changes depend on whether they substantially increase the risk of additional incarceration.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and SCC precedent — Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h), building on R. v. Wigglesworth, R. v. Shubley, R. v. Rodgers, and Cunningham v. Canada.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Essence-of-the-crime test for determining whether a charge falls within an extradition arrangement
BaselineA: Statute and treaty: s. 2 of the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, and s. 17 of the 1925 Supplementary Convention
CaseB_TestB: Purpose-of-use test distinguishing credibility impeachment from incriminating use of prior testimony
BaselineB: Constitution and statute: s. 13 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and s. 5(2) of the Canada Evidence Act, informed by R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Temporal-priority test for statutory wage liens: the lien attaches when wages are earned, does not affect an earlier mortgage, and reaches only the employer’s equity in previously mortgaged property.
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), ss. 5 and 5A, especially s. 5A(1)-(2).
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive-law framework for forced dissolution: special legislation applies first, but Civil Code of Québec arts. 355-364 fill gaps where no specific scheme governs the case of dissolution.
BaselineB: Statute — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334 and 355-364, read with the Companies Act, ss. 28, 29, 224, 227 and 231, and the Code of Civil Procedure, art. 829.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Identifiable-or-traceable trust property test: if collected tax remains identifiable or traceable, it is trust property excluded under s. 47(a); if it cannot be traced, it is a Crown claim governed by s. 107(1)(j).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j); Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18; and general principles of trust law, informed by Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board.
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 framework for determining whether numbers warrant local minority-language facilities and whether the minority-language board's location decision prevails over the Minister's decision.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional, statutory, regulatory, and precedential sources: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23(3); Prince Edward Island School Act, particularly ss. 112 and 128(2); School Act Regulations, particularly ss. 6.01(f), 6.07, 6.08, and 6.11; and the sliding-scale and management-and-control framework from Mahe v. Alberta.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Manslaughter liability under Criminal Code s. 21(2): a party to a common unlawful purpose may be convicted where the principal commits murder, the party did not foresee the probability of murder, but a reasonable person in all the circumstances would have foreseen at least a risk of harm.
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(2), and the principles from R. v. Kirkness, R. v. Creighton, and R. v. Trinneer.
CaseB_TestB: Erroneous GST payment rebate and set-off test: the person who actually paid and was out of pocket may receive a rebate under s. 261(1), and the Minister must apply an otherwise allowable rebate under s. 296(2.1), notwithstanding an expired claim period, where the statutory conditions are met.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for an arbitrator’s authority to substitute a lesser penalty in a discharge grievance
BaselineA: Statute and collective agreement: s. 25(3) of The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, read with arts. 6(4) and 12(12)(a) of the collective agreement.
CaseB_TestB: Contribution-based test for complicity under article 1F(a): a voluntary, significant, and knowing contribution to the organization’s crime or criminal purpose
BaselineB: Statute, treaty, and international law: s. 98 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act incorporates article 1F(a) of the Refugee Convention; the test is informed particularly by arts. 25, 30, and 31(1)(d) of the Rome Statute and replaces the personal and knowing participation test from Ramirez.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust for unjust enrichment: enrichment, corresponding deprivation, absence of juristic reason, a causal connection to the property, and an interest proportionate to the claimant's contribution
BaselineA: Common law and equity, principally the unjust enrichment framework stated in Rathwell v. Rathwell and the constructive trust approach introduced in Murdoch v. Murdoch
CaseB_TestB: Substantive solicitor-client confidentiality framework governing privilege and searches of lawyers' offices
BaselineB: Combination of common law solicitor-client privilege, especially Solosky v. The Queen, and the search-warrant authority in Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore four-part test for case-by-case privilege: the communication must originate in confidence; confidentiality must be essential to the relationship; the relationship must be one the community ought to foster; and the injury from disclosure must outweigh the benefit to the correct disposal of litigation.
BaselineA: Common law — Wigmore's four criteria, previously discussed by the SCC in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness test for a Crown corporation's selection of the effective tax rate for payments in lieu of taxes: the corporation retains discretion, but must calculate the rate using the tax system that actually exists where the property is located, as if the property were taxable property belonging to a private owner, rather than using a fictitious or abolished tax system.
BaselineB: Combination of common law administrative-law reasonableness review under Dunsmuir and Khosa and the statutory scheme in ss. 2, 2.1, 4, 9, 11.1 and 15 of the Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act and ss. 2, 7(1) and 12.1 of the Crown Corporation Payments Regulations.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual arbitrator’s award for error of law on its face
BaselineA: Common law, principally Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd. and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131, applied in light of the submission and the collective agreement’s limits on arbitral authority.
CaseB_TestB: Morin balancing test for unreasonable trial delay under Charter s. 11(b)
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), as interpreted in R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use: applying new knowledge to achieve a commercially valuable result is a “new and useful art” if it has a method of practical application; no further inventive step in implementation is required.
BaselineA: Statute—Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, ss. 2 and 36, informed by Hickton’s Patent Syndicate v. Patents and Machine Improvements Co.
CaseB_TestB: Purchaser-assistance exception to trafficking liability: incidental assistance rendered solely to a drug purchaser is treated as aiding possession, but a concerted effort going beyond the acts of a mere purchaser may constitute aiding trafficking if accompanied by the required intent.
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(b) and (c), and Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-1, ss. 2, 3(1), and 4(1) and (2), informed by Poitras v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention under s. 2(c) of the Canadian Bill of Rights requires compulsory restraint, associated with custody or actual physical restraint; merely obeying a lawful roadside breath-demand direction is not detention.
BaselineA: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii), read with Criminal Code, s. 234.1(1)-(2) and the analogous breath-demand provisions in s. 235.
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch tort of civil conspiracy: liability arises where the defendants' predominant purpose is to injure the plaintiff, or where unlawful conduct is directed toward the plaintiff and the defendants should know that injury is likely and actual damage results.
BaselineB: Common law: Quinn v. Leathem, Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch, Sorrell v. Smith, Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd., Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Ltd., and International Brotherhood of Teamsters v. Therien.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 13 use-immunity test for prior testimony tendered at a retrial
BaselineA: Constitutional text: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 13 and 11(c)-(d)
CaseB_TestB: K.G.B. test for substantive admissibility of a witness's prior inconsistent statement
BaselineB: Common law hearsay principles from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith, replacing the orthodox rule recognized in Deacon v. The King, with a voir dire under s. 9 of the Canada Evidence Act
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Territorial jurisdiction under art. 68 C.C.P.: a purely personal action must be brought in the court of the defendant’s domicile or, failing that, residence
BaselineA: Statute: Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68, supplemented by the residence presumption under Canadian Citizenship Act, s. 10
CaseB_TestB: Considering related state misconduct as a mitigating circumstance when imposing a fit and proportionate sentence, subject to statutory sentencing limits
BaselineB: Statute and constitutional provision: Criminal Code, ss. 718 to 718.2, and Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for conspiracy to prevent or lessen competition unduly: the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt both an intended agreement and that, if implemented, the agreement would prevent or lessen competition unduly in the relevant industry as a whole.
BaselineA: Statute: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c), as informed by Howard Smith Paper Mills Ltd. v. The Queen, Weidman v. Shragge, Stinson-Reeb Builders Supply Co. v. The King, and Container Materials Ltd. v. The King.
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable-verdict appellate review test: whether a properly instructed jury or judge could reasonably have rendered the verdict, including whether an essential factual finding is plainly contradicted by the evidence relied upon or incompatible with evidence not otherwise contradicted or rejected; credibility findings may be disturbed only if unsupported on any reasonable view of the evidence.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i), as interpreted in R. v. Yebes, R. v. Biniaris, R. v. Sinclair, R. v. Beaudry, and R. v. Burke.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid consent to intercept: consent must be knowing and voluntary, meaning a conscious, intended act free from external coercion; promised or expected leniency does not by itself invalidate consent.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, s. 178.11(2)(a), read with s. 178.16(1)(a).
CaseB_TestB: Identifiable-group targeting under s. 319(2): determine from the totality of the evidence whether the accused intended to target the particularized group; exact interchangeability between the words used and the group’s name is unnecessary.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 319(2) and 318(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rule prohibiting the joint trial of separate informations or indictments
BaselineA: Common law rule from Crane v. Public Prosecutor, incorporated by implication into the Criminal Code and applicable under provincial summary-conviction legislation unless expressly displaced.
CaseB_TestB: Credibility assessment using motive to lie and lack of embellishment
BaselineB: Common law credibility principles, including R. v. W.(D.) and R. v. Stirling.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Three-part GAAR test, particularly whether a tax benefit frustrates the object, spirit or purpose of the relied-upon provisions after a unified textual, contextual and purposive analysis
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 18(13), 96(1), 245(1)-(4) and 248(10)
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun two-stage informer-privilege procedure, including the minimum-openness requirements for fully in camera proceedings
BaselineB: Common law — Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional boundary for provincial inquiries: a province may investigate alleged criminal acts by members of the RCMP, but may not, under the guise of that investigation, inquire into or recommend changes to the administration and management of the federal police force.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91 and 92, particularly s. 92(14), together with the Public Inquiry Commission Act and the constitutional doctrine of colourability; informed by Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail and Faber v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Paramount-welfare-of-the-child test: in contested custody proceedings, the court must consider all relevant factors affecting the child's physical, psychological, spiritual and emotional welfare and choose the course best supporting the child's healthy development, with parental claims subordinated where the child's welfare requires.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 39 of the Domestic Relations Ordinance, which preserves the rules of equity, and the equitable parens patriae jurisdiction developed in Re Moores and Feldstein, Beson v. Director of Child Welfare and Racine v. Woods; ss. 28(1), 35(2) and 37 of the Ordinance provide additional statutory context.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Defence of necessity as an excuse: the accused's act must be a morally involuntary response to an imminent and direct peril, with no reasonable legal alternative, and the harm inflicted must be less than the harm avoided; once sufficiently raised, the Crown must disprove necessity beyond a reasonable doubt.
BaselineA: Common law necessity doctrine, previously addressed in Morgentaler v. The Queen, and preserved by s. 7(3) of the Criminal Code.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in an alias-based online sting: under the totality-of-the-circumstances test, an adult has no objectively reasonable expectation of privacy when communicating online with a child who is a stranger where police created the fictitious child and therefore knew the relationship's nature from the outset.
BaselineB: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework developed in Marakah, Cole, Spencer, Edwards, Patrick and Tessling.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant-purpose test for exemption from compelled testimony
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 13, and R. v. S. (R.J.), applied in the context of Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1)
CaseB_TestB: Timing and voir dire procedure for a Corbett application
BaselineB: Canada Evidence Act, s. 12, as interpreted in R. v. Corbett, together with the common-law and Charter s. 7 case-to-meet principle
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory entitlement to payment from the Highway Victims Indemnity Fund without first exhausting remedies against the judgment debtor's insurer
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39. A claimant holding a qualifying final, unsatisfied judgment must apply within one year and satisfy the prescribed declaration requirements; the Fund must then pay within seven days, subject to the statutory limits. The Court clarified that this remedy is neither subsidiary nor ultimate and does not require prior proceedings against an insurer.
CaseB_TestB: Present-value method for calculating dependency damages under the Fatal Accidents Act
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common-law damages principles: The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164, together with the present-value approach discussed in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Thornton v. Board of School Trustees and Arnold v. Teno. The Court held that the award should replace the dependants' net lost support through an exhausting lump-sum fund, using a discount rate based on long-term investment returns adjusted for inflation, with allowances for income tax and contingencies.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion under s. 52 to vary the statutory default for judgment interest where the circumstances warrant intervention
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, s. 52; Interest Act, ss. 13-14; and Supreme Court Rule 61
CaseB_TestB: Statutory-construction test for implying procedural fairness in Governor in Council review under s. 64(1)
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: National Transportation Act, s. 64(1), interpreted against the procedural-fairness principles in Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk Regional Board of Commissioners of Police and Martineau v. Matsqui Institution (No. 2)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory owner and lien-entitlement test under the Mechanics’ Lien Act
BaselineA: Statute — The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 1(1)(d), 5(1), 7 and 11
CaseB_TestB: Realistic potential for juror partiality test for challenges for cause
BaselineB: Combination of statute and prior jurisprudence — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b), as interpreted in R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exclusive statutory obscenity test for publications: an item is obscene where it is a publication whose dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex, or of sex with crime, horror, cruelty, or violence; publicly displayed wares accompanied by descriptive material may constitute publications.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), together with Brodie v. The Queen on the exclusivity of the statutory obscenity test for publications.
CaseB_TestB: Individualized accommodation test for a disability-related termination clause: the negotiated absence period is a significant but non-determinative factor, and undue hardship must be assessed globally from the beginning of the absence in light of the employee's particular circumstances.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law — Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20, and the duty-to-accommodate and undue-hardship framework from Meiorin, applied in the context of collective agreement clause 12.11(5).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith-basis test for cross-examination on disputed or unproven facts
BaselineA: Common law, particularly R. v. Bencardino and R. v. Shearing, with R. v. Howard clarified and confined to its evidentiary context; the right of cross-examination is also protected by ss. 7 and 11(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test for operational conflict or frustration of federal purpose
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine developed in cases including Multiple Access, Rothmans, Canadian Western Bank, COPA, Mangat, and Ryan Estate, applied here to s. 243 of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act and Part II, ss. 9 to 22, of The Saskatchewan Farm Security Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment requires each publisher to prove that the defamatory comment was an honest expression of the opinion asserted; a republisher is “in exactly the same position as the original writer.”
BaselineA: Common law fair-comment doctrine, principally as stated in Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd., Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., Jones v. Skelton, and “Truth” (N.Z.) Ltd. v. Holloway.
CaseB_TestB: Contempt requires personal service or actual personal knowledge of the court order, proved beyond a reasonable doubt; knowledge may be inferred from supporting circumstances but is not automatically imputed from service on counsel.
BaselineB: Common law knowledge requirement from Kimpton v. Eve, Ex parte Langley, and Baxter Travenol Laboratories of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Canada), Ltd.; Federal Court Rules 308, 311, and 355 were considered but held not to alter that requirement.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable and probable grounds for warrantless arrest: the officer must consider all available information and may disregard only information reasonably believed unreliable
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, 1953-54 (Can.), c. 51, s. 435, applied within the civil-liability framework of Civil Code arts. 1053 and 1054
CaseB_TestB: Effective dismissal of a probationary constable must be made by the Board holding the exclusive, non-delegable dismissal power
BaselineB: Combination of Regulation 680, s. 27(b), section 9 of the collective agreement, and The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fully paid share non-assessment test: an amendment to corporate articles is invalid if it imposes any financial burden on a shareholder in respect of fully paid shares.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: The Companies Act of Alberta, R.S.A. 1970, c. 60, ss. 2(1)(10), 15(1), 16(c), 42(1), 68(4), and 193(1)(d), together with the limited-liability principle reflected in Ooregum Gold Mining Company of India, Ltd. v. Roper, Bisgood v. Henderson's Transvaal Estates, Ltd., and Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co. Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for an Aboriginal right: precisely characterize the claimed activity, then determine whether, before European contact, it formed an integral, central, significant, or defining feature of the distinctive culture of the claimant Aboriginal group.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law: s. 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, as interpreted through the Aboriginal-rights framework established in R. v. Van der Peet.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown-binding test: an enactment binds the Crown only if it mentions or refers to the Crown; s. 16 excludes binding by necessary implication, while at common law necessary implication requires that the legislation's purpose would otherwise be wholly frustrated.
BaselineA: Combination of statute (Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, ss. 16 and 28) and common law (Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation).
CaseB_TestB: Contractual-breach test for a materially inaccurate cargo-weight undertaking: a substantial deviation from a material contractual term breaches a subsisting contract and attracts damages under art. 1065 rather than nullity for error under art. 992.
BaselineB: Statute (Civil Code, arts. 992 and 1065) applied to the terms of the contract of carriage.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional and integral-part test for federal jurisdiction over labour relations: federal jurisdiction exists only where the undertaking's normal operations are federal in nature or regulating its labour relations forms an integral part of primary federal jurisdiction
BaselineA: Common-law constitutional jurisprudence, particularly the Stevedoring case and related labour-jurisdiction precedents, applying ss. 91 and 92 of the British North America Act, 1867; also Canada Labour Code, ss. 2 and 108(1)
CaseB_TestB: Two-step substantive equality test under s. 15(1), without a mandatory mirror comparator group
BaselineB: Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the equality jurisprudence established in Andrews, Law, and Kapp
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Proof of breach of the municipal sewer-servicing covenant: the developer must show an existing or foreseeable inadequacy in the project’s sewer service and connect any general report to that inadequacy.
BaselineA: Section 31 of the 1966 development agreement, applied through common-law principles governing contractual breach.
CaseB_TestB: Non-retrospective application of the statutory abolition of the presumption of advancement: because the presumption is substantive law, the new statute does not govern prior circumstances unless it says so expressly or by necessary implication.
BaselineB: Section 1(3)(d) of The Family Law Reform Act, 1975 and the common-law presumption against retrospectivity recognized in Phillips v. Eyre and applied through Wilson v. Dagnall.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Four-factor test for whether an administrative decision must be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis
BaselineA: Section 28 of the Federal Court Act, informed by common-law procedural fairness principles discussed in Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works, Russell v. Duke of Norfolk, and Durayappah v. Fernando
CaseB_TestB: Section 24(2) trial-fairness test based on conscription and discoverability
BaselineB: Section 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the exclusion framework established in R. v. Collins and developed in subsequent cases
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking in the restricted drug actually sold, rebuttable by evidence of an honest belief raising a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: ss. 40 and 42 of the Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, and the mens rea principles from Beaver v. The Queen, R. v. Blondin, and The Queen v. King.
CaseB_TestB: Limits on judicial intervention: a judge may question or interrupt witnesses where necessary but must act so that justice is seen to be done and must not create doubt as to impartiality
BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy and R. v. Darlyn, informed by Jones v. National Coal Board, R. v. Torbiak and Campbell, Yuill v. Yuill, and R. v. Bateman.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 2(b) counter-advertising test: consumer criticism is protected expression, and restricting its accessible sign medium to designated places directly infringes freedom of expression.
BaselineA: Constitutional text and precedent: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b), as interpreted in Irwin Toy, Ford, Rocket and Ramsden.
CaseB_TestB: Bill of Rights due process framework for property deprivation: no pre-enactment hearing is required, adjudicative process applies only to individualized determinations, and clearly and unambiguously legislated expropriation is permitted.

CaseA_TestA: School-tax valuation under s. 373: value at real value only the property taxable in each municipality, without extending one municipality's machinery exemption to others
BaselineA: Statute—Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373, read with Cities and Towns Act, s. 488
CaseB_TestB: Elements of corruptly accepting a secret commission under Criminal Code s. 426(1)(a)(ii), including adequate and timely disclosure and no corrupt-bargain requirement
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a)(ii) (formerly s. 383(1)(a))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trustee liability for failing to maintain or replace insurance on all insurable bankrupt property, including hypothecated property, or to notify the secured creditor if insurance cannot be obtained
BaselineA: Statute and hypothec deed: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 2(o), 2(r), 9(1), 9(2), and 171, together with the deed's insurance clause
CaseB_TestB: Charitable-status test under the fourth Pemsel head: public benefit in a way recognized as charitable, assessed through precedent and analogy, the Income Tax Act scheme, and the distinction between incremental and wholesale reform
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 149(1)(l), 149.1(1), and 248(1); the common law framework from Commissioners for Special Purposes of the Income Tax v. Pemsel, as elaborated in D’Aguiar v. Guyana Commissioner of Inland Revenue and Vancouver Society of Immigrant and Visible Minority Women v. M.N.R.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown remarks: remarks sufficiently prejudicial to prevent the defence from being fairly put require judicial comment; absent application of the curative proviso, nondirection requires a new trial.
