BaselineB: Common law principles for interpreting standard-form insurance contracts from Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co., Progressive Homes Ltd. v. Lombard General Insurance Co. of Canada, Non-Marine Underwriters v. Scalera, and Co-operators Life Insurance Co. v. Gibbens, applied to SEF 44 clauses 2, 4(a), and 4(b)(vii)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 119 substantial-alteration versus clarification test for reviewing a bargaining-unit certification
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Labour Code, s. 119 and ss. 124 et seq., informed by the Board's framework in The Employees of the Regional Comptroller and the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers
CaseB_TestB: Palpable and overriding error threshold for appellate intervention in a trial court's factual findings
BaselineB: Common law — Schreiber Brothers Limited v. Currie Products Limited and Gulf Oil Canada Limited, Stein v. "Kathy K.", and Lewis v. Todd
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency: the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt a significant risk of legally cognizable harm and harm incompatible with the proper functioning of society.
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1), and the common law principles from R. v. Butler, refined in the companion case R. v. Labaye.
CaseB_TestB: “Made with a view to expropriation” test for determining whether an enactment forms part of the expropriation scheme and must be ignored when assessing compensation.
BaselineB: Combination of Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a), and the common law Pointe Gourde principle from Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory tribunal test: a tribunal is statutory where the parties must resort to it by statute or, once selected, it is invested with sufficiently wide statutory powers and duties and issues binding decisions defining the parties’ rights.
BaselineA: Combination of the common law certiorari doctrine from R. v. National Joint Council, Howe Sound and Port Arthur, and Code of Civil Procedure art. 846, applied with Canada Labour Code ss. 156, 157, 159 and 160(5).
CaseB_TestB: Sublicence test: a sublicence exists where a licensee expressly or impliedly grants a third party an independent right to do something otherwise prohibited to it that the licensee may do only by virtue of its licence.
BaselineB: Common law licensing, sale-of-licensed-goods and contractual interpretation principles, applied to a compulsory licence issued under former Patent Act s. 39(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple exception for Criminal Code s. 83: where a firearm is used in committing robbery, s. 83 creates a separate offence permitting multiple convictions and requiring additional consecutive punishment.
BaselineA: Combination of the common law rule against multiple convictions for the same matter or delict from Kienapple v. The Queen and Cox and Paton v. The Queen, and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 83(1)(a) and 83(2).
CaseB_TestB: Pith and substance test for a municipal measure: determine its true purpose from intrinsic and extrinsic evidence and its legal and practical effects, then classify the resulting matter under the constitutional heads of power.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional pith and substance doctrine, including Canadian Western Bank, COPA, Lacombe and Morgentaler, applied under the Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(29), 92(10)(a), 92(13) and 92(16).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment through random virtue-testing and the bona fide geographic inquiry exception
BaselineA: Common law — the two-branch entrapment test established in R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903.
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s voluntariness determination only upon a serious, specific and determining error
BaselineB: Common law — appellate deference to a trial judge’s evidentiary weighing on a voluntariness voir dire; no originating precedent is identified in the decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fairness test for whether the statutory order of jury addresses interferes with the accused’s right to make full answer and defence under Charter ss. 7 and 11(d)
BaselineA: Constitution, statute, and common law — Charter ss. 7 and 11(d), Criminal Code ss. 651(3)-(4), and the full-answer-and-defence principles recognized in Dersch, Stinchcombe, and Lyons.
CaseB_TestB: Three-step honest-belief-in-legal-age and reasonable-steps framework under Criminal Code s. 172.1(4)
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code ss. 172.1(1), (3), and (4), as previously interpreted in R. v. Levigne.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single transaction test for classifying murder as first degree: the Crown must first establish that the accused committed, or was a party to, both the underlying offence and the murder; only then may the court determine whether the offences were sufficiently closely connected in time. The test is unavailable for manslaughter.
BaselineA: Statute and precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5) (now s. 231(5)), as interpreted in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618.
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test: the party seeking a stay must demonstrate, through a global assessment of the context-dependent factors, that an alternative forum is clearly more appropriate.
BaselineB: Common law, principally the forum non conveniens framework in Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17, and Amchem Products Inc. v. British Columbia (Workers’ Compensation Board), [1993] 1 S.C.R. 897.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable expectation of injury test for withholding personal information under Privacy Act s. 22(1)(b)
BaselineA: Statute: Privacy Act, ss. 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47 and 49, read harmoniously with Official Languages Act, ss. 60 and 72 to 74.
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary adverse inference or presumption of fact concerning causation in medical liability cases
BaselineB: Statute and prior SCC jurisprudence: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2846 to 2849, as interpreted in Snell v. Farrell and St-Jean v. Mercier.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 letters rogatory test: documentary evidence may be ordered without ancillary oral testimony, subject to the established judicial-assistance guidelines
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43, informed by the comity principle recognized in Zingre v. The Queen and common-law guidelines requiring trial rather than discovery evidence, relevance, a permissible scope of inquiry, and adequately defined documents.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led evidence concerning an unknown third-party suspect
BaselineB: Common law — the defence-evidence admissibility framework from R. v. Seaboyer and R. v. Corbett, the air-of-reality test from R. v. Cinous, and the sufficient-connection principle from McMillan v. The Queen and R. v. Grandinetti.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh-pursuit test: a peace officer with lawful authority to arrest under s. 450 retains peace-officer status and s. 25(4) protection after crossing a provincial border if the pursuit began lawfully and remains fresh, until local authorities take over.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 25(4), 449(1)(b), and 450.
CaseB_TestB: Specific-penalty test: an arbitrator loses penalty-substitution authority only where the collective agreement assigns a specific penalty to the particular infraction; an employer-selected or randomly specified penalty does not qualify.
BaselineB: Statute — Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d), interpreted in conjunction with the collective agreement.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Guidelines Order applicability test: a federal “decision making responsibility” exists only where the federal government has an affirmative regulatory duty under an Act of Parliament relating to the proposal; the department responsible for that duty is the initiating department.
BaselineA: Combination of regulation and statute: ss. 2, 3, 6, 10, 12 and 14 of the Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, enabled by s. 6 of the Department of the Environment Act and applied alongside s. 5 of the Navigable Waters Protection Act and ss. 35 and 37 of the Fisheries Act.
CaseB_TestB: Contextual test for reversible error in a jury charge: the alleged error must be assessed in the context of the entire charge, the evidence and the trial as a whole, and must engage one of the grounds for appellate intervention in s. 686(1)(a).
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: s. 686(1)(a) of the Criminal Code and the common law governing appellate review and contextual interpretation of jury charges.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 70(1) preservation test: a contractual right to invoke interest arbitration survives expiry if it exists when notice to arbitrate is served; it need not remain in force when the award is issued.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and collective agreement: s. 70(1) of The Labour Relations Act and the interest-arbitration provisions in art. 16 of the Haldimand agreement and art. 15 of the Perth agreement.
CaseB_TestB: Exception to the collateral-attack rule permitting a trial judge to review and set aside an erroneous pre-trial division or severance order regulating the judicial process within the same litigation.
BaselineB: Common law rule against collateral attack stated in Wilson v. The Queen, applied in the procedural context of Criminal Code ss. 590(3), 591(3)-(4), and 645(5).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) is satisfied where the insured has an insurable interest; a tenant contractually obliged to insure the leased property need not separately state the nature of that interest
BaselineA: Statute: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240, statutory condition 10(a), read with Civil Code arts. 2480, 2571 and 2572 and the interpretation in Wandlyn Motels v. Commerce General Insurance Company
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 test for bodily samples initially seized for a non-criminal purpose and later appropriated by police: determine whether police conduct constitutes an independent seizure or makes the initially valid seizure unreasonable
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional and statutory law: s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and ss. 16(2), 16(4) and 16(5) of the Coroners Act, informed by Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Dyment
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Justification for departing from the knock-and-announce rule: the Crown must provide contemporaneous evidence of reasonable grounds to fear harm to officers or occupants, or destruction of evidence, with greater departures requiring stronger justification.
BaselineA: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the common law knock-and-announce rule established in Eccles v. Bourque and developed in R. v. Genest.
CaseB_TestB: Implied-assertion hearsay test: a verbal implied assertion is hearsay when tendered for the truth of its contents without a contemporaneous opportunity to cross-examine the declarant, and is presumptively inadmissible unless covered by an exception or supported by necessity and reliability.
BaselineB: The common law hearsay rule and principled approach developed in R. v. Khan, R. v. Mapara, and R. v. Khelawon.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Employed-and-risked property test: property is used or held in a business when its withdrawal would have a decidedly destabilizing effect on corporate operations, including where it fulfils a mandatory condition precedent to trade
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) and (b), informed by the employed-and-risked test from The Queen v. Marsh & McLennan, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal from acquittal test: the Crown must establish with a reasonable degree of certainty that the verdict would not necessarily have been the same absent the legal error
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law — Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Morin
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper two-stage duty-of-care test for a statutory regulator
BaselineA: Common law—Anns v. Merton London Borough Council and Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen, as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart—and the Law Society Act, particularly ss. 9, 27, 33, 51, 60 and 61.
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) contextual discrimination test for legislation targeting acquired pay-equity rights
BaselineB: Constitutional statute—s. 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms—as interpreted through the contextual framework established in Law v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effective termination of a continuing guarantee: written notice must unequivocally exercise the termination right and leave the creditor in no doubt; a mere wish or preference is insufficient.
BaselineA: Contract—s. 4 of the Bank's Guarantee and Postponement of Claim, which permitted termination of liability for future advances by written notice.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of an accused's investigative silence: unless the Crown establishes "real relevance and a proper basis" for admission, questions by investigators and evidence of the ensuing silence are inadmissible and support no adverse inference.
BaselineB: Common law right to silence and evidentiary relevance principles, protected by s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and developed in Rothman v. The Queen, R. v. Robertson, R. v. Symonds, and Hebert v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Article IV treaty-residence test: a person must be liable to tax by reason of an enumerated or genuinely similar criterion imposing full taxation on worldwide income, not merely source-based taxation
BaselineA: Treaty and statute: Article IV(1) of the Canada–United States Income Tax Convention (1980), enacted by the Canada–United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I
CaseB_TestB: Valid-refusal test for triggering the insurance limitation period: the insurer must adequately explain the entire dispute-resolution process in clear language directed to an unsophisticated person
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, ss. 279–283 and 281(5), and the Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, especially s. 71
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory limiting instruction for highly prejudicial bad-character evidence
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. D. (L.E.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 111; the Court extended its warning requirement beyond similar-act evidence to other highly prejudicial evidence tending to show bad character.
CaseB_TestB: Recent-fabrication exception for prior consistent statements, limited to proving that the statements were made
BaselineB: Common law rule governing prior consistent statements and allegations of recent fabrication; no originating case is identified in the decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Treatment of testimony from a witness who breached an exclusion order, including presumed consideration of weight without an express caution for every witness
BaselineA: Common law, as reflected in Cook v. Nethercotte, Thomas v. David, Chandler v. Home, Black v. Besse, and R. v. Carefoot.
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal legislative abrogation of Crown immunity from discovery, with s. 27 of the CLPA applying only where the Crown is a party
BaselineB: Common law Crown immunity combined with statute and regulation, principally s. 17 of the Interpretation Act, ss. 27 and 34 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, and s. 7 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings (Provincial Court) Regulations.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec inter vivos trust created for unborn primary beneficiaries
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code arts. 981a et seq., especially arts. 981a, 981b and 981l, read with the provisions governing gifts and beneficiaries, including arts. 608, 755, 765, 771, 772 and 929; informed by Curran v. Davis.
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdiction to issue and enforce injunctions against non-parties
BaselineB: Combination of common law and statute: the courts' inherent and equitable jurisdiction, the common law contempt principle reflected in cases including International Longshoremen's Association, Local 273 v. Maritime Employers' Association, and s. 36 of British Columbia's Law and Equity Act; Criminal Code, s. 11 confirms that criminality does not displace civil remedies.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fraud by “other fraudulent means”: objectively dishonest conduct that wrongfully uses something in which another has an interest, extinguishing or placing that interest at risk, coupled with subjective knowledge of the conduct and possible deprivation
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1), as previously interpreted in R. v. Olan and applied with the fraud framework in R. v. Théroux
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining, including the residual duty toward former bargaining-unit employees
BaselineB: Statute: Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, s. 47.2, informed by Noël v. Société d’énergie de la Baie James and Centre hospitalier Régina Ltée v. Labour Court
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge's matrimonial-property discretion only where the judge misdirected himself or the decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice
BaselineA: Common law appellate-review principles from Harper v. Harper, applied to discretion under ss. 43 and 51 of the Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121
CaseB_TestB: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown remarks where they are sufficiently prejudicial that comment is required to ensure the defence is fairly put to the jury
BaselineB: Common law governing jury instructions and prejudicial advocacy, with the remedial proviso in s. 686(1)(b)(iii) of the Criminal Code
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Three-essential-ingredients test for a valid partnership under s. 96: carrying on a business, in common, with a view to profit
BaselineA: Combination of Income Tax Act, s. 96, and the common law partnership test established in Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada and elaborated in Backman v. Canada
CaseB_TestB: Substantive W. (D.) test for adequate jury instructions where credibility is central
BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. W. (D.), as clarified in R. v. S. (W.D.) and R. v. Avetysan
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for whether a proceeding forms part of the “whole of the trial” requiring the accused’s presence under s. 577(1), including jury-partiality inquiries after arraignment and plea
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 577(1), informed by ss. 569(2), 598-600 and 613(1)(b)(iii), and Nova Scotia Juries Act, S.N.S. 1969, c. 12, s. 4(2).
CaseB_TestB: Test for an appellate court to set aside an acquittal and substitute a conviction rather than order a new trial
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4)(b)(ii), and the common-law test stated in Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Courville, affirmed in Courville v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law test for a search incident to lawful arrest: no reasonable and probable grounds are required, but the search must pursue a valid criminal-justice objective and must not be conducted abusively; any constraint must be proportionate.
BaselineA: Common law, principally as developed in R. v. Brezack, R. v. Morrison, and R. v. Miller, and informed by the common law police-power framework in Dedman v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 test for warrantless child apprehension: apprehension without prior judicial authorization may occur only as a last resort where there are reasonable and probable grounds to believe the child faces serious harm or a risk of serious harm, followed by a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and The Child and Family Services Act, especially ss. 17, 21(1), 24, 27, 29, and 30-37, informed by B. (R.) v. Children’s Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto and New Brunswick (Minister of Health and Community Services) v. G. (J.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused an identification line-up: it is admissible where the Crown must explain the absence of a line-up or risk an adverse inference, but ordinarily should not be tendered otherwise.
BaselineA: Common law of evidence, particularly relevance and admissibility principles reflected in R. v. Brager and R. v. John.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional limit on provincial inquiries: an inquiry is ultra vires where, in pith and substance, it uses coercive powers as a substitute police investigation or preliminary inquiry into specific criminal conduct by named persons.
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(27) and 92, informed by Faber v. The Queen, Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, Attorney General (Que.) and Keable v. Attorney General (Can.), and O'Hara v. British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Homicide causation: the accused’s unlawful act must be a contributing cause of death outside the de minimis range, proved beyond a reasonable doubt.
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 205(1), supplemented by the causation and thin-skull principles discussed in R. v. Larkin, R. v. Cato, R. v. Garforth, R. v. Blaue, and R. v. Nicholson.
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage duty-of-care test for novel pure economic loss arising from commercial negotiations.
BaselineB: Common law: the two-stage framework from Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, adopted in Canada in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and applied to pure economic loss in cases including Canadian National Railway Co. v. Norsk Pacific Steamship Co.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rule of specialty: an unqualified extradition undertaking must be interpreted in context, in light of its object and purpose and general international-law principles; absent clear terms, immunity ends once the fugitive has had an opportunity to return and remains voluntarily rather than by reason of surrender.
BaselineA: Combination of the extradition arrangement, the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, ss. 2, 3, 33 and 40, and international-law principles governing specialty and treaty interpretation.
CaseB_TestB: No-separate-leave rule for the curative proviso: an alleged error of law and the application of s. 686(1)(b)(iii) are always intertwined, so the Court may address the proviso within an appeal as of right without a separate grant of leave.
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), and the common law framework stated in R. v. Keegstra, [1995] 2 S.C.R. 381.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal licensing discretion: a council may refuse a licence only on grounds peculiar to the applicant and cannot use licensing power to prohibit a lawful type of business absent express statutory authority.
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, especially s. 455, read in light of Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo and related municipal-law authorities.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonably informed disclosure test: a security-certificate subject must receive an incompressible minimum of disclosure sufficient to give meaningful instructions to public counsel and meaningful guidance to special advocates; otherwise the undisclosed evidence must be withdrawn or the certificate quashed.
BaselineB: Statute and Constitution: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, especially ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(e) and (i), and 85.1 to 85.5, interpreted under s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Charkaoui I.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Charged-but-untried offence evidence may be considered at sentencing only through Criminal Code s. 725(1)(b) or (b.1), including the offender-consent requirement and the other enumerated conditions.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 725(1)(b) and (b.1).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in an online child-luring sting: an adult has no objectively reasonable expectation of privacy when communicating online with a child who is a stranger and police know that relationship from the outset because they created the fictitious child.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8, and the common-law reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework from Marakah, Cole, Spencer, Tessling and Edwards; Criminal Code, ss. 183 and 184.2.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation: words or conduct must induce detrimental reliance, and silence or inaction constitutes a representation only where there is a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law—estoppel by representation, including Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd. and Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha v. Dawson’s Bank, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the presumption under Criminal Code s. 212(3): the jury must consider all relevant evidence, without requiring a particular and severable item of evidence to the contrary
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fingerprint-based inference of possession: whether fingerprints support possession depends on all the circumstances and the totality of the evidence; no hard-and-fast rule applies, and fingerprints on a container rather than the prohibited substance are merely one factor.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: possession under Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-27, ss. 46 and 48(2), and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 4(3), informed by the fingerprint-inference principles in R. v. O'Keefe and R. v. Mehrabnia.
CaseB_TestB: Review Board treatment-condition jurisdiction: a Board may bind hospital authorities and impose conditions supervising or regarding treatment, including requiring reconsideration and exploration of alternatives, but may not prescribe or impose treatment; the conditions must also be reasonable and supported by the evidence.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, principally ss. 672.54, 672.55(1), and 672.78, read within the broader statutory scheme.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 three-stage test for whether adjudicative authority may be conferred on a provincially appointed tribunal
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, together with the common law three-stage framework established in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714
CaseB_TestB: Three-factor discretionary test for public interest standing
BaselineB: Common law framework established in Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility under s. 12 of a Criminal Code-based juvenile-delinquency finding as a prior conviction
BaselineA: Statute — Canada Evidence Act, s. 12(1), read with the Juvenile Delinquents Act, especially ss. 2(1), 3 and 20(1), and supplemented by Criminal Code, s. 593.
CaseB_TestB: Amendment of an indictment where the evidence proves a different particular of the same narcotics offence
BaselineB: Statute — Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 and 4 and Schedule item 3; Criminal Code, ss. 529(4)-(5) and 613(1)(b)(i), (3), as informed by Elliott v. The Queen and Lake v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional approach and rough upper limit for non-pecuniary personal-injury damages: $100,000 is the upper limit absent rare exceptional circumstances, subject to proven or agreed inflation adjustments.
BaselineA: Common law established in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Arnold v. Teno, and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees, and refined in Lewis v. Todd.
CaseB_TestB: Inadequately insured motorist coverage test: the tortfeasor must be at fault as a motorist, and an unbroken chain of causation—more than incidental, fortuitous, or merely 'but for'—must link that conduct to the injuries; a severable intervening tort breaks the chain.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 3 of the Ontario Policy Change Form 44R, s. 239(1)(a) of the Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, and the common law purpose-and-causation framework from Amos v. Insurance Corp. of British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 27(2)(e) hypothetical-infringement test: an exclusive licensee may sue third parties, but cannot establish infringement against the owner-licensor, whose liability lies only in contract
BaselineA: Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, principally ss. 2.7, 13(4)-(7), 27(1)-(2)(e), and 36(1)-(2), together with the secondary-infringement framework from CCH Canadian Ltd. v. Law Society of Upper Canada
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) test for whether a retrospective change to sentence conditions constitutes additional punishment by thwarting an offender's settled expectation of liberty
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h), informed by R. v. Wigglesworth, R. v. Shubley, R. v. Rodgers, and Cunningham v. Canada
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Voluntary-association bylaw test: a corporation’s breach of its privately agreed, member-only bylaws, including incident natural-justice duties, is contractual and attracts the contractual prescription period.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and jurisprudence: Civil Code arts. 361, 1024, 1057, 2242 and 2261(2); Part III and s. 214 of the Quebec Companies Act; and prior contractual-association jurisprudence.
CaseB_TestB: Residual lien-priority test: where the Mechanics’ Lien Act prescribes no priority between competing interests, priority is determined by registration under the Registry Act, subject to actual notice.
BaselineB: Statute: Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, particularly ss. 7, 14(1), 16, 20, 21 and 22, together with Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Essence-of-the-crime test for determining whether an offence falls within a treaty-defined extradition category
BaselineA: Statute and treaty: s. 2 of the Extradition Act and s. 17 of the 1925 Supplementary Convention concerning crimes against laws suppressing narcotics trafficking.
CaseB_TestB: Purpose-of-use test for prior testimony: credibility impeachment is permitted, but incriminating use to establish guilt is prohibited
BaselineB: Constitutional and statutory: s. 13 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and s. 5(2) of the Canada Evidence Act, informed by R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unified three-step bona fide occupational requirement (Meiorin) test
BaselineA: Statute and common law: British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 3 and 13(1), (4), building on the separate direct- and adverse-effect discrimination frameworks from O’Malley, Etobicoke, Central Alberta Dairy Pool and related cases.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage pursuit-of-profit test for a business or property source of income
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Income Tax Act, principally ss. 3(a) and 9(1)-(2), informed by the reasonable-expectation-of-profit approach from Moldowan v. The Queen and the traditional common law definition of business.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory wage-lien priority test: the lien attaches when wages are earned, leaves prior mortgages unaffected, and attaches only to the employer’s equity in encumbered property.
BaselineA: Statute: Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), ss. 5 and 5A, particularly s. 5A(1)-(2).
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive-law framework for forced dissolution: apply any governing special statutory scheme first, but use arts. 355-364 C.C.Q. insofar as necessary to fill its gaps; dissolution may then be ordered on any ground in art. 355(2).
BaselineB: Statutes: Civil Code of Québec, preliminary provision and arts. 300, 334 and 355-364, read with the Companies Act, ss. 28, 29, 224, 227 and 231, and the Code of Civil Procedure, art. 829.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal criminal law power test: a prohibition with a penalty, directed at a legitimate criminal public purpose, and not colourable
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(27), together with the common law framework from Proprietary Articles Trade Association, the Margarine Reference, and Scowby
CaseB_TestB: Individualized reasonable-accommodation test for applying a collectively negotiated termination-of-employment clause
BaselineB: Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20; the Meiorin undue-hardship framework; and the collective agreement
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-trust classification in bankruptcy: if collected tax is identifiable or traceable, it is “property held ... in trust” excluded under s. 47(a); if it cannot be traced, it is a Crown claim governed by s. 107(1)(j).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j); Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18; general trust-law principles, informed by Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board.
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 minority-language facility location and management-control framework: the minority-language board determines the location and mode of services where numbers warrant, subject to constitutional requirements and legitimate provincial norms; the Minister may verify compliance but may not substitute his own criteria or decision.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text, statute, regulation, and precedent: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23; School Act, R.S.P.E.I. 1988, especially ss. 112 and 128(2); School Act Regulations, especially ss. 6.01(f), 6.07, 6.08 and 6.11; and the sliding-scale and management-control framework established in Mahe v. Alberta.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory accomplice-evidence caution applies equally to an accessory after the fact
BaselineA: Common law rule of practice concerning warnings about uncorroborated accomplice evidence, derived from Davies v. Director of Public Prosecutions and Horsburgh v. The Queen and applied as in R. v. Riezebos.
CaseB_TestB: Six-part framework for unlawful-object murder, including actual knowledge of surrounding circumstances and the relevance of intoxication
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Manslaughter liability under Criminal Code s. 21(2): a party to a common unlawful purpose may be convicted where the principal commits murder, the party did not foresee the probability of murder, but a reasonable person in all the circumstances would have foreseen at least a risk of harm.
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(2), and the principles from R. v. Kirkness, R. v. Creighton, and R. v. Trinneer.
CaseB_TestB: GST overpayment rebate and mandatory reassessment offset: the person who actually paid and was out of pocket may obtain the s. 261(1) rebate, and an allowable rebate must be applied under s. 296(2.1) despite an expired claim period.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable interest test for an improperly withheld just debt: interest is awarded where compensation is fair and equitable, at the rate and for the period the court considers appropriate.
BaselineA: The common law principle stated in Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto and followed in The Custodian v. Blucher, grounded in s. 46 of The Queen’s Bench Act and applied alongside Interest Act, ss. 3, 12 and 13, and Supreme Court Act, s. 52.
CaseB_TestB: Two-step post-conviction non-disclosure test: whether there is a reasonable possibility that the undisclosed information affected the conviction’s reliability or, alternatively, the overall fairness of the trial process.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1), as developed through R. v. Stinchcombe, R. v. C. (M.H.), R. v. Carosella and R. v. Collins.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 25(3) test for an arbitrator's authority to substitute a lesser penalty when dismissal cannot be sustained and the collective agreement specifies no penalty for the infraction
BaselineA: Statute: The Trade Union Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. T-17, s. 25(3), applied in conjunction with arts. 6(4) and 12(12)(a) of the collective agreement.
CaseB_TestB: Contribution-based test for complicity under article 1F(a): serious reasons for considering that the claimant voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to an organization's crime or criminal purpose
BaselineB: Statute and treaty: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, s. 98, incorporating Refugee Convention art. 1F(a), informed by international criminal law, particularly Rome Statute arts. 25, 30 and 31(1)(d); the test replaces the personal and knowing participation approach from Ramirez.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Recent-possession jury-instruction test: once the Crown proves possession of recently stolen goods, possession alone raises a prima facie case permitting—but not requiring—a guilty verdict; the Crown need not prove that no explanation was given, and any explanation that may reasonably be true must result in acquittal if it raises a reasonable doubt.
BaselineA: Common-law evidentiary rule established in R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch and adopted in prior SCC cases, especially R. v. Graham, interpreted consistently with s. 4(5) of the Canada Evidence Act.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage Imperial Tobacco framework for the territorial validity of provincial legislation: characterize and classify the law by its purpose and effects, then determine whether it has a meaningful connection to the province and respects other provinces’ legislative sovereignty.
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 92(13) and (14), as interpreted through the constitutional framework established in British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.; applied to s. 11 of the Opioid Damages and Health Care Costs Recovery Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust for unjust enrichment: enrichment, corresponding deprivation, absence of juristic reason, a causal connection to the property, and a proportionate proprietary interest
BaselineA: Common law and equity—Rathwell v. Rathwell established the three unjust-enrichment requirements, building on the constructive-trust approach introduced in Murdoch v. Murdoch.
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality and lawyer-office search warrant framework
BaselineB: Combination of common law solicitor-client privilege and the broader confidentiality right recognized in Solosky v. The Queen, applied to Criminal Code, s. 443(1)(b).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Framework for catastrophic personal-injury damages: actual future-care costs, projected net lost earnings, and substitute-amenities non-pecuniary damages subject to a flexible upper limit
BaselineA: Common law compensatory-damages principles, including The Queen v. Jennings and the approaches adopted in Andrews v. Grand & Toy and Thornton; Income Tax Act provisions were considered for tax treatment.
CaseB_TestB: Fire-damage election and repudiation test under clause 5: the purchaser must either complete for whatever insurance proceeds are owing or cancel; imposing restoration or insurance-collectibility conditions constitutes repudiation
BaselineB: Common law of contract, applied through clause 5 of the agreement of purchase and sale.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore four-criteria test for case-by-case journalist-source privilege
BaselineA: Common law: Wigmore’s four criteria, previously discussed with approval in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness test for PILT effective-rate decisions: calculations must use the actual municipal tax system and the private-owner comparator
BaselineB: Combination of statute, regulation, and common law: Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, especially ss. 2, 2.1 and 4(1); Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, especially ss. 2 and 7(1); and the reasonableness framework from Dunsmuir and Khosa.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual arbitrator’s award for error of law: an award is protected from review only where the parties specifically submitted a question of law for a binding determination; a legal question arising during an ordinary grievance remains reviewable, particularly where the collective agreement restricts the arbitrator from making an inconsistent decision.
BaselineA: Common law — Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd. and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131 — applied in light of clause 17 of the collective agreement.
CaseB_TestB: Morin reasonable-delay balancing test under Charter s. 11(b): assess the length of delay after defence waiver, the reasons and attribution of delay, prejudice to the accused, and the interests protected by s. 11(b); prejudice may be inferred from prolonged delay and defence counsel need provide reasonable cooperation, not perpetual availability.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), as interpreted through the framework established in R. v. Morin and R. v. Askov.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use as a new and useful art: new knowledge must be practically applied to achieve a desired commercially useful result, but its implementation need not involve a further inventive step.
BaselineA: Statute — Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, ss. 2 and 36, with s. 41 considered.
CaseB_TestB: Purchaser-assistance test for trafficking: merely incidental assistance rendered solely to a drug purchaser is treated as aiding possession, but a concerted effort to effect the transfer, accompanied by an intention to assist it, constitutes aiding trafficking.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 21(1)(b) and (c), and Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-1, ss. 2, 3(1), and 4(1) and (2), interpreted in light of Poitras v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention under s. 2(c) of the Canadian Bill of Rights requires “some form of compulsory restraint”; a motorist merely complying with a roadside breath demand is not detained and cannot claim denial of counsel as a reasonable excuse for refusal.
BaselineA: Statute: Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(c)(ii)-(iii), read with Criminal Code, ss. 234.1(1)-(2) and 235.
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for civil conspiracy: liability arises where injury to the plaintiff is the defendants’ predominant purpose, or where unlawful conduct is directed toward the plaintiff and the defendants should know that injury is likely to, and does, result; actual damage is required.
BaselineB: Common law, particularly Quinn v. Leathem, Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch, Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd., Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Limited, and Southam Co. Ltd. v. Gouthro.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 13 test barring the incriminating use of prior testimony in other proceedings, including a retrial
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13, interpreted in light of ss. 11(c) and 11(d)
CaseB_TestB: Principled admissibility test for substantive use of a witness's prior inconsistent statement
BaselineB: Common law hearsay principles from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith, replacing the orthodox rule recognized in Deacon v. The King, with the voir dire procedure under s. 9 of the Canada Evidence Act
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Article 68 jurisdiction based on the defendant’s domicile or, failing that, residence
BaselineA: Statute — Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68, with the Canadian Citizenship Act, s. 10 informing the evidentiary assessment of residence and domicile
CaseB_TestB: Framework for considering related state misconduct as a mitigating factor in determining a fit and proportionate sentence
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law — Criminal Code, ss. 718 to 718.2, particularly s. 718.2(a), and Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright reproduction test: a literal physical transfer of an existing image to a new substrate, without multiplication or creation of a new copy or manifestation, is not production or reproduction under s. 3(1); modification without reproduction is governed by moral rights.
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, ss. 2, 3(1), 27(1), 28.2 and 38(1), together with Code of Civil Procedure, art. 734.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter test: after a somewhat probing examination, a reviewing court may intervene only if no tenable line of analysis in the reasons, considered as a whole, could reasonably support the administrative decision.
BaselineB: Common law — the reasonableness standard from Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., selected through the pragmatic and functional approach established in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and elaborated in Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework, including the public-interest weighing test
BaselineA: Statute — Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, ss. 137.1(2)-(4), especially s. 137.1(4)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Purposive, contextual, and pragmatic corporate attribution test for one-person corporations
BaselineB: Common law — the corporate attribution doctrine established and refined in Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen, Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of), Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd., and Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Additional recovery and statutory subrogation where a compensated worker was contributorily at fault
BaselineA: Statute: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) and 8, together with Civil Code arts. 1056 and 1157.
CaseB_TestB: Mandatory independent review of any government change affecting judicial remuneration conditions
BaselineB: Constitutional law: s. 11(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Preamble to the Constitution Act, 1867, as developed in Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory obscenity test for publications: material is obscene where its dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex, and displayed articles accompanied by printed descriptions may constitute publications
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), informed by Brodie v. The Queen
CaseB_TestB: Union duty to take reasonable measures short of undue hardship to accommodate an employee affected by adverse-effect discrimination
BaselineB: Statute and prior jurisprudence — Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, principally s. 8, as interpreted in O'Malley and Central Alberta Dairy Pool
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Paragraph 12 “right of access” test: if the laws in force permit any limited hunting on the land, a right of access exists and Indigenous persons may hunt any game there for food, non-dangerously, “at all seasons of the year,” regardless of provincial seasonal restrictions.
BaselineA: Constitutional statute/agreement: para. 12 of the 1930 Saskatchewan Natural Resources Agreement, confirmed by 1930 Saskatchewan, Canadian, and United Kingdom enactments, as previously interpreted in R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson.
CaseB_TestB: Charter purpose-and-effects validity test: legislative purpose is examined first; an unconstitutional purpose is dispositive, while effects need be considered only if the law passes the purpose inquiry, and effects cannot save a law with an invalid purpose.
BaselineB: Constitutional statute: ss. 1 and 2(a) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, informed by Hunter v. Southam Inc. and distinguished from Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional and structural test for whether a court or tribunal has power to grant a Charter remedy under s. 24
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text and common law: Charter s. 24(1), the tribunal's enabling legislation (here, Provincial Offences Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.33), and the three-part court-of-competent-jurisdiction test from Mills v. The Queen, as developed in Weber v. Ontario Hydro and Mooring v. Canada (National Parole Board).
CaseB_TestB: Three-stage framework for the honest-belief-in-legal-age defence and reasonable-steps requirement in child-luring prosecutions
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 172.1(1), (3), and (4), informed by the prior interpretation in R. v. Levigne and constrained by Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sufficient nexus with the employment context test for discrimination “regarding employment”
BaselineA: Statute: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, principally ss. 1, 3 and 13(1)(b)
CaseB_TestB: Context-specific test for when in-court incivility amounts to professional misconduct
BaselineB: Regulation and statute: the Professional Conduct Handbook and Rules of Professional Conduct made under the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8, particularly former rr. 2.01, 4.01(1), 4.01(6) and 6.03(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol notice test: a carrier may invoke Article 22 only upon exact compliance, and the required notice must be in a form calculated to attract attention.
BaselineA: Statute: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14, incorporating the Hague Protocol, especially arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c) and 22.
CaseB_TestB: Post-severance breathalyzer-presumption rebuttal test: the accused must raise a reasonable doubt that the approved instrument malfunctioned or was operated improperly; Carter consumption evidence alone cannot do so.
BaselineB: Statute and Constitution: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), 258(1)(d.01) and 258(1)(d.1), assessed under Charter ss. 7, 11(c), 11(d) and 1.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant-purpose test for exemption from compelled testimony: determine whether the evidence is sought primarily to incriminate the witness or to advance a legitimate public purpose; if the former is established, the compelling party must justify the resulting prejudice, and significant prejudice jeopardizing a fair trial makes the witness non-compellable.
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 13, and the self-incrimination framework from R. v. S. (R.J.), applied to compulsion under s. 128(1) of the British Columbia Securities Act.
CaseB_TestB: Section 15(1) prima facie adverse-effects discrimination test: the claimant must show that a law creates a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground and imposes disproportionate, arbitrary disadvantage, supported by evidence linking the law to the disparate impact.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), and the substantive-equality framework articulated in Quebec (Attorney General) v. A, Withler v. Canada (Attorney General), R. v. Kapp, and Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Conspiracy to prevent or lessen competition unduly: the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt an intended agreement that, if carried into effect, would unduly prevent or lessen competition in the relevant market.
BaselineA: Statute: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c), informed by Howard Smith Paper Mills Ltd. v. The Queen, Weidman v. Shragge, Stinson-Reeb Builders Supply Co. v. The King, and Container Materials Ltd. v. The King.
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable-verdict appellate review: whether a properly instructed trier of fact could reasonably have rendered the verdict, including whether an essential finding is plainly contradicted by or incompatible with the evidence; credibility findings are reviewable only if unsupported on any reasonable view of the evidence.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i), as interpreted in R. v. Yebes, R. v. Biniaris, R. v. Sinclair, R. v. Beaudry, and R. v. Burke.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid consent to interception: consent must be knowing and voluntary—an intended, conscious act resulting from the consenter’s own decision and free from external coercion; promised or expected leniency alone does not vitiate consent.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, s. 178.11(2)(a), read with s. 178.16(1)(a) (Part IV.1).
CaseB_TestB: Proof that hate speech targeted the particularized identifiable group: the court must determine beyond a reasonable doubt, from the totality of the evidence and appropriate inferences, whether the accused’s statements targeted the named group; lexical interchangeability is unnecessary.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 318(4) and 319(2), as previously interpreted in R. v. Keegstra.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Separate-informations rule: a trial judge lacks jurisdiction to try separate informations or indictments together, even with consent, unless governing legislation expressly provides otherwise.
BaselineA: Combination of common law (Crane v. Public Prosecutor) and statute: the rule is incorporated by implication into the Criminal Code and applies under New Brunswick's Summary Convictions Act absent an express contrary provision.
CaseB_TestB: Framework governing the use of absence of motive to lie and lack of embellishment in assessing a complainant's credibility.
BaselineB: Common law credibility principles, particularly R. v. Stirling, together with the burden-of-proof framework in R. v. W.(D.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR abusive tax avoidance test for preserving and transferring partnership losses to arm’s-length taxpayers
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 18(13), 96(1), 245(1)-(4) and 248(10), informed by Canada Trustco Mortgage Co. v. Canada, 2005 SCC 54
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage Vancouver Sun procedure for protecting informer privilege while minimizing impairment of the open court principle
BaselineB: Common law — Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43, supplemented by the common law rules governing informer privilege and court openness
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Provincial inquiry jurisdiction test: a province may inquire into criminal acts committed by members of a federal agency, but may not, under the guise of that inquiry, investigate the agency's administration or management
BaselineA: Constitutional and statutory: British North America Act, ss. 91 and 92(14), and Quebec's Public Inquiry Commission Act, informed by Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, Faber v. The Queen, and the doctrine of colourability
CaseB_TestB: Paramount-welfare-of-the-child test for contested custody: consider all relevant factors and choose the course best serving the child's overall welfare, with parental claims subordinated where necessary
BaselineB: Combination of statute and equity/common law: Domestic Relations Ordinance, ss. 37 and 39, and the parens patriae authorities Re Moores and Feldstein, Beson v. Director of Child Welfare, and Racine v. Woods
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law defence of necessity based on moral involuntariness, requiring imminent peril, no reasonable legal alternative, and proportionality
BaselineA: Common law necessity doctrine, preserved by s. 7(3) of the Criminal Code and previously addressed in Morgentaler v. The Queen, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 616.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy test for online communications with an unknown child during a police-created sting
BaselineB: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework stated in R. v. Marakah, R. v. Cole, R. v. Spencer, R. v. Tessling, and related cases.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant-purpose test for exemption from compelled testimony
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional text and common law: ss. 7 and 13 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, informed principally by R. v. S. (R.J.), and applied to s. 128(1) of the British Columbia Securities Act.
CaseB_TestB: Timing and procedure for deciding a Corbett application
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: s. 12 of the Canada Evidence Act as interpreted in R. v. Corbett, together with the common law case-to-meet principle protected by s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory Fund payment upon a compliant application, without prior exhaustion of remedies against the insurer
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39.
CaseB_TestB: Fatal Accidents Act dependency-damages calculation using net lost support, present-value capitalization, inflation-adjusted discounting, taxation, and contingencies
BaselineB: Statute and common-law damages principles: The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164, with the prior approaches in Gehrmann v. Lavoie and The Queen v. Jennings reconsidered or distinguished.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion under s. 52 to depart from automatic judgment-interest accrual where the circumstances make intervention appropriate
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. S-19, s. 52; Interest Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-18, ss. 13-14; and Supreme Court Rule 61
CaseB_TestB: Procedural fairness for Governor in Council decisions under s. 64(1): construe the statutory scheme as a whole; no hearing is required for this legislative function, and review is confined to compliance with statutory boundaries
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, s. 64(1), interpreted against the procedural-fairness principles in Nicholson v. Haldimand-Norfolk Regional Board of Commissioners of Police and Martineau v. Matsqui Institution (No. 2)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory owner and requesting-owner test for mechanics’ lien liability
BaselineA: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, principally ss. 1(1)(d) and 5(1), read with ss. 7 and 11
CaseB_TestB: Realistic potential for juror partiality test for a challenge for cause
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b), Charter s. 11(d), and the common law framework from R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exclusive statutory obscenity test for publications: material is obscene where its dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex; publicly displayed articles accompanied by explanatory descriptions may constitute “publications”.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), informed by Brodie v. The Queen, which held the statutory obscenity test exclusive for publications.
CaseB_TestB: Individualized reasonable-accommodation test for applying a collectively negotiated termination-of-employment clause: the negotiated absence period is significant but not determinative, and undue hardship must be assessed globally from the beginning of the absence.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: ss. 10 and 20 of Quebec’s Charter of human rights and freedoms and the Meiorin reasonable-accommodation framework, applied in the context of the collective agreement.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith-basis test for cross-examining a witness about unproven facts
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. Bencardino (drawing on Fox v. General Medical Council) and reaffirmed in R. v. Shearing; informed by Charter ss. 7 and 11(d).
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy test for operational conflict or frustration of federal purpose

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment honest-belief test for republishers: each publisher relying on the defence must prove that the comment was an honest expression of the opinion it published.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable and probable grounds for warrantless arrest require consideration of all available information; information may be disregarded only for good reason as unreliable.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of financial obligations imposed on fully paid shareholders: an amendment is invalid if it imposes “any financial burden whatsoever” on a shareholder in respect of fully paid shares.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: The Companies Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 60, ss. 2(1)(10), 15(1), 16(c), 42(1), 68(4) and 193(1)(d), the memorandum of association, and the limited-liability principle reflected in Ooregum Gold Mining Co. of India v. Roper, Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates Ltd. and Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co. Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for an Aboriginal right to exchange fish: precisely characterize the claimed activity, then determine whether, before European contact, it was a “central, significant or defining feature” integral to the distinctive culture of the claimant group.

CaseA_TestA: Proof of breach of the municipal sewer-servicing covenant requires evidence of an existing or foreseeably imminent inadequacy in the project’s sewer service, including a demonstrated connection between any general planning report and the project’s serviceability.

CaseA_TestA: Four-factor test for whether an administrative decision must be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis under s. 28 of the Federal Court Act
BaselineA: Statute and common law: ss. 2 and 28 of the Federal Court Act, interpreted against common-law natural justice principles.
CaseB_TestB: Stillman trial-fairness framework for excluding conscriptive evidence under Charter s. 24(2)
BaselineB: Constitutional text and precedent: s. 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Collins exclusion-of-evidence framework.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea upon proof of trafficking in a restricted drug, displaced only by evidence raising a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 and 42, informed by Beaver v. The Queen, R. v. Blondin, and The Queen v. King.
CaseB_TestB: Whether a trial judge's interventions, assessed in their manner and context, create doubt about impartiality such that justice is not seen to be done
BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy and R. v. Darlyn, with guidance from Jones v. National Coal Board, R. v. Torbiak and Campbell, Yuill v. Yuill, and R. v. Bateman.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trustee’s duty to preserve or replace insurance on all insurable property, including hypothecated property, and to notify the secured creditor if insurance cannot be obtained

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

BaselineA: Constitutional text—Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8 and 32(1)—as previously interpreted in Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Terry

Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board, informed for the government claim by the Mining Safety Act, especially ss. 42-43, and the Mining Safety Regulations
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a factual finding supporting an acquittal constitutes an error of law permitting a Crown appeal

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a factual finding supporting an acquittal constitutes an appealable question of law alone: only where the legal burden has shifted to the accused and there is no evidence to the contrary

CaseB_TestB: Section 65.1 interim-release test: a serious question, irreparable harm, and a balance of convenience favouring the applicant
BaselineB: Combination of Supreme Court Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-26, ss. 65 and 65.1, and the stay criteria reaffirmed in RJR—MacDonald Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Application of retrospective legislation during an SCC appeal: legislation applicable to suits pending before a court may be applied where it supports dismissal of the appeal, because s. 47 does not limit the grounds on which the Court may dismiss an appeal.

CaseB_TestB: Extradition-refusal test: the person sought must show that surrender would “shock the conscience” and violate Charter s. 7, or would be “unjust or oppressive” under s. 44(1) of the Extradition Act, assessed in light of all relevant circumstances.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional and statutory law — s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and s. 44(1) of the Extradition Act, informed by United States v. Burns and Argentina v. Mellino.

CaseA_TestA: Autonomous exemplary-damages test under s. 49(2) of the Quebec Charter: an unlawful and intentional interference is required, but compensatory damages are unnecessary outside public compensation systems, and denunciation alone may justify an award.

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for accepted services where no remuneration was agreed: the recipient must pay a reasonable rate

CaseA_TestA: Workers’ compensation entitlement exclusion: an insured is “entitled to receive benefits” once the facts establishing statutory entitlement exist, regardless of whether a formal claim has been made or approved

CaseB_TestB: Section 8 reasonableness test for cross-border disclosure of lawfully intercepted wiretap information

CaseA_TestA: Effect of a worker’s compensation election: upon election, subrogation occurs automatically; only the Commission may claim the compensation portion, while the worker may claim only the additional loss, and the worker’s overclaim neither creates an interest to intervene nor interrupts prescription for the Commission

CaseB_TestB: Collins three-category test for excluding evidence under Charter s. 24(2), emphasizing the seriousness and cumulative effect of Charter violations and the long-term consequences of admission or exclusion
BaselineB: Constitutional provision and precedent: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), as structured in R. v. Collins and Simmons, with the underlying violations arising under ss. 8 and 10
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Temporal limit on the Canadian Transport Commission’s authority to extend notice or postpone the effective date of a freight tariff
BaselineA: Statute: Railway Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. R-2, ss. 275(2) and 275(4), read with National Transportation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-17, ss. 3(a) and 64(5)
CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on a criminal appeal
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 683, and Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mental disorder test for incapacity to know an act was wrong: whether, at the time of the act, the disorder deprived the accused of the capacity to rationally assess the particular act against ordinary public standards of right and wrong
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 16(1), informed by R. v. Chaulk and the M'Naghten Rules
CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on an appeal from sentence: due diligence, relevance, credibility, and a reasonable expectation that the evidence could have affected the result
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 683 and 687, and the four criteria established in Palmer v. The Queen
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Collective-agreement exclusivity and illegal-strike continuity rule: while a collective agreement remains in force and the duty to bargain collectively subsists, common law repudiation and fundamental breach are inapplicable, and an unlawful strike does not by itself terminate employment; the employer must take positive disciplinary or discharge action.
BaselineA: Combination of statute, collective agreement, and prior common law: Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), ss. 6, 8 and 23; the Labour Relations Act; arts. VII and XX of the collective agreement; and Syndicat catholique des employés de magasins de Québec Inc. v. Compagnie Paquet Ltée, Re Polymer Corp. and Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers International Union, and C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri.
CaseB_TestB: Test for restricting defence cross-examination using evidence already possessed: relevant cross-examination may be excluded only where its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs its probative value; an omitted diary entry is probative only if there is a reasonable expectation that the omitted matter would have been recorded.
BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. Seaboyer and R. v. Osolin. The Court clarified that the production framework in R. v. O’Connor and Criminal Code ss. 278.1 to 278.9 does not govern the admissibility or use in cross-examination of a record already possessed by the defence.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reverse-onus compatibility test under the presumption of innocence: an accused may be required to prove an essential fact on a balance of probabilities only if it is rationally open to proof or disproof and the accused can reasonably be expected to prove it; for lawful importation, the Crown must first show knowledge or means of knowledge enabling the accused to discharge that burden.
BaselineA: Combination of statutes and precedent: ss. 205(1), 205(3), and 248(1) of the Customs Act and s. 2(f) of the Canadian Bill of Rights, building on R. v. Appleby.
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party test for bargaining-unit investigations: under ss. 32 and 39 of the Quebec Labour Code, the employer and concerned employee associations constitute the exhaustive class of interested parties, so an individual employee has no right to attend, intervene, call or cross-examine witnesses, or make representations.
BaselineB: Statute, principally ss. 32 and 39 of the Quebec Labour Code, interpreted contextually with ss. 25, 28, 43, 59, and 129 and the administrative-law principle that an interested party ordinarily has rights to attend and be heard.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Public-interest test for disclosure of compelled OSC material: balance the respondent’s full-answer-and-defence interests against third-party privacy and confidentiality, and disclose only what is necessary to carry out the OSC’s statutory mandate.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and regulation—Ontario Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16 and 17(1), and OSC Rules of Practice, rr. 3.3(2) and 3.7—supplemented by the common law relevance standard from R. v. Stinchcombe.
CaseB_TestB: Two-question framework for classifying records as first-party or third-party criminal disclosure: ask whether the prosecuting Crown possesses or controls the information, or whether another Crown entity ought to have supplied it because it is a fruit of the investigation or obviously relevant; an affirmative answer to either question triggers first-party disclosure, otherwise the third-party regime applies.
BaselineB: Common law disclosure regimes established in R. v. Stinchcombe and R. v. O’Connor and supplemented by R. v. McNeil, applied in the statutory context of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 258(1)(c).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Applicability of the Criminal Code search-warrant power to offences under any federal statute, whether or not that statute has its own search-and-seizure provisions

CaseB_TestB: “Risks willingly assumed” test: the visitor must assume both the physical risk and the legal risk by consenting to waive recourse against the occupier

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Priority rule for provincial Crown tax claims under Bankruptcy Act s. 107(1)(j): such claims rank pari passu notwithstanding a provincially created statutory privilege
BaselineA: Statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 2, 107(1)(j) and 107(3), read with Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, s. 30 and Civil Code art. 1989.
CaseB_TestB: Flexible three-factor test for discretionary public interest standing

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable foreseeability for highway-authority liability: whether a reasonable person should have anticipated the class or character of injury as a natural result, without foreseeing the precise sequence of events
BaselineA: Common law foreseeability from University Hospital Board v. Lépine and Overseas Tankship (U.K.) Ltd. v. Miller Steamship Co. Pty. (Wagon Mound No. 2), applied in the context of s. 33(1) of the Highway Improvement Act, R.S.O. 1960
CaseB_TestB: Environmental-assessment tracking and scoping: the assessment track is determined by the project as proposed; if it is listed in the Comprehensive Study List, a comprehensive study is mandatory, and the responsible authority may enlarge but not reduce its scope
BaselineB: Canadian Environmental Assessment Act, S.C. 1992, c. 37, especially ss. 2, 15, 18 and 21, together with s. 3 and Schedule s. 16 of the Comprehensive Study List Regulations, SOR/94-638

CaseA_TestA: Section 10(b) implementation-duty trigger: absent evidence that the detainee did not understand the right to counsel, police duties beyond promptly informing the detainee arise only when the detainee indicates a desire to exercise the right; the detainee bears the onus of proving that a request or opportunity was denied.

CaseB_TestB: Employee disgorgement for abuse of position: an employee who obtains profits through a breach of contractual good faith and loyalty must account for and turn those profits over to the employer, with the intensity of the obligation increasing according to the employee's responsibility, trust, and authority.
BaselineB: Civil Code of Lower Canada, principally arts. 411 and 1713, together with the civil-law obligation of good faith and loyalty in employment contracts.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Informed-layperson test for whether a substance is produced by a “chemical process” under s. 41(1) of the Patent Act

CaseB_TestB: Test for whether a proven conspiracy falls within the scope of the conspiracy charged in an indictment

CaseA_TestA: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown remarks: a trial judge must comment where the remarks are “prejudicial to a degree sufficient” to require intervention so that the defence is fairly put to the jury.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-limit test for groundwater pumping: in a negligence or nuisance action, a landowner's pumping right is no defence for pumping exceeding the quantity authorized by law or permit
BaselineA: Combination of common law nuisance and negligence principles and s. 37 of The Ontario Water Resources Commission Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 332
CaseB_TestB: Assessment of solatium doloris based on the circumstances of the death, the parties' ages, their relationship, the parent's personality and coping ability, and the death's effect on the parent's life, among other factors

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estate-tax “passing on death” test for community property subject to a complete survivorship clause
BaselineA: Estate Tax Act, 1958, ss. 3(1)(a), 3(2)(a) and (e), and 58(1)(i), interpreted with the civil-law doctrine of retroactive ownership and the decisions in Sura v. Minister of National Revenue and Royal Trust Co. v. Minister of National Revenue.
CaseB_TestB: “Visible, incompatible land use” test for Treaty No. 8 hunting access to privately owned land
