CaseA_TestA: Public access to executed search warrants and supporting informations: access is presumed after execution when objects are seized and brought before a justice, subject to overriding interests of superordinate importance
BaselineA: Common-law open-court principle, applied to the search-warrant regime under ss. 443 and 446 of the Criminal Code
CaseB_TestB: Two-branch bona fide occupational qualification test: the requirement must be imposed honestly and in good faith, and must be objectively reasonably necessary to accomplish the employment's legitimate objectives
BaselineB: Section 8 of the British Columbia Human Rights Code, informed by the two-branch test from Ontario Human Rights Commission v. Etobicoke (Borough of)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseB_TestB: Collateral immigration consequences may be considered in sentencing only within the range of fit, proportionate sentences, with their weight determined from the circumstances of the particular case

BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 10(b), as interpreted in R. v. Brydges, R. v. Bartle, and R. v. Prosper
CaseB_TestB: Test for whether a late-payment penalty constitutes criminal-rate interest

CaseB_TestB: Sherman three-part test for discretionary limits on the open court principle

Quebec (Commission d’appel en matière de lésions professionnelles) and the pragmatic and functional approach from U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault, informed by the presumption of legislative coherence and an analogy to constitutional paramountcy.

CaseB_TestB: Interest deductibility test: whether, considering all the circumstances, the taxpayer had a reasonable expectation of taxable income when the investment was made

CaseB_TestB: Youth-appeal advertising test under s. 22(3): the prosecution must prove reasonable grounds to believe that the advertisement could be particularly attractive and of interest to young persons, as distinguished from the general population.
BaselineB: Statute: Tobacco Act, ss. 4(b) and 22(2)-(4), interpreted in light of ss. 1 and 2(b) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Separate-mine test under s. 83(5): a mine exists where a body of ore has workings, equipment and machinery capable of producing it, and a separate ore body becomes a separate mine when extracted through separate and distinct extraction facilities; shared processing facilities are irrelevant.
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 148, ss. 83(5) and 83(6), interpreted in light of North Bay Mica Co. Ltd. v. M.N.R. and M.N.R. v. MacLean Mining Co. Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Mancini test for leave under s. 215 BIA: leave should be granted where the evidence discloses a prima facie factual basis and cause of action; only frivolous, vexatious, manifestly unmeritorious, or factually unsupported claims are screened out, without deciding the merits.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and precedent: s. 215 of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act and the test established in Mancini (Bankrupt) v. Falconi.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Article 1053 civil-law occupier-fault and trap test: an intrinsically dangerous, hidden, abnormal or surprising condition assessed contextually, without common-law entrant categories.
BaselineA: Civil Code of Lower Canada, art. 1053, informed by Quebec civil-law jurisprudence.
CaseB_TestB: Unified operating-mind or limited cognitive capacity test for confessions, the right to silence, and exercising or waiving the right to counsel.
BaselineB: Combination of the common-law operating-mind doctrine in Ward, Horvath, Nagotcha and Hebert; Charter ss. 7 and 10(b); and the fitness standard codified in Criminal Code s. 2.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Deduction of wage benefits from damages for lost earnings, subject to subrogation and limited trust exceptions
BaselineA: Common law compensatory and collateral-benefits principles from Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Thornton v. Prince George School Board, Arnold v. Teno, and Parry v. Cleaver.
CaseB_TestB: Necessarily incidental test for federal legislation intruding on provincial jurisdiction
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(3) and 92(13), as interpreted through the ancillary-powers framework in General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. City National Leasing and Reference re Exported Natural Gas Tax.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario Municipal Board jurisdiction to make equitable asset-and-liability adjustments under incorporated statutory powers
BaselineA: Statute: The Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 407, ss. 135 and 137, incorporating The Municipal Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 284, s. 14(11)(a), (b) and (d).
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt of subjective foresight of death for murder
BaselineB: Combination of statute and precedent: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d), applied to Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 213(a), building on R. v. Vaillancourt.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Whole-process test for legislative instruments: if the net effect of a series of discrete acts is legislative, each component act is legislative and subject to s. 133 bilingualism requirements.
BaselineA: Constitutional statute: s. 133 of the Constitution Act, 1867, as interpreted in the Reference re Manitoba Language Rights decisions and Quebec (Attorney General) v. Brunet.
CaseB_TestB: Responsive-answer test when a jury asks for clarification about reasonable doubt: the trial judge must attempt to answer the question and must not discourage further questions.
BaselineB: Common law: the jury-instruction principles established in R. v. Lifchus and R. v. S. (W.D.), with the reasonable-doubt formulation further explained in R. v. Starr.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 74 whistleblower protection: “lawful authority” includes public enforcement authorities and persons within the employer organization who have lawful authority over the complained-of employees or activity.
BaselineA: Statute — The Labour Standards Act, R.S.S. 1978, c. L-1, s. 74(1)(a), interpreted in light of The Interpretation Act, 1995, S.S. 1995, c. I-11.2, s. 10.
CaseB_TestB: Two-part Clunas joinder test: the charges must share a sufficient factual nexus, and a joint trial must be in the interests of justice based on a weighing of its costs and benefits.
BaselineB: Combination of common law and statute — the joinder test established in R. v. Clunas, applied alongside the Criminal Code and Ontario’s Provincial Offences Act, particularly ss. 2(1) and 47(1) of the latter.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal test: the Crown must satisfy the court that the verdict would not necessarily have been the same absent the trial judge's legal error.
BaselineA: Statute and precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4), as interpreted in White v. R. and R. v. Gauthier.
CaseB_TestB: Group defamation personal-injury test: whether an ordinary person, considering all the circumstances and non-exhaustive contextual factors, would believe that each group member personally sustained reputational damage.
BaselineB: Statute and civil law precedent: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 1457, 1607 and 1611; Quebec Charter, ss. 4 and 49; Code of Civil Procedure provisions governing sufficient interest and class actions; and the ordinary-person test from Prud’homme v. Prud’homme and Gilles E. Néron Communication Marketing Inc. v. Chambre des notaires du Québec.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for whether tangible or intangible subject matter is “anything” capable of theft: it must be property capable of being taken or converted in a way that deprives the owner of a proprietary interest.
BaselineA: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 283(1), informed by R. v. Scallen and R. v. Hardy.
CaseB_TestB: Test for whether an interest in a Henson trust is an “asset” under a means-tested assistance program: interpret “assets” objectively in the specific program and contractual context, asking whether the interest can actually be used to discharge the applicant’s debts and liabilities.
BaselineB: Common law principles of contractual interpretation and trust law, particularly Sattva Capital Corp. v. Creston Moly Corp., Ontario v. Henson, and the rule in Saunders v. Vautier, applied to the Tenancy Agreement and Assistance Application.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for amending an indictment to correct a variance between a narcotic particular and the evidence: amendment is available unless it would cause irreparable prejudice or injustice to the accused.
BaselineA: Statute — Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2 and 4 and Schedule item 3; Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) and 613(1)(b)(i) and (3).
CaseB_TestB: Two-part ineffective-assistance-of-counsel test: the appellant must show both counsel's incompetence and a resulting miscarriage of justice.
BaselineB: Common law — R. v. G.D.B., 2000 SCC 22, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 520.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Proper construction of a contractual warranty using the distinct technical meanings of “depreciation” and “capital cost allowance”
BaselineA: Common-law contractual interpretation applied to paragraph 3(g) of the sale agreement and the incorporated auditor’s letter.
CaseB_TestB: Clear legislative intention test for displacing prosecutorial discretion under the Young Offenders Act
BaselineB: Combination of common-law prosecutorial discretion and ss. 3(1), 3(2), 19(1)-(2), 20(1)(a), and 51 of the Young Offenders Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. Y-1.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence to establish guilty intent: such evidence may be admitted when relevant to intent, including whether the charged conduct was designed or accidental, but not merely to prove disposition or commission of the charged offence.
BaselineA: Common law—Makin v. Attorney-General for New South Wales, as developed in Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and R. v. Wray.
CaseB_TestB: Exceptional-property valuation test: when special circumstances make the usual valuation methods impossible to apply, whatever method is appropriate in the circumstances may be used to estimate the property's actual value.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law—the Charter of the City of Montreal's actual-value requirement and appeal provisions in ss. 873-874, interpreted through Sun Life Assurance Co. of Canada v. City of Montreal and related valuation cases.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “burglary” under the constructive-murder provision: the statutory offence defined in the 1892 Criminal Code, requiring a dwelling-house and nighttime breaking
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, ss. 213 and 306; Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, s. 36(f); and Criminal Code, 1892, ss. 228, 410 and 407.
CaseB_TestB: Damages for repudiation of a contract with alternative modes of performance: adopt the mode least profitable to the plaintiff and least burdensome to the defendant
BaselineB: Common law: Cockburn v. Alexander, as explained in Withers v. General Theatre Corp. and adopted in Canadian decisions including Park v. Parsons Brown & Co. and Aldo Ippolito & Co. v. Canada Packers Inc.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Immovable-by-nature test: a structure is immovable when it adheres directly or indirectly to land or another immovable structure and thereby acquires a fixed foundation; common ownership or functional complementarity is unnecessary.
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code arts. 374 et seq., especially arts. 375-376, applied through the Retail Sales Tax Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 71, ss. 2(3) and 6; informed by Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated v. City of Westmount and Lower St. Lawrence Power Co. v. L’Immeuble Landry Ltée.
CaseB_TestB: Punitive damages for breach of contract: the plaintiff must establish an actionable wrong causing the complained-of injury and extreme conduct deserving punishment as harsh, vindictive, reprehensible or malicious.
BaselineB: Common law punitive-damages principles from Rookes v. Barnard, McElroy v. Cowper-Smith and Woodman, H. L. Weiss Forwarding Ltd. v. Omnus, and related Canadian jurisprudence.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 93 test for whether legislation prejudicially affects a historically protected denominational-school right or privilege
BaselineA: Constitutional statute: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 93(1)-(2), read with the denominational-school rights conferred by the pre-Confederation education legislation, particularly ss. 24(1), 55(2), 57(3), 73, 74 and 131 of the 1861 Act.
CaseB_TestB: Integral-connection and practical-necessity test for determining whether an activity falls within federal maritime law
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional statute and common law: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(10) and 92(13), and the maritime-jurisdiction principles established in ITO — International Terminal Operators Ltd. v. Miida Electronics Inc., Whitbread v. Walley, and Ordon Estate v. Grail.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Pleadings-based potential-coverage test for an insurer's duty to defend
BaselineA: Insurance policy wording and common-law insurance principles, including the pleadings rule reflected in Bacon v. McBride and the potential-coverage principle reflected in Prudential Life Insurance Co. v. Manitoba Public Insurance Corp.
CaseB_TestB: Test for permitting cross-examination of a sexual-assault complainant on medical records: the evidence must serve a legitimate purpose, and its probative value must not be substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice, with rape-myth reasoning excluded and fair-trial rights balanced against protection of the complainant
BaselineB: Common-law evidence principles, particularly R. v. Seaboyer, informed by Criminal Code s. 276 and Charter ss. 7, 11(d), 15 and 28.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step test for post-conviction Crown non-disclosure: whether there is a reasonable possibility that the undisclosed information affected the conviction’s reliability or, alternatively, the overall fairness of the trial process, including realistic lost investigative opportunities and defence diligence
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 24(1), building on R. v. Stinchcombe, R. v. C. (M.H.), R. v. Carosella and R. v. Collins
CaseB_TestB: Standard-form insurance interpretation: give unambiguous policy language its ordinary meaning as understood by the average insured; a “policy of insurance” means a private insurance contract and excludes the statutory CPP regime
BaselineB: Common law principles of standard-form insurance contract interpretation from Ledcor Construction Ltd. v. Northbridge Indemnity Insurance Co., Progressive Homes Ltd. v. Lombard General Insurance Co. of Canada, Non-Marine Underwriters, Lloyd’s of London v. Scalera and Co-operators Life Insurance Co. v. Gibbens, applied to cl. 4(b)(vii) of the SEF 44 Endorsement
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Substantial-alteration test for distinguishing a bargaining-unit review under s. 119 from a new certification application
BaselineA: Statute—Canada Labour Code, s. 119 and ss. 124 et seq., informed by the Board's three-category framework in The Employees of the Regional Comptroller and the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers
CaseB_TestB: Palpable and overriding error test for appellate intervention in findings based on the evidence as a whole
BaselineB: Common law—Schreiber Brothers Limited v. Currie Products Limited and Gulf Oil Canada Limited; Stein v. "Kathy K."; and Lewis v. Todd
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-step harm-based test for criminal indecency: the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt both significant harm or risk of harm threatening a formally endorsed value and harm incompatible with society’s proper functioning.
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 210(1), and the common-law indecency framework from R. v. Butler, as developed in the companion case R. v. Labaye.
CaseB_TestB: Pointe Gourde scope-of-scheme test: whether an enactment was made with a view to expropriation or was an independent enactment, assessed through its purposes and effects.
BaselineB: Combination of Expropriation Act, R.S.N.L. 1990, c. E-19, s. 27(1)(a), and the common-law Pointe Gourde principle from Pointe Gourde Quarrying and Transport Co. v. Sub-Intendent of Crown Lands.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory tribunal test: whether the parties must resort to the tribunal by statute or, once arbitration is chosen, the tribunal is invested with wide statutory duties and powers
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: R. v. National Joint Council for the Craft of Dental Technicians, as adopted in Howe Sound and Port Arthur; applied through art. 846 C.C.P. and Canada Labour Code, ss. 156, 157, 159 and 160(5).
CaseB_TestB: Sublicence test: whether the licensee expressly or impliedly granted a third party the independent right to do something otherwise prohibited and permitted to the licensee only by its licence
BaselineB: Common law principles of licensing, sublicensing, and contractual interpretation, applied to the compulsory licence issued under the former Patent Act, s. 39(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Clear-legislative-intent exception to the Kienapple rule: Criminal Code s. 83 permits separate convictions for robbery and firearm use arising from the same event.
BaselineA: Combination of the common law rule against multiple convictions from Kienapple v. The Queen and Cox and Paton v. The Queen, and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 83(1)-(2).
CaseB_TestB: Two-step interjurisdictional immunity test: determine whether a measure trenches on the core of another government's power and, if so, whether its effect is sufficiently serious to constitute impairment.
BaselineB: Common law constitutional doctrine established in Canadian Western Bank v. Alberta and Quebec (Attorney General) v. Canadian Owners and Pilots Association, grounded in the Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(29) and 92(10)(a), and applied by analogy from Toronto Corporation v. Bell Telephone Co. of Canada.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Area-based bona fide inquiry branch of the entrapment and random virtue-testing test
BaselineA: Common law — the entrapment test established in R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention threshold for a trial judge’s voluntariness and admissibility ruling
BaselineB: Common law appellate review standard; no originating precedent is cited in the decision
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation: words or conduct must induce detrimental reliance; silence or inaction is a representation only where there is a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law estoppel by representation, including Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd. and Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha v. Dawson’s Bank, Ltd., with Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 14.04 governing pleading
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the statutory presumption of living on the avails of prostitution by considering all evidence, without isolating a particular and severable item of evidence to the contrary
BaselineB: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Refined three-stage Residential Tenancies test for whether provincial conferral of adjudicative jurisdiction contravenes s. 96
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: s. 96 of the Constitution Act, 1867 and the three-stage framework established in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979
CaseB_TestB: Flexible, cumulative three-factor test for public interest standing, including the sufficient-factual-setting inquiry
BaselineB: Common law: the public interest standing framework established in Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional approach and rough upper limit for non-pecuniary personal-injury damages: awards provide reasonable solace tailored to the victim, but are capped at $100,000 save in rare exceptional circumstances or for proven inflation
BaselineA: Common law: Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Arnold v. Teno, and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57 (Prince George), as refined in Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: Inadequately insured motorist coverage test: the tortfeasor must be at fault as a motorist, and an unbroken chain of causation—more than incidental, fortuitous, or merely 'but for'—must link that conduct to the injuries, without a severable intervening act
BaselineB: Combination of statute and insurance policy: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a), and s. 3 of Ontario Policy Change Form 44R, informed but distinguished from the test in Amos v. Insurance Corp. of British Columbia
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single-cause-of-action test for characterizing damages as contractual or delictual for prescription
BaselineA: Quebec civil law: Civil Code arts. 2242 and 2261(2), informed by Vézina v. Corporation de la Ville de Mégantic, Pilon v. Samson, and Larichelière v. Hôpital Sainte Jeanne d’Arc de Montréal.
CaseB_TestB: Priority-of-registration test for a mechanic’s lien and a mortgage where statutory priority provisions do not govern
BaselineB: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, particularly ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21 and 22, together with The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unified three-step bona fide occupational requirement (Meiorin) test: the employer must prove a rationally job-connected purpose, an honest and good-faith belief in the standard's necessity, and reasonable necessity, including impossibility of accommodation without undue hardship.
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1)(a)-(b) and 13(4), building on the workplace-discrimination tests in O'Malley, Etobicoke, Central Alberta Dairy Pool, Brossard, Saskatoon, Large, and Renaud.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage source-of-income test: determine whether the activity is pursued for profit or is personal, and, if it is not personal, classify the source as business or property; clearly commercial activities without a personal element are sources without further inquiry.
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Income Tax Act, ss. 3(a), 9(1)-(2), 18(1)(a), 18(1)(h), 20(1)(c)(i), 67 and 248(1), together with the reasonable-expectation-of-profit approach from Moldowan v. The Queen, which the Court restricted and replaced as a stand-alone source test.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal criminal law power test: a valid criminal law must contain a prohibition backed by a penalty, pursue a legitimate criminal public purpose, and not be colourable; the prohibited conduct may be ancillary to a lawful activity and need not reflect a traditional crime.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(27), as interpreted in Reference re Validity of Section 5(a) of the Dairy Industry Act (Margarine Reference), Scowby v. Glendinning, and related criminal-law-power jurisprudence.
CaseB_TestB: Assessment of a collectively negotiated termination clause under the duty to accommodate: the negotiated absence period is a significant but non-determinative factor, accommodation must be individualized, and undue hardship must be assessed globally from the beginning of the absence.
BaselineB: Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20, together with the accommodation framework established in British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU (Meiorin) and related jurisprudence.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory accomplice-evidence caution for testimony from an accessory after the fact
BaselineA: Common-law rule of practice governing uncorroborated accomplice evidence, as stated in Davies v. Director of Public Prosecutions and accepted in Horsburgh v. The Queen, with R. v. Riezebos extending it to accessories after the fact.
CaseB_TestB: Section 212(c) unlawful-object murder framework requiring an indictable mens rea object, actual knowledge of the relevant circumstances, and objective foresight of likely death
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Equitable interest for improper withholding of a just debt, measured by the creditor’s borrowing rate
BaselineA: Combination of statute and precedent: s. 46 of The Queen’s Bench Act, ss. 3, 12 and 13 of the Interest Act, and s. 52 of the Supreme Court Act, informed by Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto and The Custodian v. Blucher.
CaseB_TestB: Two-step test for whether post-conviction non-disclosure impaired the right to make full answer and defence
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and precedent: ss. 7 and 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, as developed in R. v. Stinchcombe, R. v. Egger, R. v. Carosella, R. v. C. (M.H.) and R. v. Collins.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Recent possession jury-instruction test where no explanation is in evidence: once possession of recently stolen goods is proved, it raises a prima facie case permitting conviction; the instruction should omit the phrase “in the absence of any reasonable explanation” when no explanation has been advanced.
BaselineA: Combination of common law and statute: the common law doctrine of recent possession from R. v. Schama; R. v. Abramovitch, as approved in Richler v. The King, Ungaro v. The King, Graham v. The Queen, Tremblay v. The Queen and R. v. Graham, interpreted consistently with s. 4(5) of the Canada Evidence Act.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage constitutional-territoriality test: characterize and classify the law by its pith and substance, then determine whether it has a meaningful connection to the enacting province and respects the legislative sovereignty of other governments.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text and common law doctrine: s. 92, particularly ss. 92(13) and 92(14), of the Constitution Act, 1867, applied through the framework established in British Columbia v. Imperial Tobacco Canada Ltd.; the challenged provision was s. 11 of the Opioid Damages and Health Care Costs Recovery Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional approach and presumptive upper limit for non-pecuniary personal-injury damages
BaselineA: Common law, principally Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd. and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees, drawing on Warren v. King
CaseB_TestB: Fire-loss election and repudiation test under clause 5 of a real-property sale agreement
BaselineB: Contractual clause 5, interpreted against the common-law rules governing risk and repudiation in land-sale agreements
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright reproduction test: a literal physical transfer of an existing image to a new substrate is not a reproduction under s. 3(1) where it creates no additional or new copy or manifestation of the work; modification without reproduction is governed by moral rights.
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, principally ss. 3(1), 27(1), 28.2 and 38(1), read with art. 734 of the Quebec Code of Civil Procedure.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter test: a decision is unreasonable only if no line of analysis in the reasons could reasonably lead from the evidence to the conclusion; if any sufficient supporting reason is tenable under a somewhat probing examination, the court must not interfere.
BaselineB: Common law — the reasonableness simpliciter standard from Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., within the pragmatic and functional framework established in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and elaborated in Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under s. 137.1, including the threshold, merits-based, and public-interest hurdles
BaselineA: Statute — Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, ss. 137.1(2) to 137.1(4)
CaseB_TestB: Purposive, contextual, and pragmatic corporate attribution test, applicable to one-person corporations
BaselineB: Common law — Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen; Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of); Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd.; and Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Workers’ compensation top-up test: compare the compensation received with the claimant’s fault-adjusted third-party claim; no additional sum is recoverable if compensation equals or exceeds that claim, and the Commission is subrogated to the claim.
BaselineA: Statute: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) and 8, read with Civil Code arts. 1056 and 1157.
CaseB_TestB: Judicial-remuneration commission trigger: any government measure affecting any aspect of judges’ remuneration conditions must pass through an independent, effective and objective body.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and precedent: s. 11(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Preamble to the Constitution Act, 1867, as developed in Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference; applied to the Provincial Court Act and Bill 7.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exclusive statutory obscenity test for publications: material is obscene where it is a publication whose dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex, alone or with crime, horror, cruelty, or violence; displayed articles accompanied by printed descriptions may constitute publications.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), informed by Brodie v. The Queen and replacing the common law Hicklin obscenity test for publications.
CaseB_TestB: Union duty to accommodate adverse-effect discrimination: a union that contributes to a discriminatory rule or impedes reasonable accommodation must take reasonable measures short of undue hardship, subject principally to significant interference with other employees' rights.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, principally s. 8, and the accommodation doctrine established in O'Malley v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd. and Central Alberta Dairy Pool v. Alberta (Human Rights Commission).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Paragraph 12 right-of-access test: once any hunting is permitted on the land, Indigenous persons may hunt any species there for food "at all seasons of the year," provided the hunting is non-dangerous, regardless of provincial limits on season, method, or quantity.
BaselineA: Combination of paragraph 12 of the 1930 Saskatchewan Natural Resources Agreement, constitutionally confirmed by Saskatchewan, Canadian, and United Kingdom legislation; provincial game regulations; and R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson.
CaseB_TestB: Charter purpose-and-effects test: legislative purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity; an unconstitutional purpose invalidates the law, while effects need be considered only if the law passes the purpose test, and permissible effects cannot save an invalid purpose.
BaselineB: Constitutional statute, principally ss. 1 and 2(a) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, informed by Hunter v. Southam Inc. and Attorney General of Quebec v. Quebec Association of Protestant School Boards.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional and structural test for whether a court or tribunal has power to grant a Charter remedy under s. 24

CaseA_TestA: Exception to the Kienapple rule: Criminal Code s. 83 permits a separate conviction and consecutive punishment for using a firearm during an armed robbery arising from the same event.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Entrapment through random virtue-testing: police may offer an opportunity based on reasonable suspicion about the person or during a bona fide inquiry into a sufficiently precise location where the offence is reasonably suspected
BaselineA: Common law entrapment test established in R. v. Mack, [1988] 2 S.C.R. 903
CaseB_TestB: Appellate intervention in a trial judge's voluntariness determination requires a serious, specific and determining error
BaselineB: Common law standard of appellate review for a trial judge's weighing of evidence on a confession's voluntariness; no prior case is identified in the decision
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-stage framework for remedying an improper closing address: curative instructions ordinarily, and a limited reply only in the clearest cases where instructions cannot cure the unfairness
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 651, the common-law inherent jurisdiction recognized in R. v. Osborn and Amato v. The Queen, and Charter ss. 7 and 11(d)
CaseB_TestB: Three-step framework governing the defence of honest belief in legal age and proof of culpable belief under Criminal Code s. 172.1(4)
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 172.1(1), (3), and (4), as previously interpreted in R. v. Levigne
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single transaction test for first degree murder: the Crown must first prove that the accused committed, or was a party to, both the underlying offence and the murder; only then may the court ask whether the offences were sufficiently closely connected in time. The test is unavailable for manslaughter.
BaselineA: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 214(5), and the single transaction principle established in R. v. Paré, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 618.
CaseB_TestB: Forum non conveniens test: the party seeking a stay must show that another forum is clearly more appropriate, based on a global assessment of numerous, context-dependent factors rather than a numerical tally.
BaselineB: Common law, principally the forum non conveniens framework reviewed in Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda, 2012 SCC 17, with statutory analogues used as helpful references.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable expectation of injury test for refusing access to personal information under s. 22(1)(b) of the Privacy Act
BaselineA: Statute: Privacy Act, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47 and 49, read harmoniously with Official Languages Act, ss. 60 and 72 to 74.
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary adverse inference of causation under the presumption-of-fact framework
BaselineB: Statute and prior SCC jurisprudence: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2846 to 2849, particularly art. 2849, as informed by Snell v. Farrell and St-Jean v. Mercier.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 letters rogatory test for documentary production: documentary evidence may be ordered without ancillary oral testimony, subject to requirements concerning use at trial rather than discovery, relevance, permissible scope, and adequate identification of the documents.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: s. 43 of the Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, interpreted in light of the comity principle recognized in Zingre v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third party suspect evidence: the evidence must be relevant through a sufficient connection between the incidents and evidence that the accused could not have committed the other offence, and is then admitted unless its prejudicial effects substantially outweigh its probative value.
BaselineB: Common law: the defence-evidence balancing test from R. v. Seaboyer, the air-of-reality test from R. v. Cinous, and the sufficient-connection principles from McMillan v. The Queen and R. v. Grandinetti.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh-pursuit test for retaining peace-officer status under s. 25(4)
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 25(4), 449(1)(b), and 450
CaseB_TestB: Specific-penalty test limiting an arbitrator's power to substitute discipline
BaselineB: Statute — Canada Labour Code, s. 157(d), applied to the collective agreement
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Guidelines Order applicability test: a federal “decision making responsibility” exists only where an Act of Parliament imposes an affirmative regulatory duty relating to the proposal; the department assigned that duty is the “initiating department”.
BaselineA: Regulation and statute — Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467, especially ss. 2, 3, 6, 10, 12 and 14, authorized by s. 6 of the Department of the Environment Act and applied alongside the relevant regulatory statutes.
CaseB_TestB: Contextual test for reviewable jury-charge error under s. 686(1)(a): the impugned words must be read in the context of the entire charge, the evidence and the trial as a whole, without automatically resolving ambiguity in the accused’s favour.
BaselineB: Statute and common law — Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a), applied through the common-law principle that a jury charge is reviewed contextually as a whole.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 70(1) preservation test: once the contractual prerequisites are met, the right to invoke interest arbitration is preserved if it exists when notice to arbitrate is served during the statutory status quo period; it need not continue until the award.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and collective agreement: The Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, s. 70(1) (now s. 79), read with Haldimand agreement arts. 16 and 18 and Perth agreement arts. 15 and 16, building on Bradburn v. Wentworth Arms Hotel Limited.
CaseB_TestB: Exception to the rule against collateral attack permitting a trial judge to review and, if erroneous, set aside a pre-trial division and severance order regulating the judicial process within the same litigation.
BaselineB: Common law rule against collateral attack established in Wilson v. The Queen and reaffirmed in R. v. Meltzer, R. v. Garofoli, and Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) is satisfied if the insured has an insurable interest; the nature of that interest need not be stated unless the policy requires it.
BaselineA: Statute: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240, statutory conditions 1 and 10(a), read with Civil Code arts. 2480, 2571 and 2572; informed by Wandlyn Motels v. Commerce General Insurance Company.
CaseB_TestB: When bodily samples initially seized for a non-police purpose are later used in a criminal prosecution, the court must determine whether police conduct constituted an independent state seizure or made the initially valid seizure unreasonable.
BaselineB: Combination of Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8, Coroners Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 93, ss. 16(2), (4) and (5), and the search-and-seizure principles established in Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Dyment.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Justification for departing from the knock-and-announce rule: the Crown must establish reasonable grounds for concern about harm or destruction of evidence based on information available when police acted, with a heavier onus for greater departures and latitude for operational judgment.
BaselineA: Constitutional and common law: s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the search-reasonableness and knock-and-announce principles from R. v. Collins, Eccles v. Bourque, R. v. Genest, and R. v. Gimson.
CaseB_TestB: Hearsay test for implied verbal assertions: an implied assertion tendered for the truth of its contents is hearsay and is presumptively inadmissible unless a traditional exception applies or necessity and reliability are established.
BaselineB: Common law hearsay doctrine, including the defining features stated in R. v. Khelawon and the principled necessity-and-reliability framework developed in R. v. Khan and summarized in R. v. Mapara.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Property used or held in carrying on a business: employed-and-risked or destabilizing-withdrawal test
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii), applied to foreign investment income through s. 129(4)(b).
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal from acquittal: verdict-would-not-necessarily-have-been-the-same test
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Morin.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper test for recognizing a duty of care owed by a statutory regulator
BaselineA: Common law: the Anns/Kamloops duty-of-care framework, as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart; statutory-regulator proximity is grounded in the Law Society Act, particularly ss. 9, 33, 51 and 61.
CaseB_TestB: Law contextual discrimination test for legislation targeting acquired pay-equity rights
BaselineB: Constitutional law: s. 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the contextual framework from Law v. Canada, applied to s. 9 of the Public Sector Restraint Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequivocal written notice test for terminating future liability under a guarantee
BaselineA: Contract—s. 4 of the Guarantee and Postponement of Claim, interpreted through common law contractual principles
CaseB_TestB: Presumptive inadmissibility of an accused’s silence unless the Crown establishes real relevance and a proper basis
BaselineB: Common law right to silence and evidence principles from Rothman, Robertson, and Symonds, constitutionally protected by s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms as recognized in Woolley and Hebert
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Treaty-residence test requiring liability to tax by reason of a listed or similar criterion that imposes comprehensive taxation on worldwide income
BaselineA: Statute and international tax treaty: Canada-United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I, particularly Article IV(1) of the Canada-United States Income Tax Convention (1980), read with Articles I and XII.
CaseB_TestB: Valid-refusal test for triggering the two-year insurance limitation period
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, ss. 279 to 283, especially s. 281(5), and the Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, especially ss. 62(8), 71, 72 and 94.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory limiting instruction for highly prejudicial bad-character evidence: the jury must be told the evidence's limited permissible purpose and specifically warned not to infer guilt from propensity.
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. D. (L.E.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 111.
CaseB_TestB: Recent-fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: once recent fabrication is alleged, an earlier complaint is admissible to prove that it was made, but not to prove the truth of its contents.
BaselineB: Common law rule governing prior consistent statements and recent fabrication; no earlier case is identified in the decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Treatment of a witness who remains in court despite an exclusion order: the witness is not necessarily disqualified, admission may be discretionary, and weight is determined by the trier of fact
BaselineA: Common law, including Cook v. Nethercotte, Thomas v. David, Chandler v. Home, R. v. Briggs, R. v. Thompson, Black v. Besse, and R. v. Carefoot
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal-legislative-intent test for lifting Crown immunity from discovery, with s. 27 applying only where the Crown is a party
BaselineB: Common law Crown immunity combined with Interpretation Act, s. 17; Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, ss. 27 and 34; and Crown Liability and Proceedings (Provincial Court) Regulations, s. 7
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec inter vivos trust for unborn primary beneficiaries: public-order prohibitions apply, but constraints inherent in direct gifts do not
BaselineA: Statute: Quebec Civil Code, arts. 981a, 981b and 981l, read with arts. 608, 754-55, 765-72 and 929; informed by Curran v. Davis and Masson v. Masson.
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdiction and safeguards for interim injunctions enforceable against non-parties through contempt
BaselineB: Common law and equity: inherent jurisdiction and contempt principles recognized in Attorney-General v. Times Newspapers Ltd., Seaward v. Paterson, Bartle & Gibson Co. v. Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union, Local 580, and International Longshoremen's Association, Local 273 v. Maritime Employers' Association; reinforced by the Law and Equity Act, s. 36, and the Criminal Code, s. 11.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fraud by “other fraudulent means”: conduct is dishonest if a reasonable person would stigmatize it as dishonest and unscrupulous, particularly where it wrongfully uses something in which another has an interest so as to extinguish or endanger that interest; the accused must knowingly undertake the conduct and appreciate the risk of deprivation.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1), as interpreted in R. v. Olan and R. v. Théroux.
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of representation in collective bargaining: the union owes diligent and competent representation to the bargaining unit as a whole, generally as an obligation of means; a residual duty may extend to former employees regarding employment-period interests, but they have no acquired right to retroactivity or entitlement to a particular bargaining result, and the claimant must prove breach contextually.
BaselineB: Statute: Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, especially s. 47.2 and the statutory scheme of exclusive representation, informed by Noël v. Société d’énergie de la Baie James and Centre hospitalier Régina Ltée v. Labour Court.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge's discretionary matrimonial-property reapportionment only where the judge misdirected himself or the decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice
BaselineA: Common law appellate non-intervention principle from Harper v. Harper, applied to the statutory discretion under ss. 43 and 51 of the Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121
CaseB_TestB: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown remarks where they are sufficiently prejudicial that judicial comment is required to ensure the defence is fairly put to the jury
BaselineB: Common law governing the trial judge's duty to ensure a fair jury charge, together with the curative proviso in s. 686(1)(b)(iii) of the Criminal Code
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid partnership test: carrying on a business, in common, with a view to profit, assessed pragmatically from all surrounding circumstances
BaselineA: Combination of the common law partnership test stated in Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada and applied in Backman v. Canada, and s. 96 of the Income Tax Act
CaseB_TestB: Substantive W. (D.) test for adequate jury instructions on credibility and reasonable doubt, assessed from the charge as a whole
BaselineB: Common law, principally the jury-instruction test established in R. v. W. (D.) and clarified in R. v. S. (W.D.) and R. v. Avetysan
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 577 right-to-presence test for proceedings examining prospective jurors for partiality
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 577(1), 569(2), 598-600 and 613(1)(b)(iii), together with Nova Scotia Juries Act, S.N.S. 1969, c. 12, s. 4(2).
CaseB_TestB: Test for substituting a conviction for an acquittal on a Crown appeal
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4)(b)(ii), as previously interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Courville.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law test for a frisk search incident to arrest: a lawful arrest permits the search without reasonable and probable grounds, but the search must pursue a valid criminal-justice objective and must not be abusive; any constraint should be proportionate to the objective and circumstances.
BaselineA: Common law search-incident-to-arrest power, particularly as recognized in R. v. Brezack, R. v. Morrison, and R. v. Miller.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 minimum for warrantless child apprehension: apprehension must be a last resort based on reasonable and probable grounds of serious harm or risk of serious harm, and must be followed by a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Manitoba’s Child and Family Services Act, particularly ss. 17, 21(1), 24, 27(1), 29(1), and 30-37, informed by B. (R.) v. Children’s Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto and New Brunswick (Minister of Health and Community Services) v. G. (J.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused an identification line-up: the evidence is admissible where the Crown must explain the absence of a line-up or risk an adverse inference; otherwise, it should not normally be tendered.
BaselineA: Common law of evidence and the privilege against self-incrimination, informed by Curr v. The Queen, Attorney-General of Quebec v. Begin, R. v. Brager, and R. v. John; also Canada Evidence Act, s. 5, and Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(d).
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional validity of a provincial public inquiry: its pith and substance must be anchored to a provincial head of power and must not, by purpose or effect, substitute for a criminal investigation or preliminary inquiry into specific offences by named individuals.
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(27) and 92(4), (7), (13), (14), and (16), together with the pith-and-substance jurisprudence in Faber v. The Queen, Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, Attorney General (Que.) and Keable v. Attorney General (Can.), and O'Hara v. British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Factual causation for unlawful-act manslaughter: the unlawful act must be a contributing cause of death outside the de minimis range, proved beyond a reasonable doubt
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 205(1) (with ss. 207 and 208), and common-law causation and thin-skull principles reflected in R. v. Larkin, R. v. Cato, R. v. Garforth, R. v. Blaue, and R. v. Nicholson
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage Anns/Kamloops test for recognizing a duty of care for novel pure economic loss claims arising from commercial negotiations
BaselineB: Common law: the two-stage duty-of-care framework from Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen, together with the pure economic loss jurisprudence in Rivtow, Norsk, D’Amato, and Bow Valley
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duration of specialty immunity under an unqualified extradition undertaking: absent clear terms, immunity ends once the extraditee has had a reasonable opportunity to return and remains voluntarily rather than because of the surrender.
BaselineA: Combination of the Canada-Brazil extradition arrangement, Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, ss. 2, 3 and 33, and principles governing the interpretation of international agreements.
CaseB_TestB: No-separate-leave rule for the curative proviso: where an error of law is properly before the Court, application of the proviso is always intertwined with that error and requires no separate leave, provided the Crown invokes it.
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), and the common law framework stated in R. v. Keegstra.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal licensing discretion: a council must act judicially on applicant-specific licensing grounds and cannot use a licensing power to prohibit a lawful type of business absent express statutory authority
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, especially ss. 455, 458, 458M, 458N, 870 and 871; the non-prohibition principle from Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 fair-process test for the IRPA security-certificate scheme, including the incompressible minimum of disclosure needed to keep the named person reasonably informed
BaselineB: Constitution and statute: s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and IRPA, especially ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1), 85.1, 85.2, 85.4 and 85.5, informed by Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence of other charged or uncharged offences at sentencing
BaselineA: Criminal Code, Part XXIII, particularly ss. 718 to 718.2, 724(3)(e), 725 and 726.1, informed by Lees v. The Queen and R. v. Gardiner
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in online communications with a police-created child persona
BaselineB: Charter s. 8 reasonable-expectation-of-privacy jurisprudence, particularly R. v. Marakah, R. v. Cole, R. v. Spencer, R. v. Tessling, R. v. Edwards and Hunter v. Southam Inc.; Criminal Code ss. 183 and 184.2
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation: words or conduct must induce detrimental reliance, and silence or inaction constitutes a representation only where there is a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law estoppel by representation, including Greenwood v. Martins Bank Ltd. and Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha v. Dawson’s Bank Ltd.; pleading is also governed by Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 14.04
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the statutory presumption of living on the avails: the jury may consider all relevant evidence, without isolating a particular and severable item as evidence to the contrary
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fingerprint inference of possession: whether fingerprints support an inference of possession depends on all the circumstances and all the evidence, rather than a hard-and-fast rule.
BaselineA: Combination of common law (R. v. O'Keefe and R. v. Mehrabnia) and statute (Criminal Code, s. 4(3), incorporated by Food and Drugs Act, ss. 46 and 48(2)).
CaseB_TestB: Review Board authority over treatment-related conditions: a Board may bind hospital authorities and supervise or question treatment, but may not prescribe or impose treatment.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, Part XX.1, principally ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Refined three-stage s. 96 test for determining whether a province may confer jurisdiction on a provincially appointed tribunal
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, and the three-stage common law framework established in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714
CaseB_TestB: Flexible three-factor test for granting public interest standing, including the sufficient factual setting inquiry
BaselineB: Common law public interest standing framework established in Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of cross-examination on a former juvenile delinquent’s record under s. 12(1) of the Canada Evidence Act
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1), read with the Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3, and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593.
CaseB_TestB: Amendment of an indictment where the proven narcotic differs from the narcotic particularized in the charge
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) and 613(1)(b)(i), (3), read with the Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2 and 4 and Schedule item 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rough $100,000 upper limit for non-pecuniary personal-injury damages, exceeded only in rare exceptional circumstances or adjusted upon proof or agreement of inflation
BaselineA: Common law established in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Arnold v. Teno, and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57, and refined in Lewis v. Todd

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: The “essence of the crime charged” test for determining whether an offence falls within an extradition arrangement
BaselineA: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2, and s. 17 of the 1925 Supplementary Convention concerning crimes against laws suppressing narcotics trafficking
CaseB_TestB: Purpose-based test permitting use of prior testimony solely to impeach credibility, but not to incriminate or establish the truth of its contents

CaseA_TestA: Statutory wage-lien priority test: the lien attaches when wages are earned, leaves prior mortgages unaffected, and reaches only the employer's equity

Workers' Compensation Board.

CaseB_TestB: Valid dismissal requires the Board itself to exercise its exclusive, non-delegable dismissal authority; an unauthorized dismissal by the police chief is not validated by uncommunicated informal confirmation.
BaselineB: Combination of Regulation 680, s. 27(b), and s. 9 of the collective agreement made pursuant to The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, s. 29.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fully paid shares non-assessment test: an amendment imposing “any financial burden whatsoever” on a shareholder in respect of fully paid shares is invalid.
BaselineA: Combination of common law limited-liability principles (Ooregum Gold Mining Co. v. Roper, Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates, and Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy) and The Companies Act of Alberta, especially ss. 2(1)(10), 15(1), 16(c), 42(1), 68(4), and 193(1)(d), together with the memorandum of association.
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for an Aboriginal right: precisely characterize the claimed activity, then determine whether, before European contact, it was an integral—central, significant, or defining—part of the distinctive culture of the claimant Aboriginal group.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 and the common law framework established in R. v. Van der Peet.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown-binding test: under s. 16, the Crown must be mentioned or referred to; alternatively, at common law, necessary implication exists only where excluding the Crown would wholly frustrate the legislation’s purpose.
BaselineA: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, ss. 16 and 28, together with the common-law Crown-immunity test from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation.
CaseB_TestB: Material contractual breach test: a substantial departure from an express and material undertaking constitutes breach of a subsisting contract attracting damages under art. 1065, rather than nullity for error under art. 992.
BaselineB: Civil Code, arts. 992 and 1065, applied to the contract of carriage.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional and integral-part test for federal labour-relations jurisdiction: provincial jurisdiction is the rule; federal jurisdiction arises where the undertaking's normal operations are federal or labour relations form an integral part of primary federal jurisdiction.
BaselineA: Combination of constitutional statute and common law: s. 91(24) of the British North America Act, 1867, ss. 2 and 108(1) of the Canada Labour Code, and the functional/integral-part jurisprudence, particularly the Stevedoring case and Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider.
CaseB_TestB: Two-part substantive equality test under s. 15(1): whether the law creates a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground and whether it perpetuates disadvantage or prejudice, or imposes disadvantage through stereotyping.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: s. 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the equality jurisprudence established in Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia, Law v. Canada, and R. v. Kapp.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Proof of breach of the municipality’s contractual sewer-servicing obligation: the claimant must show an existing or foreseeable inadequacy connected to the Scotia Square sewer system; a general sewer report or development charge alone does not establish breach.
BaselineA: Contract—s. 31(a)(iii) of the August 31, 1966 development agreement; Ordinance No. 153 supplied only the agreed measure of damages upon proof of breach.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the common law presumption of advancement for a gratuitous transfer from husband to wife by proving that the husband lacked an intention to advance her.
BaselineB: Common law presumption of advancement, as addressed in Goodfriend v. Goodfriend and Tinker v. Tinker; s. 1(3)(d) of The Family Law Reform Act, 1975 did not apply retrospectively.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Four-factor test for determining whether an administrative decision must be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis
BaselineA: Statute and common law: s. 28 of the Federal Court Act, interpreted in light of common-law natural justice principles reflected in Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works, Russell v. Duke of Norfolk and Durayappah v. Fernando.
CaseB_TestB: Conscriptive-evidence and discoverability framework for trial fairness under Charter s. 24(2)
BaselineB: Constitutional statute and precedent: s. 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the three-group admissibility framework established in R. v. Collins, as developed in cases including R. v. Black, R. v. Borden and R. v. Burlingham.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking in the drug actually sold, unless evidence raises an honest-belief doubt
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 and 42; Beaver v. The Queen, R. v. Blondin, and The Queen v. King
CaseB_TestB: Limits on trial-judge intervention: intervention must not create doubt about impartiality and justice must be seen to be done
BaselineB: Common law: R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy and R. v. Darlyn

CaseA_TestA: Section 2(b) protection for consumer counter-advertising: consumer criticism of a business is protected expression, and restricting accessible means such as signs infringes freedom of expression
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b), as interpreted in Irwin Toy, Ford, Rocket and Ramsden

CaseA_TestA: Municipality-specific taxable-property valuation rule under s. 373 of the Education Act
BaselineA: Statute: Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373, read with the Cities and Towns Act, s. 488
CaseB_TestB: Actus reus and mens rea test for accepting a secret commission under s. 426(1)(a)(ii) of the Criminal Code
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a)(ii) (formerly s. 383(1)(a))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trustee’s duty to preserve or replace insurance on all insurable bankrupt property, including hypothecated property, and to notify the secured creditor if insurance cannot be obtained
BaselineA: Statute and contract: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 2(o), 2(r), and 9(1)-(2), read with the hypothec deed’s insurance clause

BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 149(1)(l), 149.1(1), and 248(1), together with the Pemsel approach as adopted and elaborated in Vancouver Society of Immigrant and Visible Minority Women v. M.N.R.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent tort and contract liability test for negligent performance of contractual professional services
BaselineA: Common law — the proximity-based duty of care from Donoghue v. Stevenson, Hedley Byrne & Co. v. Heller & Partners Ltd., and Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, as previously constrained in Canada by Nunes Diamonds.
CaseB_TestB: Mandatory enforcement of a valid and exclusive foreign choice of forum clause in an incidental action in warranty
BaselineB: Statute — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148, para. 2, 3139, and 3135, informed by Code of Civil Procedure art. 940.1 and international arbitration instruments.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Election of delictual liability despite a contract: the plaintiff may proceed delictually only if the contractual fault would independently constitute a fault under art. 1053 in the absence of the contract.
BaselineA: Statute and precedent: art. 1053 of the Civil Code, as previously applied in Ross v. Dunstall; Ross v. Emery and Alliance Assurance Co. v. Dominion Electric Protection Co.
CaseB_TestB: Effect of reasonable apprehension of bias: once established, the trial judge loses further jurisdiction, subsequent orders are retroactively void, and a new trial is mandatory.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 engagement test for Canadian requests leading to foreign searches: assess whether the specific action of Canadian officials itself intrudes on privacy through a search or seizure; a mere request to independent foreign authorities does not engage s. 8
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8 and 32(1), as interpreted in Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Terry
CaseB_TestB: Duty-of-care test for failure to prevent intentional third-party harm: sufficient foreseeability and proximity establish a prima facie duty, subject to compelling residual policy considerations that negate or limit it
BaselineB: Common law duty-of-care framework from Cooper v. Hobart, Edwards v. Law Society of Upper Canada, Childs v. Desormeaux, Odhavji Estate v. Woodhouse and Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board, informed for the government defendant by the Mining Safety Act and Mining Safety Regulations
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Comprehensive statutory human-rights enforcement scheme forecloses parallel civil actions for statutory breach or a common-law discrimination tort
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: The Ontario Human Rights Code, particularly ss. 4, 14b(6), 14c and 14d, and common-law principles governing civil actions based on statutory duties
CaseB_TestB: Undue-obstacle reasonable-accommodation test for transportation accessibility
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canada Transportation Act, ss. 5 and 170-172; Canadian Human Rights Act, ss. 5(a) and 15; and the reasonable-accommodation jurisprudence in Meiorin, Grismer and Chambly
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 4 test for departing from presumptive Table child-support amounts where the paying parent earns over $150,000
BaselineA: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, s. 4, read with ss. 1, 3, 7 and 21, and Divorce Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 3 (2nd Supp.), s. 26.1(2)
CaseB_TestB: Part 2 default classification rule for comprehensive multi-risk insurance policies that do not fit a specific statutory category
BaselineB: British Columbia Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, Parts 2 and 5, especially ss. 3(a) and 119 and statutory condition 14, read with Insurance Classes Regulation, B.C. Reg. 337/90, s. 2
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When an acquittal based on a finding of fact raises a question of law alone permitting a Crown appeal
BaselineA: Statute and precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 605(1)(a), interpreted through Lampard v. The Queen and Sunbeam Corporation (Canada) Ltd. v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Section 137.1 anti-SLAPP dismissal framework
BaselineB: Statute: Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, principally ss. 137.1(1) to (4), with procedural context from ss. 137.2 to 137.5.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office: the plaintiff must prove (1) deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions and (2) subjective awareness that the conduct was unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff, together with causation and compensable injury.
BaselineA: Common law, originating in Ashby v. White and recognized in Canada in Roncarelli v. Duplessis, with guidance from Three Rivers District Council v. Bank of England (No. 3); the unlawfulness in this case was supplied by ss. 41(1)(b) and 113(9) of Ontario's Police Services Act.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional amending-formula framework for the Supreme Court: substantive changes to its composition, including the eligibility requirements in ss. 4(1), 5 and 6 of the Supreme Court Act, require unanimity under s. 41(d); changes to other essential features require the 7/50 procedure under s. 42(1)(d), while routine maintenance remains within Parliament's s. 101 authority.

JudgeB: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ. in joint reasons
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown remarks: a trial judge must comment where the remarks are prejudicial to a degree sufficient to require intervention so that the defence is fairly put to the jury.
BaselineA: Common law duty governing jury charges, adopting Ayles J.A.'s dissenting formulation; the curative proviso is governed by s. 686(1)(b)(iii) of the Criminal Code.
CaseB_TestB: Seller-fault test for voluntarily preventing free performance of a brokerage contract: the broker must prove a valid brokerage contract, performance of its own obligations, and prevention of the compensation conditions through the seller's fault, meaning breach of an identified obligation to act or refrain from acting.
BaselineB: Clause 6.1(4) of the brokerage contract, which mirrors art. 1503 of the Civil Code of Québec.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal negligence requires conduct that is a marked departure from the norm from which wanton or reckless disregard may be inferred; resulting consequences matter only when sufficiently interwoven with the accused’s conduct to characterize it.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202-203 (now R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 219-220), as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392.
CaseB_TestB: CITT procurement-complaint standing under the AIT requires a designated contract involving a Canadian supplier, meaning a supplier with a place of business in Canada.
BaselineB: Combination of statute, regulation, and incorporated trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1 and 30.11(1); Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, ss. 3(1), 7(1), and 11; and Agreement on Internal Trade, arts. 101, 501, 502, and 518.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Three-part test for establishing a constitutional convention: precedents, belief by the actors that they were bound by a rule, and a reason for the rule, with actor recognition or acceptance as an essential and dispositive requirement
BaselineA: Non-statutory constitutional-convention doctrine from Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753, which adopted the Jennings three-question test
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable suspicion test for a warrantless drug-detection dog search, assessed from the totality of objectively ascertainable circumstances and requiring a particularized nexus to drug-related criminal activity
BaselineB: Common law search power constrained by s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, based on R. v. Collins, R. v. Kang-Brown, and R. v. A.M.

CaseA_TestA: Contextual test for the effectiveness of an order while its appeal period remains open, considering the purpose for which finality is asserted, who is affected, the surrounding context, and whether any prospect of appeal is merely ephemeral.
BaselineA: Common law principles concerning the finality and effectiveness of appealable orders, including Re West and Leonard v. Wharton, applied to a discharge order made under s. 62 of The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 85.
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary-inquiry committal test: direct evidence on every element requires committal, while circumstantial evidence requires limited weighing of the whole evidence to determine whether a properly instructed reasonable jury could infer guilt, without assessing credibility or reliability or drawing factual inferences.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 548(1) of the Criminal Code and the common law committal test established in United States of America v. Shephard and applied in Mezzo, Monteleone, and Charemski.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Child-witness screen test: whether a screen is necessary to obtain a full and candid account without rendering the trial fundamentally unfair
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 486(2.1), and Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d)
CaseB_TestB: Prior-conviction similar-fact admissibility test: a conviction may provide 'some evidence' linking the accused to a disputed prior act, subject to probative value exceeding prejudicial effect
BaselineB: Common law similar-fact evidence framework established in R. v. Arp and R. v. Handy, informed by British Columbia (Attorney General) v. Malik
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interprovincial-concern and territoriality test: a province may protect property within its territory, but it cannot legislate respecting injury caused by acts performed in another province; pollution that is truly interprovincial falls within Parliament's residual authority.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91 and 92, particularly Parliament's residual peace, order and good government power and the territorial limits on provincial authority, informed by Citizens Insurance Co. v. Parsons, Burns Foods Ltd. v. A.G. Man., and Campbell-Bennett Ltd. v. Comstock Midwestern Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Patently unreasonable decision test under a privative clause: a reviewing court may intervene only where the tribunal's finding, whether arising from law, fact, or both, is unreasonable; the decision must be so patently unreasonable that it cannot be rationally supported by the governing legislation.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: ss. 127-129 of Quebec's Act respecting labour standards, s. 139 of the Labour Code, and the patently unreasonable test from Canadian Union of Public Employees Local 963 v. New Brunswick Liquor Corporation.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Four-part test for lawful warrantless arrest on private premises
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a), together with the common law entry requirements established in Eccles v. Bourque and traced to Semayne's Case.
CaseB_TestB: Two-step section 15 test requiring denial of an equality right and discrimination in purpose or effect assessed in the larger social, political, and legal context
BaselineB: Constitutional provision and precedent: s. 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, as interpreted in Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion to refuse declaratory relief where the legislature has entrusted the issue to a specialized tribunal
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Code of Civil Procedure, art. 453; Act respecting the Olympic Village, ss. 10 and 15-34, especially s. 27; and the declaratory-relief principles in Barraclough v. Brown, City of Lethbridge v. Canadian Western Natural Gas, and Cassidy v. Stuart.
CaseB_TestB: Continuing ministerial power to revoke a fishing-licence authorization before the licence is issued
BaselineB: Statute: Fisheries Act, ss. 7 and 9, read with Interpretation Act, s. 31(3).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right and mistake test: colour of right applies only where the offence embraces that concept, and a mistake must concern facts constituting the offence rather than the law’s applicability.
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, ss. 19 and 206(1)(d), incorporating the longstanding principle that mistake of law is no defence.
