Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Conditions governing who may prefer an indictment and when additional counts may be included after a preliminary inquiry
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 507(1)-(3), read with ss. 496, 504 and 505
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility and assessment of oral-history evidence in Aboriginal-rights claims

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction-contract threshold requiring a claim against the owner based on the owner's undertaking to pay the construction price

CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation for a non-proprietary breach of fiduciary duty: compensation is limited to loss resulting from the particular fiduciary breach; unrelated and independent losses caused by intervening third parties are too remote, with equitable and common-law principles applied flexibly to achieve fairness and justice.
BaselineB: Common law and equity, principally Nocton v. Lord Ashburton, Guerin v. The Queen, Jacks v. Davis, McKenzie v. McDonald, and Day v. Mead.

CaseA_TestA: Similar-fact evidence threshold requiring some direct or circumstantial evidentiary link between the accused and the alleged similar acts
BaselineA: Common law, principally Makin v. The Attorney-General for New South Wales, Boardman v. Director of Public Prosecutions, and Harris v. Director of Public Prosecutions
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional vagueness test: whether a law so lacks precision that it fails to give sufficient guidance for legal debate

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseB_TestB: Misapprehension-of-evidence test: a conviction may be set aside only where the error concerns the substance of material evidence and plays an essential part in the reasoning process resulting in conviction.
BaselineB: Statute and precedent: Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a)(iii), as developed in R. v. Morrissey and R. v. C. (R.).

CaseA_TestA: Supreme Court amendment classification test: substantive changes to the Court's composition, including the eligibility requirements in ss. 4(1), 5 and 6 of the Supreme Court Act, require unanimity under s. 41(d), while changes to other essential features require the 7/50 procedure under s. 42(1)(d).

CaseB_TestB: Two-step s. 15(1) substantive equality test: whether the law, on its face or in its impact, draws a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground and, if so, whether it reinforces, perpetuates or exacerbates disadvantage.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), as developed in Quebec (Attorney General) v. A and Kahkewistahaw First Nation v. Taypotat.

CaseA_TestA: Clause 9 price-adjustment test: an adjustment applies only to a tax, duty, charge, or fee imposed upon Imperial in respect of bunker fuel oil or its production, manufacture, sale, or delivery by Imperial, not to increased crude-oil costs charged by affiliates
BaselineA: Contractual text—clause 9 of the parties’ agreement—interpreted under common-law principles of contract interpretation.
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for Aboriginal-right and self-government claims: precisely characterize the claimed activity, then determine whether it was an integral, defining feature of the claimant group’s distinctive culture before European contact

BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. Abbey, Morris v. The Queen, R. v. Béland, R. v. Morin, and R. v. Marquard

CaseA_TestA: Quantum meruit for accepted services where no remuneration was agreed: the recipient must pay a reasonable rate

CaseA_TestA: Effect of a worker’s compensation election and statutory subrogation on the parties’ claims, intervention, and prescription

CaseB_TestB: Collins three-category test for excluding evidence under Charter s. 24(2), emphasizing the seriousness and cumulative effect of Charter violations

CaseA_TestA: Mental disorder incapacity test: whether, at the time of the act, a mental disorder deprived the accused of the capacity to rationally assess the particular act as wrong by ordinary public standards

CaseB_TestB: Palmer test for admitting fresh evidence on an appeal from sentence: due diligence, relevance, credibility, and a reasonable possibility of affecting the result

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effect of an unlawful strike under a subsisting collective agreement: common law repudiation and fundamental breach do not terminate the employment relationship; absent positive disciplinary or discharge action by the employer, the collective agreement remains binding.
BaselineA: Combination of statute, collective agreement, and precedent: Mediation Services Act, 1968 (B.C.), ss. 6, 8 and 23; the applicable Labour Relations Act; arts. Compagnie Paquet Ltée, Re Polymer Corp. and Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers International Union, and C.P.R. Co. v. Zambri.
CaseB_TestB: Limits on defence cross-examination using records already in its possession: relevant cross-examination may be excluded only where its prejudicial effect substantially outweighs its probative value; an omission is probative only if there is a reasonable expectation that the omitted matter would have been recorded.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reverse-onus compatibility with the presumption of innocence: the Crown must prove facts making the essential fact rationally open to the accused to prove or disprove, including knowledge or means of knowledge enabling proof of lawful importation
BaselineA: Combination of statute and precedent: Customs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-40, ss. 205(1), 205(3), and 248(1); Canadian Bill of Rights, s. 2(f); and R. v. Appleby, [1972] S.C.R. 303
CaseB_TestB: Interested-party status in bargaining-unit investigations: only the associations concerned and the employer are interested parties; an individual employee has no right to attend, intervene, call or cross-examine witnesses, or make representations

CaseA_TestA: Public-interest test for disclosure of compelled OSC material: balance full-answer-and-defence interests against third-party confidentiality and disclose only what is necessary to carry out the OSC’s mandate
BaselineA: Combination of statute, regulation, and common law: Securities Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. S.5, ss. 16, 17(1) and 127; OSC Rules of Practice, rr. 3.3(2) and 3.7; and the relevance standard from R. v. Stinchcombe

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

BaselineB: Common law: Minister of Justice of Canada v. Borowski, Finlay v. Canada (Minister of Finance), and Canadian Council of Churches v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), building on Thorson v. Attorney General of Canada and Nova Scotia Board of Censors v. McNeil.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable foreseeability of the general class or character of injury, without requiring foreseeability of the precise sequence of events

CaseA_TestA: Telecommunication-service medium test: s. 287 applies to transmission by wire or cable, but not radio transmission by Hertzian waves, even where part of the transmission path uses wire or cable.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 287(1)(b) and 287(2).
CaseB_TestB: Individualized excessive-demands test: officers must assess likely demands on social services using all relevant medical and non-medical circumstances, including the family's ability and willingness to contribute; inadmissibility requires a reasonable probability—more likely than not—rather than a remote possibility of excessive demands.
BaselineB: Statute — Immigration Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-2, s. 19(1)(a)(ii), with the same analysis applicable to Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 38(1)(c).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patent disclosure sufficiency: the specification must describe the invention and its production or operation sufficiently to enable a person skilled in the art to produce it using only the disclosure; depositing a sample alone is insufficient.
BaselineA: Statute: Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, s. 36(1), informed by the disclosure jurisprudence cited in Minerals Separation, Burton Parsons Chemicals, Monsanto, and Consolboard.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of a labour arbitrator's adaptation of common law or equitable doctrines: the adaptation must reasonably respond to the distinctive nature of labour relations and be consistent with the statutory scheme, labour-relations principles, collective bargaining, and the grievance's factual matrix.
BaselineB: Combination of common law administrative-law principles from Dunsmuir and Smith and the statutory arbitral mandate under The Labour Relations Act, R.S.M. 1987, c. L10, ss. 121 and 128(2).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Facial-validity test for habeas corpus review of post-expiry parole detention: revocation after sentence expiry is authorized if the parolee is in custody pursuant to s. 16, and review on habeas corpus simpliciter is confined to the face of the warrants.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 10(1)(e), 16, 18 and 20; Federal Court Act, s. 18; and the habeas corpus rule from Re Shumiatcher, [1962] S.C.R. 38.
CaseB_TestB: Equitable compensation framework for the Crown’s breach of fiduciary duty concerning reserve land: identify what the fiduciary ought to have done, then assess the realistically most favourable lost opportunity caused in fact by the breach, with hindsight and equitable presumptions but without a foreseeability limit.
BaselineB: Common law and equity, principally Guerin v. The Queen, Canson Enterprises Ltd. v. Boughton & Co., Osoyoos Indian Band v. Oliver (Town), Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada and Blueberry River Indian Band v. Canada, informed by Indian Act, R.S.C. 1927, c. 98, ss. 48, 50 and 51, and Treaty 3.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exemption from seizure applies only to a true third-party insurance beneficiary, not a universal legatee or heir
BaselineA: Statute and contract: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 597, 735 and 1028; Code of Civil Procedure, art. 553(3); and the insurance policy's exemption-from-seizure clause
CaseB_TestB: No-fault liability for abnormal or excessive neighbourhood annoyances under art. 976 C.C.Q.
BaselineB: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, art. 976
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of similar-fact evidence to establish guilty intent where it is relevant to whether the charged act was designed or accidental, rather than merely proving propensity, subject to the limited Noor Mohamed discretion to exclude evidence of trifling probative weight that would be unjust to admit.
BaselineA: Common law—Makin v. Attorney-General for New South Wales, Thompson v. The King, Noor Mohamed v. The King, and R. v. Wray.
CaseB_TestB: Issue estoppel on a subsequent perjury charge: the Crown cannot re-litigate an issue necessarily decided in the accused's favour unless it tenders evidence that was unavailable through reasonable diligence at the first trial.
BaselineB: Common law doctrines of issue estoppel, res judicata, and double jeopardy—particularly The Duchess of Kingston's Case, Director of Public Prosecutions v. Humphrys, Gushue v. The Queen, and R. v. Gordon.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Legitimate expectations are procedural only and do not apply to the legislative process
BaselineA: Common law, principally Old St. Boniface Residents Assn. Inc. v. Winnipeg (City), with the legislative-function exclusion reflected in Attorney General of Canada v. Inuit Tapirisat of Canada and Martineau v. Matsqui Institution Disciplinary Board.
CaseB_TestB: Pension double-dipping inquiry on an application to vary spousal support
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Divorce Act, 1985, s. 17(4) and (7), informed by the overlap approach in Linton v. Linton.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 96 institutional-setting test: assess a challenged power not in isolation, but in the institutional arrangements in which it appears and is exercisable under the provincial legislation.
BaselineA: Constitution and common law: s. 96 of the British North America Act, 1867, as interpreted in Labour Relations Board of Saskatchewan v. John East Iron Works Ltd. and Tremblay v. Commission des Relations de Travail du Québec; applied to s. 49 of the Nova Scotia Trade Union Act, 1972.
CaseB_TestB: YCJA youth-sentencing rule excluding deterrence: neither general nor specific deterrence is a permissible sentencing principle or a basis for imposing a harsher sanction.
BaselineB: Statute: Youth Criminal Justice Act, especially ss. 3, 38, 42 and 50(1), considered alongside the omitted adult deterrence principle in s. 718(b) of the Criminal Code.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Attorney General’s stay power under s. 508 begins only when a summons or warrant is issued
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, especially ss. 2, 455, 455.3, 503 and 508. The Court interpreted an information as being “found” only after a justice of the peace decides to issue process.
CaseB_TestB: Five-factor procedural-fairness test for determining whether a municipality must give reasons for refusing rezoning
BaselineB: Common law: the duty-of-fairness framework from Baker v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), together with Cardinal v. Director of Kent Institution and related procedural-fairness cases, applied in the context of municipal authority under the Act respecting land use planning and development.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Conditions-precedent test for when a statutory appeal as of right is acquired, accrued or accruing
BaselineA: Statute: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. I-21, ss. 43(c) and 44(c), (d), read with former Criminal Code, s. 691(2).
CaseB_TestB: Sherman three-part test for discretionary limits on the open court principle
BaselineB: Common law: Sherman Estate v. Donovan, 2021 SCC 25.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Standard-of-review framework: interpretation of an administrative body's home statute is presumptively reviewed for reasonableness, rebuttable by established correctness categories or contextual legislative intent; a statutory appeal is not itself a correctness category.
BaselineA: Common law, principally Dunsmuir v. New Brunswick and Mouvement laïque québécois v. Saguenay (City), applied in the context of ss. 467 and 470 of Alberta's Municipal Government Act.
CaseB_TestB: Sui generis Crown fiduciary-obligation framework: the Crown must exercise discretionary control over a specific or cognizable Aboriginal interest according to fiduciary standards of loyalty, good faith, full disclosure and ordinary prudence, while fairly reconciling competing interests.
BaselineB: Combination of common law, principally Wewaykum Indian Band v. Canada, Guerin v. The Queen, Haida Nation v. British Columbia and Manitoba Metis Federation Inc. v. Canada, and ss. 14(1)(b) and 14(1)(c) of the Specific Claims Tribunal Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Paragraph 12 entitlement test: all Indians physically within Alberta, regardless of residence, may hunt, trap, and fish for food on unoccupied Crown lands or other lands to which they have access
BaselineA: Statute and treaty: para. 12 of the Alberta Natural Resources Transfer Agreement, given force of law by the British North America Act, 1930, together with s. 88 of the Indian Act and Treaty No. 6
CaseB_TestB: Qualified privilege and malice test: a communication made pursuant to reciprocal duties or interests is protected absent proof of malice, even if its language is excessive, where the speaker might honestly and on reasonable grounds have believed it true
BaselineB: Common law: Adam v. Ward, as applied by the Supreme Court of Canada in Netupsky v. Craig
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Meaning of “unlawful purpose” under Criminal Code s. 423(2)(a): the conspiracy’s purpose must be conduct prohibited by federal or provincial legislation.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 423(2)(a), read in light of s. 8.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable-journalist test for fault in Quebec media defamation: considering the entire context, the journalist or media outlet must have fallen below professional journalistic standards.
BaselineB: Statute and civil-law jurisprudence: art. 1457 of the Civil Code of Québec, informed by Société Radio-Canada v. Radio Sept-Îles Inc. and Prud’homme v. Prud’homme.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory-form test for municipal taxation: where legislation requires a tax rate to be set by by-law, a council cannot redelegate that power to itself for exercise by resolution; doing so exceeds its jurisdiction and permits a direct action in nullity.
BaselineA: Statute: Cities and Towns Act, s. 526 (as amended for Dorval), particularly the requirement to impose the tax by by-law, together with ss. 385 and 395; Code of Civil Procedure, art. 33.
CaseB_TestB: Material-contribution causation test for negligent blood-donor screening: the plaintiff must prove that the defendant's negligence materially contributed to the injury, meaning that its contribution fell outside the de minimis range; no rebuttable presumption of causation applies.
BaselineB: Common law negligence causation, based on Snell v. Farrell and Athey v. Leonati; the learned-intermediary presumption from Hollis v. Dow Corning Corp. was distinguished.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Arbitrable-grievance test: a damages claim arising from breach of a collective agreement is a grievance, whether characterized as its application or violation and whether brought by an employer or employee.
BaselineA: Statute—Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 141, ss. 1(g) and 88—together with the collective agreement and the interpretations in General Motors of Canada Ltd. v. Brunet and Imbleau v. Laskin.
CaseB_TestB: Negligence-waiver enforceability test: construed in context, a waiver applies where the parties intended a release and the accident falls within its contemplated scope, unless the clause is unenforceable for unconscionability or public-policy reasons.
BaselineB: Common law of contractual interpretation, waiver clauses, unconscionability, and public policy; no prior test-establishing case is named in the Court's reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Test for when quashing a defective charge under Criminal Code s. 529 is tantamount to an acquittal for autrefois acquit
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529, 535 and 537, together with the final-determination requirement recognized in Petersen v. The Queen and R. v. Riddle.
CaseB_TestB: Framework for determining whether an altered or intensified legal non-conforming use remains protected by acquired rights
BaselineB: Statute and judicial doctrine: Act Respecting Land Use Planning and Development, R.S.Q., c. A-19.1, s. 113(18), Saint-Romuald By-law 273-90, s. 204, and the doctrine of legal non-conforming uses reflected in Central Jewish Institute v. City of Toronto.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Audi alteram partem rule for ex parte evidence: absent express or necessarily implied authority, an appellate tribunal must not receive evidence behind a party’s back and must provide a real opportunity to correct or contradict potentially prejudicial information; possible prejudice is sufficient.
BaselineA: Common law natural justice, particularly Board of Education v. Rice, Kanda v. Government of the Federation of Malaya, and Pfizer Co. Ltd. v. Deputy Minister of National Revenue for Customs and Excise, applied to the statutory appeal under ss. 58(3) and 61 of the Universities Act, 1974 (B.C.).
CaseB_TestB: Occupational-disease causation test: employment must be of causative significance, and causation may be inferred from circumstantial evidence despite inconclusive or contrary expert opinion; evenly weighted evidence must be resolved in the worker’s favour.
BaselineB: Statute and administrative policy: ss. 6, 250(2), 250(4), and 254 of the Workers Compensation Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 492, together with the Rehabilitation Services & Claims Manual policies defining “causative significance”; informed by the common law inference principle in Snell v. Farrell.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Two-pronged framework for admitting Mr. Big confessions: presumptive inadmissibility unless the Crown proves on a balance of probabilities that probative value, assessed through reliability, outweighs prejudicial effect, supplemented by abuse-of-process review.
BaselineA: Common law—particularly the party-admissions exception to hearsay recognized in R. v. Evans, the probative-value/prejudicial-effect principle discussed in R. v. Handy, and the abuse-of-process doctrine in R. v. Mack and R. v. Babos.
CaseB_TestB: Infanticide disturbed-mind test: whether, when causing her newborn child's death, the mother had a mind that was disturbed in its ordinary sense by reason of not having fully recovered from childbirth or the effects of lactation.
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 233, interpreted alongside ss. 2, 16, 663(b), and 672.11(c).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Necessarily incidental fisheries-power test: legislation regulating provincial property and civil rights must be necessarily incidental to effective federal fisheries legislation and must link the prohibited conduct to actual or potential harm to fisheries.
BaselineA: Constitutional statute and precedent: British North America Act, ss. 91(12) and 92(13), applying the necessarily incidental doctrine stated in Attorney-General for Canada v. Attorney-General for British Columbia, [1930] A.C. 111.
CaseB_TestB: Colour of right test: the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that, at the time of the taking or conversion, the accused did not honestly believe that they had a right to the property, regardless of their actual legal entitlement.
BaselineB: Statute: the theft provisions in ss. 283 and 294(a) of the Criminal Code, including the requirement that the taking or conversion be “without colour of right.”
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Premarital-property exemption test: equal distribution is presumed, and the exemption for premarital assets is limited to their fair market value at the date of marriage; equitable discretion may reduce but cannot enlarge that exemption, and the general catch-all provision cannot circumvent the limit.
BaselineA: Statute: The Matrimonial Property Act, 1979 (Sask.), principally ss. 20, 21 and 23.
CaseB_TestB: Aggravated-assault consequence test: the Crown must prove all elements of assault plus the alleged aggravating consequence beyond a reasonable doubt, with endangerment assessed by the actual consequences for the particular complainant and coinciding with the requisite mens rea.
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, ss. 265 and 268(1), as interpreted through R. v. Godin, R. v. DeSousa and R. v. Cooper.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 2(d) test for exclusion from a statutory labour-relations regime: exclusion does not infringe freedom of association where workers remain free to establish an independent association and exercise lawful rights collectively, absent exceptional circumstances requiring positive state action
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 2(d) and 32(1), as interpreted in the 1987 labour trilogy, Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada v. Northwest Territories (Commissioner), and Canadian Egg Marketing Agency v. Richardson
CaseB_TestB: Joint/co-principal liability test: two or more individuals must come together intending to commit an offence, be present during its commission, and contribute to it; for manslaughter, the accused's actions must be a significant contributing cause of death
BaselineB: Criminal Code, s. 21(1)(a), combined with the common law of causation and party liability discussed in R. v. Pickton
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Post-August 1, 1970 sentence test for applying mandatory supervision to a combined sentence
BaselineA: Statute and proclamation: Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, ss. 14(1) and 15; Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1968-69, c. 38, s. 101(2); and Proclamation SOR/70-339
CaseB_TestB: Test for taxing accident-insurance proceeds payable by reason or on account of death
BaselineB: Statute: Succession Duties Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 70, s. 26(1), read with ss. 45(f) and 46(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 11(b) unreasonable-delay balancing test considering length of delay, waiver, reasons for delay, and prejudice, with flexible institutional-delay guidelines
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 11(b) and 24(1), as developed in Mills v. The Queen, R. v. Rahey, R. v. Conway, R. v. Smith, and R. v. Askov
CaseB_TestB: Contractor-fault defence to subcontractor liability: a subcontractor may avoid liability by proving that the loss resulted from the contractor's own fault rather than breach of the subcontractor's contractual obligations
BaselineB: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 1065, 1684 and 1688, the parties' contractual terms, and Hill, Clarke-Francis Ltd. v. Northland Groceries (Quebec) Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown appeal from acquittal under s. 686(4): no residual discretion to decline relief after a reversible error, absent abuse of process in the clearest of cases
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, ss. 676(1)(a) and 686(4), interpreted alongside the common-law abuse-of-process doctrine established in R. v. Jewitt and reaffirmed in R. v. Keyowski, R. v. Mack and R. v. Conway.
CaseB_TestB: Two-pronged framework for admitting Mr. Big confessions: presumptive inadmissibility rebutted where probative value outweighs prejudicial effect, supplemented by abuse-of-process review
BaselineB: Common law: the party-admissions exception to hearsay recognized in R. v. Evans, the probative-value versus prejudicial-effect analysis reflected in R. v. Handy, and the abuse-of-process doctrine discussed in R. v. Mack and R. v. Babos.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple procedure for charges of differing gravity: where the same delict underlies both charges, conviction on the more serious charge requires acquittal on the less serious charge; a guilty plea to the less serious charge must be held in abeyance pending disposition of the more serious charge.
BaselineA: Common law—the rule against multiple convictions established in Kienapple v. The Queen, with reference to Côté v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Habeas corpus for continued detention after a parole decision: detention becomes challengeable only when the inmate acquires parolee status, which occurs when an immediate grant is made, a future effective date arrives, or a prerequisite condition is fulfilled.
BaselineB: Combination of the common law of habeas corpus, particularly R. v. Miller, and the Parole Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-2, as amended.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Kamloops two-stage duty-of-care test for public-authority negligence
BaselineA: Common law, principally Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, applied through Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, s. 714 and Kamloops By-law No. 11-1.
CaseB_TestB: Necessary-implication test for lawful roadside sobriety screening and delayed access to counsel
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Charter ss. 1 and 10(b), Manitoba Highway Traffic Act s. 76.1(1), Criminal Code s. 254, and the principles from Therens, Thomsen, Dedman and Ladouceur.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fixed-work-pattern test for being “regularly engaged in some other occupation” under s. 44(1)(c)
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, s. 44(1)(c), read in context with s. 44 generally and s. 49 of the Regulations
CaseB_TestB: Programming-control/conduit test for whether an entity is a “broadcasting undertaking”
BaselineB: Statute: Broadcasting Act, S.C. 1991, c. 11, ss. 2(1), 2(3), and 3(1)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Single extraprovincial undertaking test: a cable system that receives extra-provincial signals and transmits them to subscribers remains one federal undertaking despite a change in transmission technology, and program-content regulation is inseparable from regulation of that undertaking.
BaselineA: British North America Act, ss. 91 and 92(10)(a), as interpreted in In re Regulation and Control of Radio Communication in Canada and Attorney-General for Ontario v. Winner.
CaseB_TestB: Embedded future-cost versus distinct-liability test for proceeds of disposition: a purchaser’s assumption of a distinct vendor liability may form part of the sale price, but an inseverable future cost embedded in the property merely depresses its value and is excluded.
BaselineB: Income Tax Act, s. 13(21), particularly the definition of “proceeds of disposition” as including the sale price, applied alongside the Forests Act, ss. 16(3) and 28(2), and Timber Management Regulations, s. 154.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Compatibility of municipal indemnification discretion with statutory collective bargaining authority
BaselineA: Statute: The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351, ss. 24(6) and 29(2), read with Regulation 790
CaseB_TestB: Exhaustive statutory-exceptions framework for civil state immunity
BaselineB: Statute: State Immunity Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. S-18, especially ss. 2, 3(1), 4 to 8 and 18
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown priority applies only against competing claims of equal degree; a prior registered second mortgage is of higher degree than a later Crown judgment
BaselineA: Combination of the common law Crown-prerogative rule recognized in The Queen v. Bank of Nova Scotia and the Registry Act, R.S.N.S. 1967, c. 265, ss. 17-18, together with Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 47.11
CaseB_TestB: International extension of article 71 jurisdiction over incidental actions in warranty
BaselineB: Statute, principally article 71 of the Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, informed by article 27 of the Civil Code and the international-jurisdiction principle recognized in Alimport and Trower and Sons
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Air-of-reality test for putting a defence to the jury: assuming the supporting evidence is true, there must be some evidence capable of supporting the defence and conveying a sense of reality to it.
BaselineA: Common law, principally Kelsey v. The Queen, Wu v. The King, and R. v. Workman and Huculak.
CaseB_TestB: Appellate-delay framework: Charter s. 11(b) does not apply during appellate proceedings after a conviction, acquittal, or judicial stay; materially prejudicial appellate delay may instead be remedied under s. 7 as an abuse of process.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(b), interpreted in light of R. v. Kalanj, R. v. L. (W.K.), R. v. Jewitt, and R. v. Keyowski.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 116(1) availability test: a charge for disobeying a civil or criminal court order is available whenever statute law, including regulations, does not expressly provide another punishment, penalty, or mode of proceeding.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 116(1), considered alongside s. 8 and the Manitoba Court of Queen’s Bench Rules.
CaseB_TestB: Public-law estoppel bar: estoppel cannot prevent enforcement of a clear legislative provision establishing a regulatory offence where the public authority lacks power to authorize the prohibited conduct.
BaselineB: Combination of common law public-law promissory estoppel from Mount Sinai Hospital Center v. Quebec, Maracle v. Travellers Indemnity Co. of Canada, and St. Ann’s Island Shooting and Fishing Club Ltd. v. The King, and City of Québec By-law VQZ-3, arts. 40, 83 and 359.
Score_Desc: Tests are approximately equal in rule-likeness.

CaseA_TestA: Scope of provincial licensing authority under s. 3(2): “into or through the province” encompasses extra-provincial undertakings operating in, across, into, and out of the province, whether interprovincial or international
BaselineA: Statute: Motor Vehicle Transport Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. M-14, ss. 2, 3(1)-(2), and 5
CaseB_TestB: Purposive Charter interpretation framework: begin with and remain constrained by the constitutional text; use international and comparative sources only as appropriate support or confirmation, with binding sources receiving greater weight than non-binding sources
BaselineB: Constitutional text and common law: the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, especially s. 12, and the purposive interpretation framework from R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supplemented by the presumption of conformity discussed in Reference re Public Service Employee Relations Act (Alta.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Manifestly frivolous” threshold for summary dismissal of criminal applications: the moving party must show an obvious, fundamental flaw making failure necessary, while alleged facts and non-frivolous inferences are assumed true and evidence is not weighed.
BaselineA: Common law summary-dismissal and criminal case-management power, particularly R. v. Vukelich and R. v. Kutynec, with prior threshold formulations discussed in R. v. Cody and R. v. Jordan.
CaseB_TestB: Combined child-luring presumption and reasonable-steps test under Criminal Code ss. 172.1(3) and (4): a representation that the interlocutor is underage triggers a rebuttable presumption, displaced only by evidence of objectively reasonable age-verification steps and a belief that the interlocutor was not underage.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 172.1(3) and 172.1(4), read with the child-luring offence in s. 172.1(1).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effective re-election of mode of trial under Criminal Code s. 492
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, ss. 492 and 496. Section 492 prescribes the sequential requirements for re-election, while s. 496 addresses the indictment following re-election.
CaseB_TestB: Common-law nuisance actionability test for injurious affection where no land is taken
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Expropriations Act, ss. 1(e)(ii) and 21, incorporating the common-law actionability requirement and the four conditions stated in The Queen v. Loiselle; the applicable nuisance inquiry asks whether there was physical injury or substantial interference with the use or enjoyment of land that was unreasonable in all the surrounding circumstances.

CaseA_TestA: Person-in-authority and proprio motu voir dire test under the confessions rule
BaselineA: Common law—principally Erven v. The Queen and Rothman v. The Queen, with the voluntariness rule originating in Ibrahim v. The King and adopted in Prosko v. The King.
CaseB_TestB: Application of Income Tax Act s. 56(2) to dividend payments allegedly diverted to another person

CaseA_TestA: Part performance overcoming a Statute of Frauds-type writing requirement, including against the Crown
BaselineA: Combination of equity and statute: the doctrine of part performance described in Steadman v. Steadman, applied to the writing requirement in s. 21(1)(a) of the Public Highways Act and the definition of an interest in land in s. 1(c) of the Expropriation Act.
CaseB_TestB: Public-order test for annulling or refusing homologation of an arbitral award
BaselineB: Statute: arts. 946.2, 946.5 and 947.2 of the Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, read with art. 2639 of the Civil Code of Québec.

CaseA_TestA: Section 6 coverage test: an insurer is directly liable to an accident victim only if the materialized risk falls within the policy; where an excluded trailer is involved, coverage turns on whether the damage was caused “first and foremost” by use of the trailer rather than the insured automobile.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and contract: s. 6 of the Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, and the policy’s civil-liability coverage and definition of “automobile,” building on General Security Insurance Company of Canada v. Bélanger.

BaselineB: Common law principles of lease interpretation, tenant liability, insurance, and subrogation, particularly Ross Southward Tire Ltd. v. Pyrotech Products Ltd. and Agnew-Surpass Shoe Stores Ltd. v. Cummer-Yonge Investments Ltd.; United Motors Service Inc. v. Hutson was distinguished.

CaseA_TestA: Article 2930 test for actions arising from the direct and immediate consequences of interference with physical integrity
BaselineA: Statute — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2925 and 2930, read with arts. 1457 and 1607, and Cities and Towns Act, s. 586.
CaseB_TestB: Appellate non-intervention in a trial judge’s factual and credibility findings
BaselineB: Judge-made appellate-review doctrine reflected in Latour v. Grenier, Maze v. Empson, Dorval v. Bouvier, Métivier v. Cadorette, and Hood v. Hood.

CaseA_TestA: Service ex juris under Rule 307: whether another forum is more convenient and appropriate for pursuing the action and securing the ends of justice

CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led evidence concerning an unknown third-party suspect: relevance through a sufficient connection, followed by Seaboyer balancing
BaselineB: Common law evidence principles from R. v. Seaboyer, R. v. Corbett, R. v. Cinous, McMillan v. The Queen and R. v. Grandinetti

BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 121(1)(a), informed by Martineau v. La Reine and general criminal-law principles of intention and subjective knowledge

BaselineB: Common law governing solicitors’ contractual duties and appellate review of factual findings; the majority identified no originating precedent for the test.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Garofoli excision test: excise unconstitutionally obtained information and determine whether the remaining information established reasonable grounds such that the search warrant could still have issued.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness simpliciter standard for reviewing an expert tribunal’s decision on a statutory appeal
BaselineA: Common law administrative-law principles from Pezim v. British Columbia (Superintendent of Brokers), informed by ss. 12 and 13 of the Competition Tribunal Act.

BaselineB: Section 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 and s. 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, together with the constitutional-remedies jurisprudence in Canada (Attorney General) v. Hislop and Ontario (Attorney General) v. G.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Secret-commission offence test: agency, knowing acceptance of a benefit concerning the principal’s affairs, and failure to make adequate and timely disclosure of the benefit’s source, amount, and nature
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a)(ii)
CaseB_TestB: Curative proviso test: whether a properly instructed jury, acting reasonably, could have reached a different conclusion absent the error

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal appeal curative-proviso test: the Crown must satisfy the appellate court that a properly instructed jury “could not, as reasonable men, have done otherwise than find the appellant guilty.”

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 88 test for applying provincial laws of general application to Indians: the law applies by federal incorporation unless, and only to the extent that, it is inconsistent with the Indian Act or covers a matter already provided for under that Act.
BaselineA: Statute and constitutional law: Indian Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-6, ss. 2(1), 11 and 88; British Columbia Adoption Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 4, s. 10; and British North America Act, 1867, s. 91(24).

BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), as interpreted through the common-law framework established in R. v. Collins and organized into three categories in R. v. Simmons.

CaseA_TestA: Staged conditional-sentence framework for Aboriginal offenders under ss. 742.1 and 718.2(e)

CaseB_TestB: Balancing a freedom-of-religion claim against countervailing rights, values, and harm

I-16, applied to the student-loan contract and the 1997 and 1998 amendments to the Act respecting financial assistance for students.

BaselineA: Statute: Canada Labour Code, s. 119 and ss. 124 et seq., informed by the Board framework in The Employees of the Regional Comptroller and the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers

BaselineB: Common law doctrine of forum non conveniens, principally as stated in Club Resorts Ltd. v. Van Breda and Amchem Products Inc. v. British Columbia (Workers’ Compensation Board), with the Uniform Court Jurisdiction and Proceedings Transfer Act, s. 11, used as a helpful reference.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable expectation of injury test for refusing access to personal information under s. 22(1)(b) of the Privacy Act
BaselineA: Statute: Privacy Act, ss. 12(1), 22(1)(b), 22(3), 47 and 49, read harmoniously with Official Languages Act, ss. 60 and 72 to 74.
CaseB_TestB: Discretionary adverse inference of causation as a presumption of fact
BaselineB: Combination of statute and precedent: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 2846 to 2849, particularly art. 2849, together with Snell v. Farrell and St-Jean v. Mercier.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 43 framework for granting letters rogatory seeking documents alone: documentary testimony need not be ancillary to oral testimony, provided the evidence is for trial rather than discovery, relevant, within the permissible local scope, and adequately defined.
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 43, informed by the comity principle in Zingre v. The Queen and established judicial-assistance guidelines.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility of defence-led unknown third-party-suspect evidence: the evidence must be relevant through a sufficient connection between similar crimes and evidence that the accused could not have committed the other offence, and is then admissible unless prejudice substantially outweighs probative value.
BaselineB: Common law: the defence-evidence admissibility rule from R. v. Seaboyer and R. v. Corbett, the air-of-reality test from R. v. Cinous, and the sufficient-connection principle from McMillan v. The Queen and R. v. Grandinetti.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Cross-border fresh-pursuit test for retaining peace-officer status and protection under s. 25(4) of the Criminal Code
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 25(4), 449(1)(b), and 450.
CaseB_TestB: Specific-penalty test: a penalty must be assigned to the particular infraction in the collective agreement to deprive an arbitrator of penalty-substitution jurisdiction
BaselineB: Statute and collective agreement: Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-1, s. 157(d), interpreted in conjunction with Article XI(b) of the collective agreement.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Guidelines Order applicability test: a federal “decision making responsibility” exists only where an Act of Parliament imposes an affirmative regulatory duty relating to the proposal; the department responsible for that duty is the initiating department.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and regulation: Department of the Environment Act, ss. 4-6; Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, especially ss. 2, 3, 6, 10, 12 and 14; and the relevant regulatory statute, including Navigable Waters Protection Act, s. 5, or Fisheries Act, ss. 35 and 37.
CaseB_TestB: Contextual test for reversible error in a jury charge: the impugned language must be interpreted in the context of the entire charge, the evidence and the trial as a whole before determining whether it engages a ground of appellate intervention.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 686(1)(a), together with common-law principles governing contextual review of jury charges and the use of post-offence conduct reflected in R. v. Arcangioli and R. v. White.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interest-arbitration jurisdiction under the statutory status quo: once the collective agreement’s conditions for invoking arbitration are met, s. 70(1) preserves that right through the statutory period, and the right need exist only when notice to arbitrate is given, not when the award is issued.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and collective agreement: s. 70(1) of The Labour Relations Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 232, together with arts. 16 and 18 of the Haldimand agreement and arts. 15 and 16 of the Perth agreement; Bradburn v. Wentworth Arms Hotel Limited supplied the prior statutory interpretation.
CaseB_TestB: Exception to the rule against collateral attack for a pre-trial division and severance order regulating the judicial process within the same litigation: the trial judge may review and set aside the order if it was erroneously made.
BaselineB: Common law rule against collateral attack established in Wilson v. The Queen and reaffirmed in R. v. Meltzer, R. v. Garofoli, and Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor, operating in the statutory context of Criminal Code ss. 590(3), 591(3)-(4), and 645(5).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a): “all that is necessary” is that the insured have an insurable interest; absent a policy requirement, the nature of that interest need not be declared.
BaselineA: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240, statutory condition 10(a), read with Civil Code arts. 2480, 2571 and 2572.
CaseB_TestB: Police appropriation of bodily samples initially seized for non-criminal purposes: determine whether police conduct constitutes an independent state seizure or makes the initially valid seizure unreasonable.
BaselineB: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the principles from Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Dyment, applied alongside ss. 16(2), 16(4) and 16(5) of the Coroners Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness test for departing from the knock-and-announce rule: the Crown must provide evidence that the police had reasonable grounds to fear harm or destruction of evidence, assessed using information reasonably available when they acted and with operational latitude afforded to police.
BaselineA: Common law knock-and-announce rule established in Eccles v. Bourque and refined in R. v. Genest, operating within the reasonable-manner requirement under s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms recognized in R. v. Collins.
CaseB_TestB: Implied-assertion hearsay test: a verbal implied assertion tendered for the truth of its contents is hearsay and presumptively inadmissible unless admitted through a traditional exception or the necessity-and-reliability framework.
BaselineB: Common law hearsay doctrine and the principled necessity-and-reliability framework developed in R. v. Khan, R. v. Mapara, and R. v. Khelawon.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Property is used or held in carrying on a business when it is truly employed and risked in the business, such that its withdrawal would have a decidedly destabilizing effect on corporate operations; the inquiry is whether it fulfilled a requirement for doing business, not whether that particular property was indispensable.
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) and (b), interpreted in light of The Queen v. Marsh & McLennan, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Crown appeal from acquittal test: the Crown must establish, with a reasonable degree of certainty, that the verdict would not necessarily have been the same absent the legal error.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Morin.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper two-stage duty-of-care test for statutory regulators
BaselineA: Common law: the Anns/Kamloops duty-of-care framework, as clarified in Cooper v. Hobart, applied in light of the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8, especially ss. 9, 33, 51 and 61.
CaseB_TestB: Exceptional fiscal-crisis justification for limiting Charter rights under s. 1
BaselineB: Constitutional law: s. 1 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the Oakes framework, informed by prior decisions addressing financial justifications, including Martin, Singh, Lee, Schachter, Figueroa and PSAC.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Effective termination of a continuing guarantee requires written notice that unequivocally communicates termination; an expression of wish or preference is insufficient, although no set form of words is required.
BaselineA: Contractual guarantee, cl. 4, interpreted under common law principles: liability for future advances could be determined by written notice delivered to the bank manager.
CaseB_TestB: Evidence of an accused's silence is inadmissible unless the Crown establishes real relevance and a proper basis for its admission; no adverse inference may ordinarily be drawn from exercising the right to silence.
BaselineB: Combination of the common law right to silence, as discussed in Rothman v. The Queen, R. v. Robertson, and R. v. Symonds, and s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, particularly as recognized in Hebert v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Article IV treaty-residence test: a person must be liable to comprehensive tax on worldwide income by reason of an enumerated or similarly personal criterion; a fact that merely informs source-based tax liability is insufficient.
BaselineA: Statute and treaty: Canada–United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I, incorporating the Canada–United States Income Tax Convention (1980), especially arts. IV(1) and XII; informed by Income Tax Act, s. 212(1)(d), and U.S. Internal Revenue Code, §§ 864, 882 and 883.
CaseB_TestB: Valid-refusal notice test: before the two-year limitation period begins, an insurer must explain the entire dispute-resolution process in clear language for an unsophisticated person, including mediation, subsequent arbitration or litigation, mediation as a prerequisite, and the applicable time limits.
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, ss. 279 to 283, especially s. 281(5), and the Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, especially ss. 71, 72 and 94.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory limiting instruction for highly prejudicial bad-character evidence: the jury must be told the evidence's limited purpose and specifically warned not to infer guilt from propensity.
BaselineA: Common law, principally R. v. D. (L.E.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 111, with the bad-character evidence framework from Morris v. The Queen, [1983] 2 S.C.R. 190.
CaseB_TestB: Recent-fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: once recent fabrication is alleged, prior complaints are admissible to prove that they were made, but not to prove the truth of their contents.
BaselineB: Common law prior-consistent-statement rule and recent-fabrication exception; no originating case is identified in the decision.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Consequences when a witness breaches an exclusion order: the witness is not necessarily disqualified, exclusion remains discretionary, and evidentiary weight is for the trier of fact; once a judge demonstrates awareness of this rule, the judge may be presumed to have applied it to other breaching witnesses without repeating an oral caution.
BaselineA: Common law, including Cook v. Nethercotte, Thomas v. David, Chandler v. Home, Black v. Besse, and R. v. Carefoot.
CaseB_TestB: Crown immunity from discovery remains unless clearly and unequivocally lifted by legislation; s. 27 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act lifts it only where the Crown is a party, not where it is a non-party.
BaselineB: Combination of the common law Crown immunity from discovery and statute and regulation, principally s. 17 of the Interpretation Act, ss. 27 and 34 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, and s. 7 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings (Provincial Court) Regulations.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of a Quebec inter vivos trust for unborn primary beneficiaries: trustee acceptance and temporary ownership permit the trust; art. 981a incorporates public-order prohibitions but not constraints inherent to direct gifts, and the trust lapses only if no actual or eventual beneficiary can exist.
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code arts. 981a, 981b and 981l, read with arts. 608, 754-55, 765-72 and 929; informed by Curran v. Davis and related trust jurisprudence.
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdiction and enforceability of injunctions against non-parties: non-parties may be held in contempt if they are apprised of the order and given an opportunity to comply, and the order must be carefully worded, fair and not unduly broad.
BaselineB: Common law and equity: courts' inherent jurisdiction and the contempt principles recognized in Attorney-General v. Times Newspapers Ltd., Seaward v. Paterson, Bartle & Gibson Co. and International Longshoremen's Association; supplemented by Law and Equity Act, s. 36, and Criminal Code, s. 11.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fraud by “other fraudulent means”: objective dishonesty and deprivation combined with subjective knowledge of the conduct and risk of deprivation
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 380(1), as interpreted in R. v. Olan and R. v. Théroux.
CaseB_TestB: Union’s duty of representation toward former employees during collective bargaining
BaselineB: Statute — Quebec Labour Code, R.S.Q., c. C-27, particularly s. 47.2, informed by Noël v. Société d’énergie de la Baie James and Centre hospitalier Régina Ltée v. Labour Court.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in discretionary family-property reapportionment: intervention is justified only if the trial judge misdirected himself or the decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice.
BaselineA: Common law appellate non-interference principles from Harper v. Harper, applied to discretion under ss. 43 and 51 of the Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to correct prejudicial Crown remarks: a trial judge must comment when the remarks are prejudicial to a degree sufficient to require correction so that the defence is fairly put to the jury.
BaselineB: Common law jury-charge and trial-fairness principles, combined with the curative proviso in s. 686(1)(b)(iii) of the Criminal Code.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid partnership test: at formation, the evidence must disclose that the parties were (1) carrying on a business, (2) in common, and (3) with a view to profit, assessed pragmatically from the true agreement, intentions, and all surrounding circumstances.
BaselineA: Combination of the common-law partnership test stated in Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada and elaborated in Backman v. Canada, applied for deductions under s. 96 of the Income Tax Act.
CaseB_TestB: Substantive W. (D.) jury-instruction test: read as a whole, the charge must make clear that the Crown always bears the burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt, that the jury must not merely choose between competing accounts, and that disbelief of the accused does not establish guilt.
BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. W. (D.), as further explained in R. v. S. (W.D.) and R. v. Avetysan.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Accused’s right to be present during jury selection and juror-partiality proceedings
BaselineA: Combination of statute and prior jurisprudence: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 569(2), 577(1), 598-600 and 613(1)(b)(iii), interpreted in light of Basarabas and Spek v. The Queen, Vézina and Côté v. The Queen, and Meunier v. The Queen; also Nova Scotia Juries Act, S.N.S. 1969, c. 12, s. 4(2).
CaseB_TestB: Test for an appellate court to set aside an acquittal and enter a conviction instead of ordering a new trial
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4)(b)(ii), with the common law test established in Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Courville, affirmed in Courville v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law test for a search incident to lawful arrest: no additional reasonable and probable grounds are required, but the search must pursue a valid criminal-justice objective and must not be abusive or disproportionate.
BaselineA: Common law search-incident-to-arrest power, particularly R. v. Brezack, R. v. Morrison, and R. v. Miller, informed by the police-powers framework in Dedman v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 test for warrantless child apprehension: apprehension may occur where there is serious harm or a risk of serious harm, as a last resort, provided that a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing is available.
BaselineB: Constitutional and statutory combination: s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, as developed in B. (R.) and New Brunswick v. G. (J.), applied to ss. 17, 21(1), 27(1), and 29(1) of Manitoba's Child and Family Services Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused to participate in a police line-up
BaselineA: Common-law principles of relevance and admissibility, including R. v. Brager and R. v. John; informed by the common-law privilege against self-incrimination
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional limit on provincial inquiries functioning as substitute criminal investigations of named persons for specific offences
BaselineB: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91(27) and 92(14), as interpreted in Faber v. The Queen, Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, Attorney General (Que.) and Keable v. Attorney General (Can.), and O'Hara v. British Columbia
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Factual causation for unlawful-act manslaughter: the unlawful act must be a contributing cause of death outside the de minimis range, proved beyond a reasonable doubt on all expert and lay evidence
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, s. 205(1), and common-law causation and thin-skull principles reflected in R. v. Larkin, R. v. Cato, R. v. Garforth, R. v. Blaue, and R. v. Nicholson
CaseB_TestB: Anns two-stage test for recognizing a novel duty of care for pure economic loss: proximity establishing a prima facie duty, followed by policy considerations that may negate or limit it
BaselineB: Common law—Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, as adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and applied to pure economic loss in cases including Canadian National Railway Co. v. Norsk Pacific Steamship Co.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Interpretation of an unqualified extradition specialty undertaking: read the undertaking in context and in light of its object, purpose, and general international-law principles; absent clear terms, immunity ends after a reasonable opportunity to return when the extraditee voluntarily remains in the requesting state.
BaselineA: Combination of the Canada-Brazil extradition arrangement, the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, ss. 2, 3, 33 and 40, and international-law principles governing specialty and treaty interpretation.
CaseB_TestB: Intertwined-issues rule for the curative proviso: when an alleged error of law is properly before the Court and the Crown invokes the proviso, the Court may determine whether the verdict can be saved under s. 686(1)(b)(iii) without a separate grant of leave.
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), and the common-law appellate principle stated in R. v. Keegstra.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal licensing jurisdiction test: a council may refuse a licence only on grounds peculiar to the applicant and within its licensing powers; absent express statutory authority to prohibit, it cannot use licensing discretion to prohibit a lawful type of business.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: s. 455 of the Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, read in the context of the Act and the principle from Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo that a power to regulate a trade does not, absent express authority, include a power to prohibit a lawful trade.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional fair-process test for the IRPA security-certificate scheme: the named person must remain reasonably informed through an incompressible minimum of disclosure sufficient to give meaningful instructions and guidance, while the designated judge uses the statutory scheme's safeguards and discretion to ensure overall fairness.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional law and statute: s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and Division 9 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, particularly ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1), 85.1, 85.2, 85.4 and 85.5, building on the fair-process principles established in Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility at sentencing of evidence tending to establish another offence for which the offender has not been convicted
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, Part XXIII, especially ss. 718 to 718.2, 724(3)(e), 725, 726.1 and 742.1, informed by Lees v. The Queen, R. v. Gardiner and R. v. Edwards.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in undercover online communications with a child who is a stranger
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 8, and the common law reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework from cases including R. v. Marakah, R. v. Cole, R. v. Spencer, R. v. Tessling and R. v. Edwards; also Criminal Code, ss. 183 and 184.2.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation: representation by words or conduct inducing detrimental reliance; silence qualifies only where there is a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law estoppel by representation, including Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd. and Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha v. Dawson’s Bank, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Rebutting the statutory presumption under s. 212(3): the jury may consider all the evidence, without isolating a particular and severable item of evidence to the contrary
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fingerprint inference of possession: whether fingerprints support possession depends on “all of the circumstances of the case and all of the evidence adduced,” not a hard-and-fast rule
BaselineA: Common law evidentiary principles from R. v. O’Keefe and R. v. Mehrabnia, applied to statutory possession under Criminal Code, s. 4(3), and Food and Drugs Act, ss. 46 and 48(2)
CaseB_TestB: Review Board treatment-condition jurisdiction: a Board may bind hospital authorities and supervise or make conditions regarding treatment, but may not prescribe or impose treatment
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, Part XX.1, principally ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1), read with ss. 672.1, 672.38, 672.72 and 672.78
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Three-stage s. 96 test for determining whether adjudicative powers may be conferred on a provincially appointed tribunal
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96, combined with the common-law three-stage framework established in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714
CaseB_TestB: Flexible, cumulative three-factor test for public interest standing
BaselineB: Common law — the public interest standing framework established in Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of juvenile delinquency findings to contradict testimony under Canada Evidence Act s. 12
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, s. 12(1), read with Juvenile Delinquents Act, ss. 2(1), 3 and 20(1). A delinquency consisting of a Criminal Code violation is an “offence”, an adjudication of delinquency is a “conviction”, and an admitted conviction requires no additional documentary proof absent exceptional circumstances clearly showing error.
CaseB_TestB: Amendment of an indictment where the evidence varies from a particular of the charged narcotic
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, ss. 529(4)-(5), 613(1)(b)(i) and 613(3), read with Narcotic Control Act, ss. 2 and 4 and Schedule item 3. A narcotic subtype is a particular rather than a distinct offence; an amendment may be made unless prejudice is irreparable, with curable prejudice addressed by adjournment.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional approach and rough upper limit for non-pecuniary personal injury damages
BaselineA: Common law — Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Arnold v. Teno, and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57 (Prince George), as refined in Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: At-fault motorist and unbroken chain of causation test for inadequately insured motorist coverage
BaselineB: Combination of statute and insurance policy — Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, s. 239(1)(a), and Ontario Policy Change Form 44R, s. 3, informed by the common law test in Amos v. Insurance Corp. of British Columbia
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hypothetical primary infringement under Copyright Act s. 27(2)(e): an exclusive licensee may sue third parties, but cannot establish infringement where the owner-licensor is the hypothetical infringer because an owner cannot infringe its own copyright.
BaselineA: Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, particularly ss. 2.7, 13(4)-(7), 27(1)-(2)(e), and 36(1)-(2).
CaseB_TestB: Retrospective punishment test under Charter s. 11(h): the dominant consideration is the extent to which retrospective legislation thwarts an offender's settled expectation of liberty; a change is generally not punitive unless it substantially increases the risk of additional incarceration, while automatic lengthening of incarceration clearly constitutes double punishment.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h), building on R. v. Wigglesworth, R. v. Rodgers, and Cunningham v. Canada.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual characterization of a voluntary association’s by-laws and natural justice obligations for prescription purposes
BaselineA: Combination of the Civil Code of Lower Canada, particularly arts. 361, 1024, 1057, 2242 and 2261(2), the Companies Act, R.S.Q. 1941, c. 276, s. 214, the association’s by-laws, and prior contractual-association jurisprudence.
CaseB_TestB: Priority-by-registration test for lien and mortgage interests not expressly ranked by the Mechanics’ Lien Act
BaselineB: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, particularly ss. 14(1), 16 and 20-22, together with The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Essence-of-the-crime test for determining whether a charge falls within an extradition-crime category
BaselineA: Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, s. 2, together with s. 17 of the 1925 Supplementary Convention; the Court held that the controlling inquiry is "what is the essence of the crime charged," regardless of the Canadian statute under which it might be prosecuted.
CaseB_TestB: Purpose-based test distinguishing permissible credibility impeachment from prohibited incriminating use of prior testimony
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 13, and Canada Evidence Act, s. 5(2), informed by R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion; prior testimony may be used solely to challenge credibility but not to establish its contents or the accused's guilt.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unified three-step Meiorin test for establishing a bona fide occupational requirement: rational connection, honest and good-faith adoption, and reasonable necessity including accommodation to the point of undue hardship
BaselineA: Statute and common law: British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1) and 13(4), building on the previously bifurcated discrimination frameworks from O’Malley, Etobicoke, Central Alberta Dairy Pool, and related cases.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage pursuit-of-profit test for determining whether an activity constitutes a business or property source of income
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Income Tax Act, principally ss. 3 and 9, with related provisions including ss. 18(1)(a), 18(1)(h), 20(1)(c)(i), 67, and 248(1); the Court restricted the reasonable-expectation-of-profit approach associated with Moldowan v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Temporal priority test for statutory wage liens: the lien attaches from the date wages are earned, affects only the employer’s property or equity, leaves prior mortgages unaffected, and prevails over later dispositions
BaselineA: Statute: Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), ss. 5 and 5A, particularly s. 5A(1)-(2)
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive-law framework for forced dissolution: special legislation applies first, but Civil Code of Québec arts. 355 to 364 fill any gap where no specific scheme governs the dissolution sought
BaselineB: Statute: Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334 and 355 to 364, read with the Companies Act, ss. 28, 29, 224, 227 and 231, and Code of Civil Procedure, art. 829
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal criminal law power test: a valid criminal law must contain a prohibition backed by a penal sanction, be directed at a legitimate criminal public purpose, and not be a colourable intrusion into provincial jurisdiction.
BaselineA: Combination of Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(27), and the common law framework from Proprietary Articles Trade Association, the Margarine Reference, and Scowby v. Glendinning.
CaseB_TestB: Individualized reasonable-accommodation test for applying a collectively negotiated termination-after-absence clause: the clause is a significant but non-determinative factor, and undue hardship must be assessed globally from the beginning of the absence in light of the employee's particular circumstances.
BaselineB: Combination of Quebec's Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20, the collective agreement, and the common law accommodation framework from Meiorin and related cases.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Identifiability and traceability test for whether a statutory tax trust falls under Bankruptcy Act s. 47(a): identifiable or traceable property is excluded as trust property; otherwise the Crown's claim falls under s. 107(1)(j).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j); Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18; general principles of trust law; Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board.
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 numbers-warrant and local-facilities framework, including the minority-language board's management and control over school location and the limits on ministerial approval.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional, statutory, and regulatory law: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23; School Act, R.S.P.E.I. 1988, c. S-2.1, especially ss. 112 and 128(2); School Act Regulations, especially ss. 6.01(f), 6.07, 6.08, and 6.11; and the sliding-scale framework established in Mahe v. Alberta.

CaseB_TestB: Stillman conscription-and-discoverability framework for trial fairness and exclusion of evidence under Charter s. 24(2)
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), building principally on the framework established in R. v. Collins and refined in subsequent cases
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking: once the accused is proved to have sold the restricted drug, a rebuttable presumption of the requisite intent arises, and conviction follows unless evidence raises a reasonable doubt based on an honest belief negating mens rea.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: ss. 40 and 42 of the Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, together with the mens rea and rebuttable-presumption principles from Beaver v. The Queen, The Queen v. King, and R. v. Blondin.
CaseB_TestB: Limits on judicial intervention: a trial judge may and sometimes must question or interrupt witnesses, but must intervene in a manner that preserves the appearance of impartiality; conduct creating doubt about impartiality or the impression that the judge assisted the prosecution requires a new trial.
BaselineB: Common law, principally the appearance-of-justice principle from R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy and the judicial-intervention principles stated in R. v. Darlyn, Jones v. National Coal Board, R. v. Torbiak and Campbell, Yuill v. Yuill, and R. v. Bateman.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 2(b) protection for consumer counter-advertising: criticism of a business is protected expression, and restricting access to effective, affordable means such as signs infringes freedom of expression through its purpose or practical effect.
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b), as interpreted in Irwin Toy, Ford, Rocket, and Ramsden.
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights property due process test: procedural protections arise only in individualized adjudication, while clear and unambiguous legislation may expropriate property without compensation or a pre-enactment hearing.
BaselineB: Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e), combined with the common law governing procedural fairness and uncompensated expropriation, including Lapointe, Manitoba Fisheries, and Wells.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 373 school-tax valuation rule: value at real value the property taxable in each municipality, without extending one municipality's machinery exemption to others
BaselineA: Statute — Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373, read with Cities and Towns Act, s. 488
CaseB_TestB: Elements of corruptly accepting a secret commission, including adequate and timely disclosure and no corrupt-bargain requirement
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a)(ii) (formerly s. 383(1)(a))
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trustee’s duty to preserve insurance protecting secured creditors: the trustee must keep or replace insurance on all insurable bankrupt property, including hypothecated property, insure it adequately as a prudent administrator, and notify the secured creditor if insurance cannot be obtained.
BaselineA: Primarily statute: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 2 definitions of “property” and “secured creditor” and 9(1)-(2), interpreted alongside the hypothec deed’s insurance clause and the reasonable-conduct standard for fault.
CaseB_TestB: Fourth-head Pemsel test for charitable status: the organization’s substantive main purpose must provide a public benefit in a way the law recognizes as charitable, assessed through analogous precedents, the Income Tax Act scheme, and whether the proposed development is incremental rather than wholesale reform.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 149.1(1) and 248(1), together with the Pemsel common law approach as adopted and refined in The King v. Assessors of the Town of Sunny Brae, Guaranty Trust Co. of Canada v. Minister of National Revenue, and Vancouver Society of Immigrant and Visible Minority Women v. M.N.R.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent tort and contract liability: a contractual relationship may create sufficient proximity for an independent common law duty of care, but tort cannot circumvent an express contractual exclusion or limitation of liability.
