CaseB_TestB: Exclusive foreign choice-of-forum clause test: where a valid clause clearly applies and indicates an exclusive intention to oust Quebec jurisdiction, art. 3148(2) C.C.Q. prevails over art. 3139 and the Quebec court must decline jurisdiction, subject to specified exceptions.
BaselineB: Statute — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 3148(2), 3139 and 3135, interpreted with reference to arts. 3149 and 3151 and the Code's private international law framework.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Independent delictual fault test for electing delictual liability despite a contract
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code, art. 1053, informed by Ross v. Dunstall; Ross v. Emery and Alliance Assurance Co. v. Dominion Electric Protection Co.
CaseB_TestB: Automatic nullity and new-trial rule upon a reasonable apprehension of judicial bias
BaselineB: Common law: Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 engagement for Canadian requests for foreign searches: assess the specific Canadian governmental action; a letter merely requesting an independent foreign search or seizure does not itself engage s. 8.

CaseB_TestB: Duty of care for failing to prevent a third party’s intentional wrongdoing: reasonable foreseeability and sufficient proximity establish a prima facie duty, subject to compelling residual policy considerations that negate or limit it.
BaselineB: Common law duty-of-care framework from Cooper v. Hobart, Childs v. Desormeaux, and Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board, informed for the government claim by the Mining Safety Act, particularly ss. 42 and 43.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exclusive statutory-remedy rule: a comprehensive human rights enforcement scheme forecloses both a direct civil action for breach and a common law discrimination action based on the statute’s public policy
BaselineA: Combination of common law and The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, particularly ss. 4(1)(a)-(b), 14b(6), 14c and 14d
CaseB_TestB: Undue-obstacle reasonable-accommodation test: a discriminatory transportation barrier must be removed unless the carrier proves that accommodation would impose undue hardship

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 4 test for departing from presumptive child-support Table amounts when the paying parent earns over $150,000
BaselineA: Regulation — Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, especially ss. 1, 3, 4(b) and 21(4), informed by Divorce Act, s. 26.1(2).
CaseB_TestB: Classification test for determining whether Part 5 or the general provisions of Part 2 govern a comprehensive multi-risk insurance policy
BaselineB: Statute and regulation — British Columbia Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, especially ss. 3(a) and 119 and Part 5 statutory condition 14, together with Insurance Classes Regulation, B.C. Reg. 337/90, s. 2.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: When a factual finding supporting an acquittal constitutes an error of law permitting a Crown appeal

CaseB_TestB: Section 137.1 anti-SLAPP dismissal framework

CaseA_TestA: Misfeasance in public office: deliberate and unlawful conduct in the exercise of public functions, coupled with subjective awareness that the conduct is unlawful and likely to injure the plaintiff, plus causation and compensable injury

CaseA_TestA: Duty to correct Crown remarks that are sufficiently prejudicial to require judicial comment so the defence is fairly put to the jury
BaselineA: Common law governing jury charges, together with the curative proviso in s. 686(1)(b)(iii) of the Criminal Code
CaseB_TestB: Broker commission for voluntary prevention: the broker must prove a valid brokerage contract, performance of its own obligations, and seller fault preventing fulfillment of the conditions for compensation
BaselineB: Clause 6.1(4) of the brokerage contract and art. 1503 of the Civil Code of Québec
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Marked-departure test for criminal negligence, including the relevance of consequences to characterizing the accused's conduct
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 202(1)-(2) and 203 (now R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 219 and 220), as interpreted in R. v. Tutton, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1392.
CaseB_TestB: Canadian-supplier standing test for procurement complaints before the Canadian International Trade Tribunal under the Agreement on Internal Trade
BaselineB: Combination of statute, regulation, and incorporated trade agreement: Canadian International Trade Tribunal Act, ss. 30.1 and 30.11(1); Canadian International Trade Tribunal Procurement Inquiry Regulations, ss. 3(1), 7(1), and 11; and Agreement on Internal Trade, especially arts. 101, 501, 502, and 518.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Three-part test for establishing a constitutional convention: identify the precedents, determine whether the actors believed themselves bound by a rule, and identify a reason for the rule; actor recognition is an essential threshold requirement and cannot remain wholly inarticulate.
BaselineA: Constitutional convention doctrine (non-statutory), particularly the Jennings test adopted in Re: Resolution to amend the Constitution, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 753.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contextual test for whether an appealable order is sufficiently effective to satisfy a purchaser’s title requisition
BaselineA: Common law principles from Re West and Leonard v. Wharton, applied to a discharge order under s. 62 of The Conveyancing and Law of Property Act
CaseB_TestB: Preliminary-inquiry committal test, including limited weighing of the whole evidence where the Crown relies on circumstantial evidence

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Child-witness screen order and constitutional fair-trial test under Criminal Code s. 486(2.1)
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, s. 486(2.1), interpreted against Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 11(d).
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility and challenge of a prior conviction on a similar-fact-evidence voir dire
BaselineB: Common law: the similar-fact-evidence framework from R. v. Arp and R. v. Handy, informed by British Columbia (Attorney General) v. Malik and R. v. Mahalingan.

CaseA_TestA: Interprovincial-matters test: pollution that is truly interprovincial falls within Parliament’s exclusive residual authority, while provincial legislative authority is territorially limited

CaseB_TestB: Patently unreasonable or flagrant-abuse threshold for judicial review of a tribunal protected by a privative clause

CaseA_TestA: Four-part test for lawful warrantless arrest on private premises
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 450(1)(a), and the common law entry requirements established in Eccles v. Bourque and traced to Semayne's Case
CaseB_TestB: Two-step section 15 test requiring denial of an equality right and discrimination in purpose or effect

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Declaratory relief should be declined where legislation assigns the disputed issue to a specialized tribunal, particularly where a declaration would serve little or no useful purpose.

CaseA_TestA: Colour of right is unavailable unless the offence embraces that concept, and a mistake of law is no defence

BaselineB: Statute and precedent — The Saskatchewan Human Rights Code, s. 14(1)(b), interpreted in light of Canada (Human Rights Commission) v. Taylor
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Conditions under Criminal Code s. 507 for preferring an indictment containing additional counts disclosed by evidence at a preliminary inquiry.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 507(1)-(3), interpreted in light of ss. 496, 504 and 505.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility and assessment of evidence in Aboriginal-rights claims: oral histories must be useful and reasonably reliable, subject to exclusionary discretion, and the claim must be proved by persuasive evidence on a balance of probabilities.

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Construction-contract status of a lessee for workmen’s privileges, requiring a claim against the owner based on an undertaking to pay the construction price
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 984 et seq., 1060, 2013e and 2013f.
CaseB_TestB: Two-part test for contractual mental-distress damages: a contemplated psychological benefit and sufficiently serious mental suffering
BaselineB: Common law: the contractual damages and remoteness principle from Hadley v. Baxendale, as recognized for mental distress in Vorvis v. Insurance Corp. of British Columbia.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Judicial-discretion test for refusing an adjournment needed to exercise the right to counsel: refusal requires reasons based on established facts and is reviewable if those reasons are not well founded in law.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 577(3) and 613, supplemented by Talbot v. Regina and Spataro v. Regina.
CaseB_TestB: Equitable-compensation test for a non-trust breach of fiduciary duty: compensate loss fairly attributable to the particular breach, informed by common-law principles of causation, remoteness, and mitigation where policy objectives coincide.

BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 1, as interpreted in prior SCC vagueness jurisprudence.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseB_TestB: Stringent conjunctive test for setting aside a conviction based on misapprehension of evidence

JudgeA: McLachlin C.J. and LeBel, Abella, Cromwell, Karakatsanis and Wagner JJ. (joint reasons)

CaseA_TestA: Kienapple two-nexus test for barring multiple convictions
BaselineA: Common law — the rule against multiple convictions established in Kienapple v. The Queen and refined in Côté v. The Queen and Krug v. The Queen.

BaselineA: Contract, specifically the price-adjustment provision in clause 9 of the parties’ agreement

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseB_TestB: Three-part test for a stay or interim release: a serious question, irreparable harm, and a balance of convenience favouring the applicant

CaseA_TestA: Duty to instruct the jury on an unadvanced defence that is revealed by, or reasonably inferable from, the evidence

CaseA_TestA: Two-stage professional-discipline participation rule: Discipline Committee members may participate when Convocation considers their report because this is the second stage of a single proceeding, and s. 39(4)'s express disqualification applies only to the specified reprimand appeals.

CaseA_TestA: Remedial constructive trust for matrimonial property: where an untitled spouse’s direct or indirect contribution enabled acquisition of an asset and the titled spouse would otherwise be unjustly enriched—requiring an enrichment, corresponding deprivation, and no juristic reason—the court may impose a trust and distribute the property equitably according to the spouses’ contributions.
BaselineA: Common law equity, particularly the unjust-enrichment and constructive-trust principles discussed in Deglman v. Guaranty Trust Company, Murdoch v. Murdoch, and Peter Kiewit Sons' Co. of Canada v. Eakins Construction Ltd.

BaselineB: Common law right of access to judicial records and the court’s supervisory power over its records, principally established in Attorney General of Nova Scotia v. MacIntyre; Nova Scotia Civil Procedure Rule 30.11(6) informed the treatment and custody of exhibits.

CaseA_TestA: Bilingual common-meaning test for interpreting “tetracycline and its derivatives”: each official-language version is read in its own language, and the concept applicable to both versions is selected—here, a thing actually derived from another.
BaselineA: Statute and regulation: Official Languages Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. O-2, s. 8(2)(b), applied to s. 4 and Schedule A, tariff item 92944-1, of Order in Council SOR/69-8 under the Customs Tariff Act.

BaselineB: Common law and constitutional structure: superior courts’ inherent jurisdiction and statutory courts’ necessarily implied powers, as described in MacMillan Bloedel Ltd. v. Simpson, R. v. BaselineB: Combination of statute, constitutional law, and precedent: the Forest Practices Code of British Columbia Act, ss. 130-141, especially ss. 131(8) and 141(1); ss. 35 and 52 of the Constitution Act, 1982; and the approach established concurrently in Nova Scotia (Workers’ Compensation Board) v. Martin. The Court extended that approach to s. 35 questions and held that practical considerations generally do not rebut the presumption.

Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Context-sensitive section 8 reasonableness test for administrative or regulatory seizures

BaselineA: Statute — Moncton Consolidation Act, 1946 (N.B.), s. 6, interpreted with the New Brunswick Interpretation Act, R.S.N.B. 1973, c. I-13, s. 17

E-10, ss. 4-6; Environmental Assessment and Review Process Guidelines Order, SOR/84-467, especially ss. 2, 3, 6, 10, 12 and 14; applied with Navigable Waters Protection Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. N-22, s. 5, and Fisheries Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-14, ss. 35 and 37.
CaseB_TestB: Contextual test for reviewing an alleged error in a jury charge: the impugned words must be interpreted in the context of the entire charge, the evidence, and the trial as a whole, and ambiguity is not automatically resolved in the accused’s favour.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a), together with the jurisprudence governing jury instructions and post-offence conduct, particularly R. v. Arcangioli and R. v. White.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Preservation of the right to invoke interest arbitration after collective-agreement expiry under s. 70(1)
BaselineA: Statute and collective agreement: s. 70(1) of The Labour Relations Act and the interest-arbitration provisions in articles 16 and 15 of the respective collective agreements
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdictional test for dividing or severing counts: the indictment must first be preferred, and only the trial judge may make the order
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Criminal Code, ss. 590(3), 591(3)-(4), and 645(5), interpreted in light of R. v. Chabot
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory condition 10(a) is satisfied if the insured has an insurable interest; a tenant contractually obliged to insure the leased property has such an interest and need not separately specify its nature
BaselineA: Combination of statute and civil law: Insurance Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 295, s. 240, statutory conditions 1 and 10(a), and Civil Code arts. 2480, 2571 and 2572; informed by Wandlyn Motels v. Commerce General Insurance Company
CaseB_TestB: Section 8 test for police appropriation of bodily samples initially seized for a non-criminal purpose: determine whether police conduct constitutes an independent seizure or makes the original seizure unreasonable
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional and statutory law: s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and ss. 16(2) and 16(5) of Ontario's Coroners Act, as interpreted through Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Dyment
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonableness test for departing from the knock-and-announce rule: the Crown must establish reasonable grounds, based on information available when police acted, for concern about harm or destruction of evidence; the search is assessed overall with operational latitude afforded to police.
BaselineA: Common law knock-and-announce rule from Eccles v. Bourque and R. v. Genest, applied through s. 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the reasonable-search framework from R. v. Collins.
CaseB_TestB: Implied-assertion hearsay test: an implied verbal assertion tendered for the truth of its contents is hearsay and presumptively inadmissible unless a traditional exception applies or necessity and reliability are established.
BaselineB: Common law hearsay doctrine and the principled necessity-and-reliability framework developed in R. v. Khan, R. v. Mapara and R. v. Khelawon.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Property employed and risked in a business test: whether the property fulfilled a requirement necessary to do business, such that its withdrawal would have a decidedly destabilizing effect on corporate operations
BaselineA: Statute: Income Tax Act, s. 129(4)(a)(ii) and (b), interpreted in light of The Queen v. Marsh & McLennan, Ltd. and March Shipping Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue
CaseB_TestB: Crown new-trial test following an acquittal: whether the Crown establishes with a reasonable degree of certainty that the verdict would not necessarily have been the same absent the legal error
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 686(4), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and reaffirmed in R. v. Morin
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Anns/Cooper two-stage duty-of-care test for a statutory regulator
BaselineA: Common law: the Anns duty-of-care test, adopted in Kamloops and clarified in Cooper v. Hobart, applied with reference to the Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8, especially ss. 9, 33, 51 and 61.
CaseB_TestB: Law contextual-factor test for discrimination under s. 15(1), as applied to acquired pay-equity rights
BaselineB: Constitutional text and precedent: s. 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the contextual equality framework established in Law v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unequivocal written notice test for terminating future liability under a continuing guarantee
BaselineA: Contract: s. 4 of the Bank’s Guarantee and Postponement of Claim, permitting termination of liability for future advances by written notice delivered to the branch manager.
CaseB_TestB: Admissibility test for questions and evidence concerning an accused’s exercise of the right to silence
BaselineB: Combination of the common law right to silence and s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, informed by Rothman v. The Queen, R. v. Robertson, R. v. Symonds, R. v. Woolley, and Hebert v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Treaty-residence test: liability to tax must arise from an enumerated or similar criterion imposing comprehensive taxation on worldwide income, not merely source taxation
BaselineA: Statute/treaty: Canada–United States Tax Convention Act, 1984, Schedule I, implementing the Canada–United States Income Tax Convention (1980), especially Article IV(1), read with Articles I and XII
CaseB_TestB: Valid-refusal test for triggering the limitation period: the insurer must clearly explain the entire dispute-resolution process and its essential steps and time limits
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: Insurance Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. I.8, ss. 279–283, especially s. 281(5), and the Statutory Accident Benefits Schedule, O. Reg. 776/93, especially ss. 71, 62, 72 and 94
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory limited-use jury instruction for highly prejudicial bad-character evidence: the jury must be told of the evidence's permitted purpose and specifically warned not to infer guilt from propensity.
BaselineA: Common law, particularly R. v. D. (L.E.), [1989] 2 S.C.R. 111.
CaseB_TestB: Recent-fabrication exception for prior consistent statements: once recent fabrication is alleged, prior complaints are admissible to rebut it only as proof that the complaints were made, not for the truth of their contents.
BaselineB: Common law prior-consistent-statement and recent-fabrication doctrine; no originating case was identified in the reasons.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Treatment of a witness who breaches an exclusion order: the witness is not necessarily disqualified, exclusion remains discretionary, and the weight of the evidence is for the trier of fact; a judge who expressly demonstrates an understanding of this rule for one witness may be presumed to apply it to similarly situated witnesses.
BaselineA: Common law, including Cook v. Nethercotte, Thomas v. David, Chandler v. Home, R. v. Briggs, R. v. Thompson, Black v. Besse, and R. v. Carefoot.
CaseB_TestB: Clear-and-unequivocal-language test for abrogating Crown immunity from discovery: section 27 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act lifts immunity only where the Crown is a party, so immunity continues in non-party proceedings absent clear legislative language.
BaselineB: Combination of common law Crown immunity and statute, principally s. 17 of the Interpretation Act and ss. 27 and 34 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act, with s. 7 of the Crown Liability and Proceedings (Provincial Court) Regulations considered.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Validity of an inter vivos Quebec trust benefiting unborn primary beneficiaries
BaselineA: Statute: Civil Code arts. 981a et seq., especially arts. 981a, 981b and 981l, read with arts. 608, 754, 755, 765, 771, 772 and 929; informed by Curran v. Davis on trustee acceptance and ownership.
CaseB_TestB: Jurisdiction to bind non-parties by injunction and enforce compliance through contempt
BaselineB: Combination of common law and statute: the courts’ inherent and equitable jurisdiction, confirmed by s. 36 of British Columbia’s Law and Equity Act and supported by s. 11 of the Criminal Code; prior authorities include Seaward v. Paterson, Bartle & Gibson Co. v. Retail, Wholesale and Department Store Union, Local 580, and International Longshoremen's Association, Local 273 v. Maritime Employers' Association.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fraud by “other fraudulent means”: objectively dishonest conduct causing deprivation or risk, with subjective knowledge of the conduct and risk
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, s. 380(1), as interpreted in R. v. Olan and R. v. Théroux.
CaseB_TestB: Union duty of diligent and competent representation toward current and former bargaining-unit employees
BaselineB: Statute — Quebec Labour Code, s. 47.2, informed by Noël v. Société d’énergie de la Baie James and Centre hospitalier Régina Ltée v. Labour Court.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Appellate intervention in a trial judge’s exercise of discretion under s. 51: intervention is justified only if the judge misdirected himself or the decision is so clearly wrong as to amount to an injustice.
BaselineA: Common law appellate non-interference principles from Harper v. Harper, applied to the statutory discretion under the Family Relations Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 121, s. 51.
CaseB_TestB: Duty to address prejudicial Crown remarks: the trial judge must comment where the remarks are prejudicial to a degree sufficient to require correction so that the defence is fairly put to the jury.
BaselineB: Common law governing jury instructions and trial fairness, combined with the curative proviso in the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid partnership for s. 96: carrying on a business, in common, with a view to profit, assessed pragmatically from all surrounding circumstances
BaselineA: Combination of the common law partnership test from Continental Bank Leasing Corp. v. Canada and Backman v. Canada, applied under s. 96 of the Income Tax Act
CaseB_TestB: Substantive adequacy of a W. (D.) credibility instruction, assessed from the jury charge as a whole
BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. W. (D.), as clarified by R. v. S. (W.D.) and R. v. Avetysan
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 577 right-to-be-present test: a post-arraignment examination of prospective jurors concerning partiality forms part of the trial, must be heard by the accused, and a breach requires a new trial without proof of prejudice.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 577(1), 569(2), 598-600 and 613(1)(b)(iii), read with Nova Scotia Juries Act, S.N.S. 1969, c. 12, s. 4(2).
CaseB_TestB: Strict test for substituting a conviction on appeal from an acquittal: the Crown must show that the accused should have been convicted but for the legal error, and every finding necessary for guilt must have been made explicitly or implicitly, or not be in issue.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 613(4)(b)(ii), as interpreted in Vézeau v. The Queen and R. v. Courville, affirmed in Courville v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Common law test for a lawful search incident to arrest: no separate reasonable and probable grounds are required, but the search must pursue a valid criminal-justice objective and must not be conducted abusively or with disproportionate constraint.
BaselineA: Common law, particularly R. v. Brezack, R. v. Morrison, and R. v. Miller.
CaseB_TestB: Section 7 test for warrantless child apprehension: apprehension must be a last resort based on reasonable and probable grounds of serious harm or risk of serious harm, followed by a fair and prompt post-apprehension hearing.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and The Child and Family Services Act, especially ss. 17, 21(1), 24, 27(1), and 29(1), informed by B. (R.) v. Children’s Aid Society of Metropolitan Toronto and New Brunswick (Minister of Health and Community Services) v. G. (J.).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of evidence that an accused refused a police line-up: the evidence is relevant and admissible where the Crown must explain the absence of a line-up or risk an adverse inference; in other circumstances it should not normally be tendered.
BaselineA: Common law of evidence, informed by R. v. Brager and R. v. John.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional limit on provincial commissions of inquiry: an inquiry is ultra vires where, in pith and substance, its overall purpose and effect make it a substitute police investigation or preliminary inquiry into specific criminal offences allegedly committed by named individuals.
BaselineB: Combination of the Constitution Act, 1867, especially ss. 91(27) and 92(14), the Public Inquiries Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 411, s. 2, and the commission-of-inquiry jurisprudence in Faber, Di Iorio, Keable and O'Hara; applied with reference to Criminal Code ss. 121, 535 and 548.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Criminal causation requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused’s unlawful act was at least a contributing cause of death outside the de minimis range.
BaselineA: Combination of Criminal Code, s. 205(1), and common law causation principles reflected in R. v. Larkin, R. v. Cato, R. v. Garforth, R. v. Blaue, and R. v. Nicholson.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage Anns test for recognizing a novel duty of care for pure economic loss arising from commercial negotiations.
BaselineB: Common law Anns duty-of-care framework, adopted in Kamloops (City of) v. Nielsen and applied to pure economic loss in cases including Canadian National Railway Co. v. Norsk Pacific Steamship Co. and Hercules Managements Ltd. v. Ernst & Young.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Duration of protection under an unqualified extradition specialty undertaking: read the undertaking in context and in light of its object, purpose, and international-law principles; absent clear terms, immunity ends once the extraditee has a reasonable opportunity to return and remains voluntarily.
BaselineA: Combination of the extradition arrangement, the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, ss. 2, 3, 33 and 40, and international-law principles governing treaty interpretation.
CaseB_TestB: Intertwined-issues rule: an alleged error of law and the Criminal Code curative proviso are always intertwined, so the Crown need not obtain separate leave to argue the proviso when it has invoked it.
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(b)(iii), and the common-law appellate principle stated in R. v. Keegstra.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Municipal licensing discretion test: a council must act judicially and within its statutory licensing powers; absent express prohibitory authority, it cannot refuse a licence on extraneous moral grounds to prohibit an otherwise lawful type of business, and “particular case” means circumstances peculiar to the applicant rather than the type of business.
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Municipal Act, R.S.B.C. 1960, c. 255, especially s. 455, interpreted in the context of ss. 458, 458M, 458N, 870 and 871; the rule against using regulatory authority to prohibit a lawful trade absent express authority from Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo.
CaseB_TestB: Constitutional fair-process test for the IRPA security-certificate scheme: the named person must receive an incompressible minimum of disclosure sufficient to give meaningful instructions and guidance, while the designated judge uses broad gatekeeping discretion to ensure the overall process remains fair.
BaselineB: Constitution and statute: s. 7 and s. 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms; Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, especially ss. 77(2), 78, 83(1)(a), (c), (e), (h) and (i), 85.1, 85.2 and 85.4; and the fair-process principles established in Charkaoui v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 SCC 9.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Framework for admitting evidence of other charged or uncharged offences at sentencing
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, Part XXIII, especially ss. 718 to 718.2, 724(3)(e), and 725, informed by Lees v. The Queen and R. v. Gardiner.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in an alias-based online police sting
BaselineB: Constitutional and common law: Charter s. 8 and the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework from R. v. Marakah, R. v. Cole, R. v. Spencer, R. v. Tessling, R. v. Edwards, and Hunter v. Southam Inc., together with Criminal Code ss. 183 and 184.2.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Estoppel by representation: words or conduct must induce detrimental reliance, and silence or inaction constitutes a representation only where there is a legal duty to disclose
BaselineA: Common law estoppel by representation, including Greenwood v. Martins Bank, Ltd. and Nippon Menkwa Kabushiki Kaisha v. Dawson’s Bank, Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Rebuttal of the living-on-the-avails presumption: the jury must consider all relevant evidence, without isolating a particular and severable item as evidence to the contrary
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 212(3)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fingerprint inference of possession: whether an accused's fingerprint on an article supports an inference of possession depends on all the circumstances of the case and all the evidence adduced, with guilt ultimately required beyond a reasonable doubt.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: possession under Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 4(3), incorporated by Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-27, ss. 46 and 48(2), together with the fingerprint-inference principles discussed in R. v. O'Keefe and R. v. Mehrabnia.
CaseB_TestB: Review Board treatment-condition jurisdiction: a Board may bind hospital authorities through conditions regarding or supervising an NCR accused's treatment, including requiring reconsideration and exploration of alternatives, but may not prescribe or impose treatment.
BaselineB: Statute: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, Part XX.1, principally ss. 672.54 and 672.55(1), read with ss. 672.1, 672.38 to 672.42, 672.58 to 672.62, and 672.72 to 672.78.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Three-stage s. 96 test for whether adjudicative jurisdiction may be conferred on a provincially appointed tribunal
BaselineA: Combination of Constitution Act, 1867, s. 96 and the common law three-stage framework established in Re Residential Tenancies Act, 1979, [1981] 1 S.C.R. 714
CaseB_TestB: Flexible three-factor test for granting public interest standing
BaselineB: Common law framework established in Canada (Attorney General) v. Downtown Eastside Sex Workers United Against Violence Society, 2012 SCC 45
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Admissibility of a former juvenile delinquency finding as a prior conviction under s. 12(1) of the Canada Evidence Act
BaselineA: Statute: Canada Evidence Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-10, s. 12(1), interpreted with the Juvenile Delinquents Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. J-3, ss. 2(1), 3 and 20(1), and Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, s. 593. A delinquency consisting of a Criminal Code violation is an "offence", and an adjudication of delinquency is equivalent to a "conviction" for s. 12(1); the witness's admission proves it without an official record absent exceptional circumstances clearly showing error.
CaseB_TestB: Amendment of an indictment where the evidence proves a different particular of the charged narcotic
BaselineB: Statute: Narcotic Control Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. N-1, ss. 2 and 4 and Schedule item 3, together with Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 529(4)-(5) and 613(1)(b)(i) and (3). Building on Elliott v. The Queen and Lake v. The Queen, the Court held that the particular narcotic is not a distinct offence and that an amendment may be made unless it causes irreparable prejudice; curable prejudice may be addressed by adjournment, while irreparable prejudice precludes amendment and requires acquittal.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional assessment of non-pecuniary damages, subject to a rough $100,000 upper limit exceeded only in rare circumstances or adjusted for proven or agreed inflation
BaselineA: Common law — Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Arnold v. Teno, and Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57 (Prince George), as refined in Lewis v. Todd
CaseB_TestB: Inadequately insured motorist coverage requires use of the vehicle as a motor vehicle and an unbroken chain of causation linking the tortfeasor's conduct as a motorist to the injuries; merely incidental, fortuitous, or but-for involvement is insufficient
BaselineB: Combination of insurance contract and statute — s. 3 of Ontario Policy Change Form 44R and s. 239(1)(a) of the Insurance Act, interpreted against the causation framework in Amos v. Insurance Corp. of British Columbia
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hypothetical primary infringement test under s. 27(2)(e): the foreign maker must have infringed copyright had it made the work in Canada, and an owner-licensor cannot infringe its own copyright at the suit of an exclusive licensee.
BaselineA: Statute: Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, principally ss. 27(1), 27(2)(e), 2.7, 13(4)-(7), and 36(1)-(2).
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(h) test for whether a retrospective change to sentence conditions constitutes additional punishment, focusing on the extent to which it thwarts the offender's settled expectation of liberty and increases the risk of additional incarceration.
BaselineB: Constitutional text and jurisprudence: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(h), building on R. v. Wigglesworth, R. v. Rodgers, and Cunningham v. Canada.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Contractual-characterization test for a voluntary association’s by-laws: where an organization’s by-laws govern only its consensual, private relationship with members, the by-laws—and natural-justice obligations incorporated into that relationship—are contractual, so their breach gives rise to a contractual action.
BaselineA: A combination of Quebec civil law and corporate legislation, principally Civil Code arts. 361, 1024, 1057, 2242 and 2261(2), Part III and s. 214 of the Companies Act, and the contractual theory of voluntary-association by-laws reflected in cases including Union St-Joseph de Montréal v. Lapierre and Vancouver Real Estate Board v. Moscrop Realty Ltd.
CaseB_TestB: Priority-of-registration test for a mechanics’ lien and mortgage where the Mechanics’ Lien Act prescribes no priority: the competing interests are governed by registration priority under the Registry Act, subject to actual notice.
BaselineB: Statute, principally The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, ss. 14(1), 16, 20, 21 and 22, together with The Registry Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 409, ss. 69(1) and 70.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Essence-of-the-crime test for determining whether a charge falls within an extradition arrangement
BaselineA: Statute and extradition arrangement: s. 2 of the Extradition Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. E-21, and s. 17 of the 1925 Supplementary Convention covering crimes against laws suppressing narcotics trafficking.
CaseB_TestB: Purpose-based test distinguishing use of prior testimony to impeach credibility from use to incriminate
BaselineB: Constitution and statute: s. 13 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and s. 5(2) of the Canada Evidence Act, informed by R. v. Dubois and R. v. Mannion.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Unified three-step bona fide occupational requirement (Meiorin) test
BaselineA: Statute and common law: Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, ss. 13(1) and 13(4), building on the BFOR and accommodation jurisprudence in Etobicoke, O’Malley, Central Alberta Dairy Pool, and related cases.
CaseB_TestB: Two-stage pursuit-of-profit test for a business or property source of income
BaselineB: Statute and common law: Income Tax Act, ss. 3(a) and 9(1)-(2), interpreted against the reasonable-expectation-of-profit approach from Moldowan v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory wage-lien priority test: the lien attaches from the date wages are earned, does not affect pre-existing mortgages, and attaches only to the employer’s equity in encumbered property
BaselineA: Statute — Payment of Wages Act, 1962 (B.C.), ss. 5 and 5A(1)-(2)
CaseB_TestB: Suppletive-law framework for forced dissolution: consider applicable special statutes first; where they provide no applicable dissolution scheme, apply the Civil Code of Québec to fill the gap
BaselineB: Statutes — Civil Code of Québec, arts. 300, 334 and 355 to 364; Companies Act, R.S.Q., c. C-38; and Code of Civil Procedure, art. 829
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Federal criminal law power test: a prohibition backed by a penalty, directed at a legitimate criminal public purpose, and not colourable
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, s. 91(27), combined with the common law framework from Reference re Validity of Section 5(a) of the Dairy Industry Act (Margarine Reference) and Scowby v. Glendinning
CaseB_TestB: Individualized accommodation test for collectively bargained termination clauses: the negotiated absence period is significant but not determinative, and undue hardship is assessed globally
BaselineB: Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20, combined with the accommodation framework from British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU (Meiorin), Commission scolaire régionale de Chambly v. Bergevin, and Central Okanagan School District No. 23 v. Renaud
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Statutory-trust priority test: tax funds fall under Bankruptcy Act s. 47(a) if they remain identifiable or traceable under general trust law; otherwise the province has only a Crown claim governed by s. 107(1)(j).
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. B-3, ss. 47(a) and 107(1)(j); Social Service Tax Act, R.S.B.C. 1979, c. 388, s. 18; general trust-law principles; Deputy Minister of Revenue v. Rainville and Deloitte Haskins and Sells Ltd. v. Workers' Compensation Board.
CaseB_TestB: Section 23 minority-language facility and management-control test: the appropriate local area and services are determined contextually under the numbers-warrant sliding scale, with the minority-language board controlling location subject to objective, Charter-compliant provincial norms and the Minister limited to verifying compliance rather than substituting his own decision.
BaselineB: Combination of constitutional text, statute, regulation, and precedent: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 23; Prince Edward Island School Act, particularly ss. 112 and 128(2); School Act Regulations, particularly ss. 6.01(f), 6.07, 6.08 and 6.11; and the sliding-scale and management-control framework established in Mahe v. Alberta.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory caution concerning conviction on the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice or an accessory after the fact
BaselineA: Common law— the rule of practice concerning accomplice evidence stated in Davies v. Director of Public Prosecutions and accepted in Horsburgh v. The Queen, with R. v. Riezebos followed.
CaseB_TestB: Section 212(c) unlawful-object murder framework: an indictable mens rea object, actual knowledge of the dangerous circumstances, and objective foresight of likely death
BaselineB: Statute—Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34, ss. 205(5)(a) and 212(c), interpreted in light of the pre-codification common law and the English Draft Code of 1878.

CaseA_TestA: Common-unlawful-purpose manslaughter under Criminal Code s. 21(2) where the principal commits murder
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, s. 21(2), informed by R. v. Trinneer, R. v. Kirkness, R. v. Creighton, and R. v. Logan.
CaseB_TestB: Entitlement to a rebate and reassessment set-off for GST paid in error
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Compensatory interest for an improperly withheld just debt, measured by the creditor’s actual borrowing rates where that withholding forced the creditor to finance the debtor’s obligation
BaselineA: Combination of statute and prior jurisprudence: s. 46 of The Queen’s Bench Act, R.S.S. 1965, c. 73, as interpreted in Toronto Railway Co. v. City of Toronto and followed in The Custodian v. Blucher; ss. 3, 12 and 13 of the Interest Act and s. 52 of the Supreme Court Act were also addressed.

BaselineB: Sections 7 and 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, together with the disclosure and remedial principles established in R. v. Stinchcombe, R. v. C. (M.H.), R. v. Carosella and related jurisprudence.

CaseA_TestA: Arbitrator’s authority to substitute a lesser penalty where dismissal is unsustainable and the collective agreement specifies no penalty for the infraction

BaselineB: Statute and treaty: Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27, s. 98, incorporating Refugee Convention art. 1F(a), informed by international criminal law, including Rome Statute arts. 25, 30 and 31(1)(d).

CaseA_TestA: Recent possession inference and jury-instruction test: proof that the accused possessed recently stolen goods raises a prima facie case permitting, but not requiring, conviction; any explanation that may reasonably be true requires acquittal if it raises a reasonable doubt.

CaseA_TestA: Constructive trust for unjust enrichment: enrichment, corresponding deprivation, absence of juristic reason, and a sufficient causal connection to the disputed property, with the interest proportionate to the claimant’s contribution.
BaselineA: Common law and equity, particularly the unjust-enrichment requirements stated in Rathwell v. Rathwell and the constructive-trust approach introduced in Murdoch v. Murdoch.
CaseB_TestB: Solicitor-client confidentiality and lawyer-office search framework: protected communications are broadly defined, privileged material cannot be seized, and any authorized search requires no reasonable alternative and confidentiality-protective execution terms.

CaseA_TestA: Structured assessment of catastrophic personal-injury damages, including future-care and income calculations and the functional approach with an upper limit for non-pecuniary damages
BaselineA: Common law, particularly Andrews v. Grand & Toy Ltd., Thornton v. Board of School Trustees, and The Queen v. Jennings
CaseB_TestB: Fire-damage election under a land-sale agreement: complete and take the available insurance proceeds or cancel; imposing different conditions constitutes repudiation
BaselineB: Clause 5 of the agreement of purchase and sale, interpreted against the common law governing risk, insurance proceeds, and contractual repudiation
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Wigmore four-criteria test for case-by-case privilege over journalist-source communications
BaselineA: Common law — Wigmore’s four criteria, previously discussed by the SCC in Slavutych v. Baker, [1976] 1 S.C.R. 254.
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness review of Crown corporations’ selection of effective tax rates for payments in lieu of taxes
BaselineB: Statute and regulation — the Payments in Lieu of Taxes Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. M-13, particularly ss. 2, 2.1 and 4(1), and the Crown Corporation Payments Regulations, SOR/81-1030, particularly ss. 2 and 7(1), applied through the reasonableness framework from Dunsmuir and Khosa.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reviewability of a consensual arbitrator’s award for error of law: an award is reviewable unless the parties specifically submitted a question of law for a binding, unreviewable determination, assessed from the submission and contractual limits on the arbitrator’s authority.
BaselineA: Common law — the distinction established in F.R. Absalom Ltd. v. Great Western (London) Garden Village Society Ltd. and applied in Faubert and Watts v. Temagami Mining Co. Ltd. and Bell Canada v. Office and Professional Employees’ International Union, Local 131.
CaseB_TestB: Section 11(b) unreasonable-delay test: assess the length of delay less defence waiver, then balance the reasons for delay, prejudice to the accused, and the interests protected by s. 11(b); prejudice may be inferred from lengthy delay.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law — Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(b), as interpreted through the framework and delay guidelines established in R. v. Morin and the Crown-responsibility principle from R. v. Askov.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Patentability of a new use for an old compound as a new and useful art where the new knowledge has practical application and commercial value, without requiring novelty in its implementation.
BaselineA: Statute — Patent Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. P-4, ss. 2 and 36, with s. 41 distinguished.

Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Detention under s. 2(c) of the Canadian Bill of Rights requires compulsory restraint associated with actual physical restraint or custody; compliance with a roadside breath-demand procedure does not itself constitute detention.

CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter test: after a somewhat probing examination, a reviewing court may intervene only if no line of analysis in the reasons, considered as a whole, could reasonably support the decision; the standard does not float with the circumstances.
BaselineB: Common law: the reasonableness simpliciter standard from Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., applied within the pragmatic and functional framework established in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and refined in Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration).

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act
BaselineA: Statute — Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, ss. 137.1(2)-(4), with related procedure under s. 137.2.
CaseB_TestB: Purposive and contextual corporate attribution test, including for one-person corporations
BaselineB: Common law — the corporate attribution doctrine established in Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen and refined in Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of), Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd., and Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co.; applied in the context of the Limitations Act, 2002 and the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act.

CaseA_TestA: Additional-recovery test after workers’ compensation: reduce the third-party claim for the victim’s contributory fault, then permit an additional recovery only if the statutory compensation is less than that adjusted claim.

CaseA_TestA: Limited-hunting right-of-access test under paragraph 12 of the Saskatchewan Natural Resources Agreement
BaselineA: Constitutional statute and precedent: paragraph 12 of the 1930 Saskatchewan Natural Resources Agreement, constitutionally confirmed by the British North America Act, 1930, as previously interpreted in R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson. If the governing laws permit any hunting on the land, a right of access exists and Indigenous persons may hunt any game for food at all seasons, provided the hunting is non-dangerous.

BaselineB: Constitutional text and precedent: ss. 1 and 2(a) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982, informed by Hunter v. CaseA_TestA: Functional and structural test for whether a court or tribunal has power to grant a Charter remedy

BaselineB: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 172.1(1), (3) and (4), informed by the prior interpretation in R. v. Levigne and common-law principles governing air of reality, burdens of proof and subjective mens rea

CaseA_TestA: Section 15(1) two-step test for adverse-impact discrimination

Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: “Financing” a labour dispute requires active and voluntary involvement by the claimant and a meaningful connection between the payment and the dispute.

CaseA_TestA: Royalties and licence fees paid as a “condition of the sale” test: the vendor must be entitled to refuse the sale or repudiate it upon non-payment

BaselineB: Combination of statutes, common law, and contract: Income Tax Act, s. 224(1); Bills of Exchange Act provisions governing holders, collecting banks, and presentment, particularly ss. 84, 86, 126, 138, and 165(3); and common law banking principles concerning debtor-creditor relationships and cheque collection.

CaseA_TestA: Detention under s. 2(c) of the Canadian Bill of Rights requires compulsory restraint, in the nature of actual physical custody.
