CaseB_TestB: Two-branch test for civil conspiracy: predominant purpose to injure, or unlawful conduct directed toward the plaintiff with actual or constructive intent to cause resulting damage.
BaselineB: Common law, principally Quinn v. Leathem, Crofter Hand Woven Harris Tweed Co. v. Veitch, Gagnon v. Foundation Maritime Ltd., and Lonrho Ltd. v. Shell Petroleum Co. Ltd.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 13 test barring the incriminating use of an accused’s prior testimony in a retrial
BaselineA: Constitutional text: s. 13 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, interpreted with ss. 11(c) and 11(d) and contrasted with s. 5 of the Canada Evidence Act and the pre-Charter rule in R. v. Brown (No. 2).
CaseB_TestB: K.G.B. test for substantive admissibility of a witness’s prior inconsistent statement
BaselineB: Common law: the principled hearsay framework from R. v. Khan and R. v. Smith, replacing the orthodox rule adopted in Deacon v. The King, and operating through the voir dire procedure under s. 9 of the Canada Evidence Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Article 68 personal-action jurisdiction test: jurisdiction lies at the defendant's domicile or, failing that, residence, determined from the evidence as a whole
BaselineA: Statute: Quebec Code of Civil Procedure, art. 68, supplemented by the residence presumption drawn from s. 10 of the Canadian Citizenship Act
CaseB_TestB: State-misconduct sentence-reduction framework: related misconduct may mitigate sentence, subject generally to statutory sentencing limits
BaselineB: Statute and Constitution: Criminal Code, ss. 718 to 718.2 and applicable statutory sentencing restrictions, together with s. 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Copyright reproduction test: a literal mechanical transfer of an existing image without creating an additional or new copy is not reproduction under s. 3(1).
BaselineA: Statute — Copyright Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-42, principally s. 3(1), read with ss. 2, 27, 28.2 and 38(1).
CaseB_TestB: Reasonableness simpliciter test: a decision is unreasonable only if no tenable line of analysis in the reasons could reasonably lead from the evidence to the conclusion, considering the reasons as a whole.
BaselineB: Common law — Canada (Director of Investigation and Research) v. Southam Inc., within the pragmatic and functional approach established in U.E.S., Local 298 v. Bibeault and developed in Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Ontario anti-SLAPP dismissal framework under s. 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act
BaselineA: Statute — Courts of Justice Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43, ss. 137.1 to 137.2, especially ss. 137.1(3) and 137.1(4).
CaseB_TestB: Purposive, contextual, and pragmatic corporate attribution test, including for one-person corporations
BaselineB: Common law — Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. The Queen, Deloitte & Touche v. Livent Inc. (Receiver of), Christine DeJong Medicine Professional Corp. v. DBDC Spadina Ltd., and Aquino v. Bondfield Construction Co.; applied in the statutory context of the Limitations Act, 2002, ss. 5 and 12, and the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Additional-compensation test: compare workers’ compensation received with the third-party claim after reducing the loss for the worker’s contributory fault; no additional sum is recoverable if the compensation equals or exceeds that adjusted claim.
BaselineA: Workmen’s Compensation Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 159, ss. 7(3) and 8, combined with Civil Code arts. 1056 and 1157.
CaseB_TestB: Institutional financial-security test: any government measure affecting any aspect of judicial remuneration must pass through an independent, effective and objective body, subject only to exceptional constitutional justification.
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 11(d), the Preamble to the Constitution Act, 1867, and the judicial-independence principles established in Valente v. The Queen and the Provincial Court Judges Reference.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Exclusive statutory obscenity test for publications: publicly displayed wares accompanied by descriptions may constitute publications and are obscene if their dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), together with Brodie v. The Queen on the exclusivity of the statutory test
CaseB_TestB: Union duty to take reasonable measures short of undue hardship to accommodate an employee affected by adverse-effect discrimination
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law — Human Rights Act, S.B.C. 1984, c. 22, principally s. 8, and the accommodation principles from O'Malley and Central Alberta Dairy Pool
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Right-of-access test under paragraph 12: if the laws in force permit any limited hunting on the land, Indigenous persons have a right of access and may hunt non-dangerously for food there “at all seasons of the year,” regardless of provincial limits on season, species, method, or quantity.
BaselineA: Paragraph 12 of the 1930 Saskatchewan Natural Resources Agreement, constitutionally confirmed by 1930 (Sask.), c. 87, 1930 (Can.), c. 41, and the British North America Act, 1930, together with R. v. Sutherland, Wilson and Wilson.
CaseB_TestB: Purpose-and-effects test for Charter constitutionality: legislation is invalid if either its purpose or its effect infringes a Charter right; purpose is examined first, and an invalid purpose is dispositive regardless of effects.
BaselineB: The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, particularly ss. 2(a), 1, and 52(1), informed by Hunter v. Southam Inc., Attorney General of Quebec v. Quebec Association of Protestant School Boards, and Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional and structural test for whether a court or tribunal has power to grant a Charter remedy under s. 24
BaselineA: Combination of Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(1), the tribunal's enabling legislation, and the Mills test as developed in Mills, Weber, and Mooring
CaseB_TestB: Three-step framework for the defence of honest belief in legal age under Criminal Code s. 172.1(4)
BaselineB: Combination of Criminal Code, ss. 172.1(1), (3), and (4), Charter ss. 7 and 11(d), and the framework previously stated in R. v. Levigne
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Sufficient-nexus contextual test for discrimination “regarding employment” under s. 13(1)(b)
BaselineA: Statute: British Columbia Human Rights Code, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 210, principally ss. 1, 3 and 13(1)(b)
CaseB_TestB: Context-specific test for when in-court incivility amounts to professional misconduct
BaselineB: Combination of statute and professional conduct rules: Law Society Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. L.8, and the applicable Professional Conduct Handbook and Rules of Professional Conduct, informed by Charter s. 2(b)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Hague Protocol notice test: a carrier may limit liability only if the prescribed notice is presented in a form calculated to attract the passenger's attention.
BaselineA: Statute: Carriage by Air Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-14, incorporating Hague Protocol arts. 3(1)(c), 3(2), 4(1)(c), and 22.
CaseB_TestB: Post-severance test for rebutting the statutory presumptions of accuracy and identity attaching to breathalyzer results.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and constitutional law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, ss. 258(1)(c), 258(1)(d.01), and 258(1)(d.1), reviewed under ss. 1 and 11(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant-purpose test for exemption from compelled testimony under s. 7
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 7 and 13, building on R. v. S. (R.J.), and applied to Securities Act, S.B.C. 1985, c. 83, s. 128(1)
CaseB_TestB: Two-part s. 15(1) test for discriminatory distinctions and disproportionate adverse effects
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1), building principally on Quebec (Attorney General) v. A
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Conspiracy to unduly prevent or lessen competition: the Crown must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended to enter the agreement and that, if carried into effect, the agreement would unduly prevent or lessen competition in the relevant industry.
BaselineA: Statute: Combines Investigation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-23, s. 32(1)(c), as previously interpreted in Weidman v. Shragge, Stinson-Reeb Builders Supply Co. v. The King, Container Materials Ltd. v. The King, and Howard Smith Paper Mills Ltd. v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Unreasonable-verdict appellate review: determine whether the verdict could reasonably have been rendered by a properly instructed trier of fact; essential findings plainly contradicted by, or incompatible with, unrejected evidence may also render it unreasonable, while credibility findings cannot be disturbed unless unsupported on any reasonable view of the evidence.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and precedent: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 686(1)(a)(i), as interpreted in R. v. Yebes, R. v. Biniaris, R. v. Sinclair, R. v. Beaudry, and R. v. Burke.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Valid consent to intercept a private communication: consent must be knowing, conscious, and voluntary in the sense of being free from external coercion; promised or expected leniency alone does not invalidate it.
BaselineA: Statute — Criminal Code, s. 178.11(2)(a), with admissibility governed by s. 178.16(1)(a).
CaseB_TestB: Proof that hate speech targeted the particularized identifiable group: the court must consider the totality of the evidence and draw appropriate inferences, without requiring proof that the hateful terminology and the group's specified name are interchangeable.
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, ss. 319(2) and 318(4).
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rule prohibiting the joint trial of separate informations or indictments, even with consent, unless legislation expressly provides otherwise
BaselineA: Common law rule established in Crane v. Public Prosecutor and incorporated by implication into the Criminal Code; extended to provincial proceedings absent express statutory authorization
CaseB_TestB: Credibility assessment based on absence of motive to lie and lack of embellishment
BaselineB: Common law credibility principles, including R. v. Stirling, within the burden-of-proof framework of R. v. W.(D.)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: GAAR test for abusive tax avoidance: after a tax benefit and avoidance transaction are established, determine through a unified textual, contextual and purposive analysis whether the benefit would frustrate the object, spirit or purpose of the provisions relied upon
BaselineA: Statute — Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 245(1)-(4), applied with ss. 18(13), 96(1) and 248(10)
CaseB_TestB: Vancouver Sun two-stage procedure for protecting informer privilege while minimizing impairment of the open court principle, including the parallel-proceeding approach for fully in camera matters
BaselineB: Common law — the informer-privilege and open-court procedure established in Named Person v. Vancouver Sun, 2007 SCC 43
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Constitutional limit on provincial inquiries: a province may investigate alleged crimes by federal police officers but may not, directly or indirectly, investigate the administration or management of the federal police institution itself.
BaselineA: Constitution Act, 1867, ss. 91 and 92(14), the Quebec Public Inquiry Commission Act, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act, and the Department of the Solicitor General Act, informed by Di Iorio v. Warden of the Montreal Jail, Faber v. The Queen, and the doctrine of colourability.
CaseB_TestB: Paramount-welfare-of-the-child test for contested custody: consider all relevant factors affecting the child's psychological, spiritual, emotional, physical, and developmental welfare, with parental claims subordinate where the child's welfare requires.
BaselineB: Combination of the Domestic Relations Ordinance, ss. 28(1), 35(2), 37 and 39, and the equitable parens patriae jurisdiction reflected in Re Moores and Feldstein, Beson v. Director of Child Welfare, and Racine v. Woods.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Defence of necessity as an excuse: moral involuntariness arising from imminent peril, no reasonable legal alternative, and proportionality
BaselineA: Common law necessity defence, as discussed in Morgentaler v. The Queen, preserved by s. 7(3) of the Criminal Code
CaseB_TestB: Reasonable expectation of privacy in police-created online child-sting communications
BaselineB: Section 8 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy framework from Marakah, Cole, Spencer, Edwards, Patrick and Tessling
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Predominant-purpose test for exemption from compelled testimony
BaselineA: Constitutional common law under ss. 7 and 13 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, building on R. v. S. (R.J.), as applied to s. 128(1) of the British Columbia Securities Act
CaseB_TestB: Timing and procedure for deciding a Corbett application
BaselineB: Section 12 of the Canada Evidence Act as interpreted in R. v. Corbett, supplemented by the common-law case-to-meet principle protected by s. 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mandatory payment by the Highway Victims Indemnity Fund without prior exhaustion of remedies against the judgment debtor or insurer
BaselineA: Statute: Highway Victims Indemnity Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 232, ss. 36-39, particularly the qualifying requirements in ss. 36-37, the Fund's seven-day payment obligation in s. 38, and the transfer of the creditor's rights under s. 39.
CaseB_TestB: Present-value method for calculating Fatal Accidents Act dependency damages, including income tax, discounting, and contingency adjustments
BaselineB: Statute and common law: The Fatal Accidents Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 164, supplemented by the damages methodology discussed in Andrews v. Grand & Toy Alberta Ltd., Thornton v. Board of School Trustees of School District No. 57, and Arnold v. Teno.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Discretion under s. 52 to depart from the default accrual of judgment interest where the circumstances make intervention appropriate
BaselineA: Statute: Supreme Court Act, s. 52, and Interest Act, ss. 13-14
CaseB_TestB: Procedural-fairness test for Governor in Council review under s. 64(1): construe the statutory scheme as a whole; no hearing or reasons are required for this quasi-legislative function, provided the Governor in Council remains within the parliamentary grant
BaselineB: Statute and common law: National Transportation Act, s. 64(1), interpreted against the procedural-fairness principles in Nicholson and Martineau (No. 2)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Mechanics’ lien “owner” and requesting-owner lien entitlement test
BaselineA: Statute: The Mechanics’ Lien Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 267, especially ss. 1(1)(d), 5(1), 7 and 11.
CaseB_TestB: Realistic potential for juror partiality test for challenges for cause
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 638(1)(b), as interpreted in R. v. Sherratt and R. v. Williams.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Publication and exclusive statutory obscenity test: an item is a “publication” under Criminal Code s. 159(8) when its character is made publicly known, including through public display accompanied by printed descriptions; publications are judged exclusively by whether their dominant characteristic is the undue exploitation of sex or of sex combined with crime, horror, cruelty, or violence.
BaselineA: Statute: Criminal Code, ss. 159(1)(a) and 159(8), as previously construed in Brodie v. The Queen.
CaseB_TestB: Individualized accommodation assessment for an automatic termination clause: the negotiated absence period is a significant but non-determinative factor, and undue hardship must be assessed globally from the beginning of the absence in light of the employee’s particular circumstances.
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Quebec Charter of human rights and freedoms, ss. 10 and 20, and the duty-to-accommodate framework from British Columbia (Public Service Employee Relations Commission) v. BCGSEU (Meiorin), applied alongside the collective agreement.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Good-faith-basis test: an otherwise permissible cross-examination question concerning an unproven matter should be allowed if counsel has a good faith basis for asking it.
BaselineA: Common law of cross-examination, particularly R. v. Bencardino and R. v. Shearing, informed by ss. 7 and 11(d) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
CaseB_TestB: Federal paramountcy conflict test: after legislative validity is established, provincial law is inoperative only where dual compliance is impossible or the law frustrates a clearly proven federal purpose, with paramountcy construed narrowly.
BaselineB: Constitutional doctrine of federal paramountcy, including Canadian Western Bank, COPA, Rothmans and Ryan Estate, applied to Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act ss. 243, 244 and 72(1) and Saskatchewan Farm Security Act ss. 9 to 22.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Fair comment requires proof that the impugned opinion was honestly held, with each publisher standing "in exactly the same position as the original writer."
BaselineA: Common law fair-comment doctrine, including Jones v. Skelton, Turner v. Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Pictures Ltd., Slim v. Daily Telegraph Ltd., and Truth (N.Z.) Ltd. v. Holloway.
CaseB_TestB: Contempt requires personal service or actual personal knowledge of the court order, proved beyond a reasonable doubt; knowledge is not automatically imputed from counsel or officials.
BaselineB: Common law contempt doctrine from Kimpton v. Eve, Ex parte Langley, and Baxter Travenol Laboratories of Canada Ltd. v. Cutter (Canada), Ltd., considered alongside Federal Court Rules 308, 311, and 355.
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Reasonable and probable grounds for warrantless arrest require consideration of all available information, including exculpatory information; information may be disregarded only for good reason as unreliable.
BaselineA: Combination of Civil Code arts. 1053-1054 and Criminal Code, 1953-54 (Can.), c. 51, s. 435, which authorized warrantless arrest where a peace officer had reasonable and probable grounds to believe the person committed an indictable offence.
CaseB_TestB: Effective dismissal of a probationary constable must be exercised by the Board holding the exclusive, non-delegable dismissal power; action by the police chief and uncommunicated later confirmation by the Board are ineffective.
BaselineB: Combination of s. 9 of the collective agreement, s. 27(b) of Regulation 680, and s. 29 of The Police Act, R.S.O. 1970, c. 351; the first two vested dismissal authority in the Board.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Non-assessability of fully paid shares: an amendment imposing “any financial burden whatsoever” on a shareholder in respect of fully paid shares is invalid
BaselineA: Combination of The Companies Act, R.S.A. 1970, c. 60, ss. 2(1)(10), 15, 16(c), 42(1), 68(4), and 193(1)(d), the memorandum of association, and the common-law limited-liability principle reflected in Ooregum Gold Mining Co. v. Roper, Bisgood v. Henderson’s Transvaal Estates, and Shalfoon v. Cheddar Valley Co-operative Dairy Co.
CaseB_TestB: Van der Peet test for an Aboriginal right to exchange fish: precisely characterize the claimed activity, then determine whether it was, before European contact, an integral—central, significant, or defining—part of the claimant group’s distinctive culture
BaselineB: Combination of s. 35(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982 and the common-law Aboriginal-rights test established in R. v. Van der Peet
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Crown-binding test: under s. 16, the Crown is bound only where it is mentioned or referred to; at common law, necessary implication arises only if excluding the Crown would wholly frustrate the enactment’s purpose.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Interpretation Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. I-23, ss. 16 and 28, and the necessary-implication rule from Bombay Province v. Bombay Municipal Corporation.
CaseB_TestB: Subsisting-contract breach and damages test under Civil Code art. 1065, as distinguished from nullity for error under art. 992.
BaselineB: Statute and contract: Civil Code of Lower Canada, arts. 992 and 1065, applied to the contract’s stipulated cargo-weight undertaking.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Functional test for federal labour-relations jurisdiction: provincial jurisdiction is the rule, and federal jurisdiction arises only where labour relations are integral to primary federal jurisdiction, assessed through the nature of the undertaking's operations and normal activities.
BaselineA: Common-law constitutional doctrine developed in Toronto Electric Commissioners v. Snider and the Stevedoring Reference, under the division of powers, together with ss. 2 and 108(1) of the Canada Labour Code.
CaseB_TestB: Two-part substantive equality test under Charter s. 15(1): whether the law creates a distinction based on an enumerated or analogous ground, and whether that distinction perpetuates disadvantage or prejudice or imposes stereotyping.
BaselineB: Section 15(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and the equality jurisprudence established in Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia and refined in Law v. Canada and R. v. Kapp.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Proof of breach of the municipality’s contractual sewer-servicing obligation requires evidence of an existing or foreseeable inadequacy in the project’s sewer service; a general report or ordinance is insufficient without evidence connecting it to that serviceability.
BaselineA: Contract: s. 31(a)(iii) of the August 31, 1966 development agreement; Ordinance No. 153 supplied only the agreed measure of damages if breach were proved.
CaseB_TestB: A substantive statutory change does not apply to pre-enactment circumstances unless the statute provides for retrospective application expressly or by necessary implication.
BaselineB: Combination of common law and statute: the common law presumption against retrospectivity recognized in Phillips v. Eyre and Wilson v. Dagnall, applied to s. 1(3)(d) of The Family Law Reform Act, 1975.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Four-factor test for whether an administrative decision must be made on a judicial or quasi-judicial basis
BaselineA: Combination of Federal Court Act, s. 28, and the common law of natural justice, including Cooper v. Wandsworth Board of Works
CaseB_TestB: Conscriptive-evidence and discoverability test for trial fairness under Charter s. 24(2)
BaselineB: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 24(2), as previously structured by R. v. Collins and subsequent jurisprudence
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Rebuttable presumption of mens rea for trafficking in a restricted drug: once trafficking is proved, guilt is presumed unless evidence raises a reasonable doubt based on an honest belief negating mens rea.
BaselineA: Combination of statute and common law: Food and Drugs Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. F-27, ss. 40 and 42, together with Beaver v. The Queen, R. v. King, and R. v. Blondin.
CaseB_TestB: Permissible judicial intervention and apparent impartiality test: a judge may and sometimes must intervene, but must remain within contextual limits and act so that justice is seen to be done.
BaselineB: Common law, principally R. v. Sussex Justices; Ex parte McCarthy and R. v. Darlyn, supplemented by Jones v. National Coal Board, R. v. Torbiak and Campbell, Yuill v. Yuill, and R. v. Bateman.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 2(b) protection and infringement test for consumer counter-advertising through signs
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 2(b), informed by Irwin Toy, Ford, Rocket, and Ramsden
CaseB_TestB: Canadian Bill of Rights due process test for legislative deprivation of property
BaselineB: Canadian Bill of Rights, ss. 1(a) and 2(e), applied to Department of Veterans Affairs Act, s. 5.1(4)
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 373 test for equalizing school-tax valuation rolls based on the real value of property taxable in each municipality
BaselineA: Statute — Education Act, R.S.Q. 1964, c. 235, s. 373, together with the municipal machinery-exclusion authority under the Cities and Towns Act, s. 488
CaseB_TestB: Actus reus and mens rea test for an agent's corrupt acceptance of a secret commission
BaselineB: Statute — Criminal Code, R.S.C., 1985, c. C-46, s. 426(1)(a)(ii), formerly s. 383(1)(a)
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Trustee’s duty to preserve or replace insurance on all insurable bankrupt property, including hypothecated property, and to notify the secured creditor if insurance cannot be obtained
BaselineA: Bankruptcy Act, R.S.C. 1952, c. 14, ss. 2(o), 2(r), 9(1), 9(2), and 171, read with the insurance clause in the hypothec deed
CaseB_TestB: Charitable-status test under the fourth Pemsel head: public benefit in a way recognized by law as charitable, assessed by analogy to precedent, the Income Tax Act scheme, and whether the proposed development is incremental
BaselineB: Combination of Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), ss. 149.1(1) and 248(1), and the common law tests from Commissioners for Special Purposes of the Income Tax v. Pemsel, D’Aguiar v. Guyana Commissioner of Inland Revenue, and Vancouver Society of Immigrant and Visible Minority Women v. M.N.R.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Concurrent liability in tort and contract: a contractual relationship may create a tort duty through sufficient proximity, provided the asserted duty does not depend on specific express contractual obligations and does not circumvent a contractual exclusion or limitation of liability.
BaselineA: Common law principles from Anns v. Merton London Borough Council, Hedley Byrne & Co. v. Heller & Partners Ltd., Donoghue v. Stevenson, and J. Nunes Diamonds Ltd. v. Dominion Electric Protection Co.
CaseB_TestB: Priority of an exclusive foreign choice-of-forum clause: where a valid clause clearly applies and ousts Quebec jurisdiction, art. 3148, para. 2 C.C.Q. prevails over incidental-demand jurisdiction under art. 3139, and the Quebec court must decline jurisdiction, subject to recognized exceptions.
BaselineB: Statute—Civil Code of Québec, principally arts. 3148, para. 2, 3139 and 3135, interpreted in light of arts. 3149 and 3151 and related international instruments.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Election of delictual liability despite a contract: the contractual fault must independently constitute a fault under art. 1053 C.C. even in the absence of the contract.
BaselineA: Civil Code, art. 1053, as previously applied in Ross v. Dunstall; Ross v. Emery and Alliance Assurance Co. v. Dominion Electric Protection Co.
CaseB_TestB: Consequences of reasonable apprehension of bias: once established, the trial judge has no further jurisdiction, affected orders are retroactively void, and a new trial is required.
BaselineB: Common law procedural fairness, particularly Newfoundland Telephone Co. v. Newfoundland (Board of Commissioners of Public Utilities).
Score_Desc: Test A is slightly more standard-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 8 threshold for Canadian requests leading to foreign searches: assess the specific Canadian governmental action; a letter merely requesting an independent foreign search does not itself engage s. 8
BaselineA: Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, ss. 8 and 32(1), as interpreted in Hunter v. Southam Inc. and R. v. Terry
CaseB_TestB: Duty of care for failing to prevent a third party’s intentional wrongdoing: sufficient foreseeability and proximity establish a prima facie duty unless compelling residual policy considerations negate or limit it
BaselineB: Common law duty-of-care framework from Cooper v. Hobart, Childs v. Desormeaux, and Hill v. Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police Services Board, supplemented for the government claim by the Mining Safety Act, especially ss. 42-43, and the Mining Safety Regulations
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Foreclosure of civil actions by a comprehensive statutory human rights enforcement scheme
BaselineA: Statute: The Ontario Human Rights Code, R.S.O. 1970, c. 318, particularly ss. 4, 14b-14d and 16, together with common law principles concerning actions for breach of statute. The Court held that the Code's comprehensive remedial regime forecloses both a civil action based directly on its breach and a common law discrimination action based on its public policy.
CaseB_TestB: Undue-obstacle and reasonable-accommodation test for transportation barriers affecting persons with disabilities
BaselineB: Combination of statute and common law: Canada Transportation Act, S.C. 1996, c. 10, ss. 5, 170-172; Canadian Human Rights Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. H-6, ss. 5(a) and 15; and the reasonable-accommodation framework from Meiorin, Grismer and Chambly. A discriminatory transportation barrier must be removed unless the carrier proves that accommodation would impose undue hardship, assessed contextually through such factors as cost, economic viability, safety and service quality.
Score_Desc: Test A is substantially more rule-like than Test B.

CaseA_TestA: Section 4 test for deviating from presumptive Table child support amounts where the paying parent earns over $150,000
BaselineA: Regulation: Federal Child Support Guidelines, SOR/97-175, principally s. 4, read with ss. 1, 3, 7 and 21 and Divorce Act, s. 26.1(2).
CaseB_TestB: Part 2 default rule for comprehensive multi-risk insurance policies that do not fit a specific statutory category
BaselineB: Statute and regulation: British Columbia Insurance Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 226, Parts 2 and 5, particularly ss. 3(a) and 119 and statutory condition 14, read with Insurance Classes Regulation, B.C. Reg. 337/90, s. 2.
